African blue tit: The African blue tit has blue upperparts, white underparts, a black eye stripe, and a white cheek. It inhabits woodlands, savannas, and gardens across sub-Saharan Africa. It feeds mainly on insects and seeds, foraging actively in trees and often joining mixed-species flocks. A fun fact is that it sometimes mimics the calls of other bird species to confuse predators.
African desert warbler: The African desert warbler has brown upperparts with pale streaks and a pale throat. It inhabits dry, rocky deserts and semi-desert scrublands across northern Africa. It feeds primarily on insects and small invertebrates, foraging singly in low vegetation with active, jerky movements. Its distinctive high-pitched "tseep" call is often heard in arid habitats.
Algerian nuthatch: The Algerian nuthatch has gray upperparts, a white face, and a dark eye stripe. It inhabits high-elevation Mediterranean forests, primarily in the Tell Atlas mountains of Algeria. It feeds on insects and seeds while climbing tree trunks and foraging in a characteristic manner. This species is one of the rarest birds globally, with a very limited range.
Alpine accentor: The Alpine accentor has brown streaked upperparts and a pale throat. It inhabits rocky mountain meadows and scree slopes across Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects and seeds, foraging actively on the ground. Its loud, varied song carries clearly through alpine valleys.
Alpine chough: Alpine choughs are entirely black birds with distinctive bright orange beaks and legs. They inhabit high mountain regions across Europe, Asia, and Africa, often nesting on cliffs above the snowline. Their diet includes insects, berries, and human food scraps, and they are highly social, noisy birds that forage in large flocks. They are known to approach mountain tourists for food scraps.
Alpine swift: Alpine swifts have dark brown plumage and long, swept-back wings. They inhabit mountainous regions across Europe and Asia, nesting on cliffs. They feed exclusively on flying insects while in continuous flight. They can sleep while flying for extended periods.
American bittern: This bird has brown and buff streaked plumage for camouflage in wetlands. It hunts fish and amphibians by standing motionless in reeds. Its loud booming call resembles a bullfrog, a distinctive trait.
American black duck: The American black duck has dark brown plumage with a distinctive dark head and lighter breast, inhabiting wetlands, marshes, and coastal areas across eastern North America. It feeds primarily on aquatic plants, seeds, and invertebrates, often remaining shy and wary near water. A fun fact is that it frequently hybridizes with mallards, creating mixed populations that complicate conservation efforts.
American golden plover: The American golden plover has a golden-brown back and white underparts in breeding plumage, with a black face mask. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters in grasslands across South America. Its diet consists mainly of insects, worms, and other invertebrates, and it forages in flocks while migrating long distances. It is known to make nonstop transatlantic flights during migration.
American robin: The American robin has a gray back, orange-red breast, and yellow beak. It inhabits gardens, woodlands, and lawns across North America. It eats earthworms, insects, and berries, often foraging on lawns and singing loudly at dawn. A fun fact is that robins are among the first birds to sing at daybreak, signaling the start of a new day.
American wigeon: Male American wigeons have a green head, white forehead, and a brown body with a white patch on the face. They inhabit freshwater wetlands, ponds, and lakes across North America. They primarily eat aquatic plants and grasses, often foraging by dabbling or stealing food from other ducks. They are highly social birds forming large flocks during migration. Fun fact: American wigeons are known for their habit of "stealing" vegetation from other dabbling ducks.
Aquatic warbler: The Aquatic warbler has a brown back, yellow underparts with dark streaks, and a pale eyebrow. It breeds in wet grasslands and marshes across northern Europe. It feeds on insects and spiders gleaned from the ground and is secretive, often flitting through dense vegetation. A fun fact is that it is Europe's rarest warbler and its song resembles a rapid series of high-pitched chips.
Arabian babbler: The Arabian babbler has brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a distinctive pale eyebrow stripe. It inhabits arid scrublands, desert oases, and cultivated areas across the Arabian Peninsula and parts of the Middle East. It feeds primarily on insects and small fruits, living in cooperative groups that defend territories and engage in communal chick-rearing. A fun fact is that these birds use complex vocalizations to coordinate group movements and alert others to predators.
Arabian green bee-eater: This bird has bright green plumage with a black eye stripe and yellow throat, inhabiting arid deserts and dry woodlands across the Arabian Peninsula. It feeds primarily on flying insects like bees and wasps, hunting in cooperative groups by sallying from perches. Fun fact: it removes stingers from prey by repeatedly beating insects against branches before consumption.
Arabian warbler: The Arabian warbler has olive-brown upperparts and a pale throat. It inhabits arid scrublands and desert edges across the Arabian Peninsula. It feeds on insects while foraging actively in dense vegetation. Its loud, repetitive song is often heard before the bird is seen.
Arctic redpoll: Arctic redpolls have a small size with a red forehead patch, streaked brown upperparts, and pale underparts. They inhabit Arctic tundra and boreal forests during summer, moving to open woodlands and gardens in winter. Their diet consists mainly of seeds from birch, alder, and conifer trees, and they often forage in noisy, nomadic flocks. They can eat snow to obtain water during cold weather.
Arctic tern: Arctic terns have gray backs, white bellies, and bright red beaks. They breed in Arctic coastal areas and migrate to Antarctic waters for winter. Their diet consists of small fish and marine invertebrates, and they are highly aerial feeders known for their long migrations. They hold the record for the longest annual migration, traveling up to 44,000 miles between breeding and wintering grounds.
Arctic warbler: The Arctic warbler has a greenish back, yellowish underparts, and a white eye ring. It breeds in boreal forests across northern Eurasia and migrates to Southeast Asia for winter. It feeds primarily on insects gleaned from foliage while being active and often seen in tree canopies. This bird undertakes one of the longest migrations of any songbird relative to its size.
Armenian gull: The Armenian gull has a pale gray back, white head and underparts, and a pale yellow bill during breeding season. It breeds in mountainous wetlands across Armenia and adjacent regions, feeding on fish, insects, and carrion while migrating in large flocks. A fun fact is that it undertakes one of the longest migratory journeys among gull species, traveling thousands of kilometers annually.
Asian brown flycatcher: The Asian brown flycatcher has plain brown upperparts and pale underparts with no distinct markings. It inhabits open woodlands, gardens, and forest edges across South and Southeast Asia. It feeds primarily on insects caught in short aerial sallies from perches. It occasionally imitates the calls of other birds.
Asian desert warbler: This small warbler has brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a distinct pale eye stripe. It inhabits arid scrublands and desert edges across North Africa and Southwest Asia. It feeds primarily on insects while foraging actively in low vegetation. A fun fact is that its loud, repetitive song sounds like 'wheee' and is often heard before the bird is seen.
Atlantic canary: The Atlantic canary has a bright yellow body with a dark head and a distinctive white eye ring. It inhabits rocky coastal areas and scrublands on the Canary Islands. Its diet includes seeds and insects, and it is known for its loud, cheerful song. Fun fact: This wild bird is the direct ancestor of the domestic canary kept as a popular pet.
Atlantic puffin: The Atlantic puffin has a stocky body, black back, white front, and a brightly colored beak during breeding season. It nests on rocky coastal cliffs across the North Atlantic and feeds mainly on small fish like sand eels. Puffins are highly social, diving underwater to catch prey and known for carrying multiple fish in their beaks at once.
Atlas pied flycatcher: This bird has black and white plumage in males with a contrasting black back, while females are browner and less marked. It inhabits montane forests and woodlands in the Atlas Mountains of North Africa. It feeds on flying insects caught mid-air using a perch-and-sally hunting style. A fun fact is that its loud, sharp call often echoes through mountain valleys during the breeding season.
Atlas wheatear: Atlas wheatears have gray upperparts, white underparts, and a distinctive black face mask. They inhabit rocky, arid slopes across North Africa including the Atlas Mountains. They eat insects and forage actively on the ground, with a loud song. A fun fact is their black face mask is so striking it aids quick identification in the field.
Audouins gull: Audouin's gull has a white head and underparts, gray back, and black-tipped wings. It nests on coastal islands in the Mediterranean Sea and Atlantic coasts. Its diet includes fish and invertebrates, and it forages in colonies near the water. It is named after the French naturalist Jean-Louis Cabanis.
Azure-winged magpie: The Azure-winged magpie has striking blue wings and tail contrasting with black head, back, and white underparts. It inhabits mixed forests and woodlands in East Asia, particularly China, Japan, and Korea. It feeds on insects, fruits, seeds, and occasionally small vertebrates, often foraging in noisy social groups. A fun fact is that it is one of the few magpie species with prominent blue wing feathers.
Baikal teal: Male Baikal teals have striking green heads with white facial stripes and chestnut bodies. They breed in wetlands across Siberia and migrate to East Asia for winter. Their diet includes aquatic plants and small invertebrates, and they fly in fast, agile flocks. A fun fact is that males produce a distinctive whistling sound during courtship displays.
Bairds sandpiper: Baird's sandpiper has brown streaked upperparts, pale underparts, and a short bill. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters in South American grasslands and wetlands. It feeds on insects and invertebrates while foraging in flocks. It undertakes one of the longest migration routes of any shorebird, traveling from Alaska to Patagonia.
Balearic shearwater: This dark brown seabird has a pale belly and a distinctive white eye patch. It nests on remote Mediterranean islands and feeds on fish and squid by skimming the ocean surface during long oceanic flights. A fun fact is that it migrates over 2,000 kilometers to winter off northwest Africa.
Balearic warbler: The Balearic warbler has olive-brown upperparts, a pale eyebrow, and a dark eye. It inhabits scrubland and maquis vegetation on the Balearic Islands. It feeds mainly on insects and spiders, being active and territorial during breeding. Its song consists of a rapid series of high-pitched notes.
Band-rumped storm petrel: This small seabird has dark brown plumage, a white rump band, and a distinctive dark bar across its rump. It inhabits open oceans worldwide, breeding on remote offshore islands in the Pacific and Atlantic. It feeds on plankton and small fish by skimming the water surface while flying low, using its feet to paddle during feeding. Its unique feeding method includes using its feet to paddle on the water while skimming for prey.
Bar-headed goose: Bar-headed geese have brown and white mottled plumage with a pale head and neck. They breed in high-altitude wetlands across Central Asia and migrate long distances to winter in South Asia. Their diet consists of grasses, sedges, and aquatic plants, and they fly in V-formations during migration. They are known to fly over the Himalayas, including Mount Everest, at altitudes exceeding 29,000 feet.
Bar-tailed godwit: Bar-tailed godwits have a barred brown back, long pale legs, and a slightly upturned bill. They breed in Arctic tundra and winter on coastal mudflats worldwide. Their diet consists of invertebrates like worms and crustaceans, and they feed in flocks during migration. They hold the record for the longest non-stop flight by a shorebird.
Bar-tailed lark: The Bar-tailed lark has a streaked brown back, pale breast, and distinctive black bars on its tail. It inhabits dry grasslands, deserts, and open fields across Asia and Africa, feeding primarily on seeds and insects while foraging on the ground. Its distinctive 'tsee-tsee' call is often heard during song flights.
Barbary partridge: This bird has brown plumage with black and white head markings and inhabits rocky, arid regions of North Africa. It feeds on seeds, insects, and vegetation while moving in social groups on the ground. Barbary partridges form lifelong monogamous pairs.
Barn owl: Barn owls have pale brown and white plumage with a distinctive heart-shaped facial disc. They inhabit open landscapes like farmlands and grasslands, nesting in buildings or tree cavities. They hunt small mammals primarily at night using silent flight and exceptional hearing. Barn owls consume over a thousand rodents annually in a single year.
Barn swallow: Barn swallows have blue upperparts, a reddish-brown throat, and long forked tails. They nest under eaves, bridges, and in barns across open country near water. They eat flying insects on the wing and are highly social, often seen in groups. Their migration spans continents, with some individuals traveling over 10,000 kilometers annually.
Barnacle goose: Barnacle geese have black heads and necks with white cheek patches, grayish-brown bodies, and white rumps. They breed in Arctic tundra regions and winter along coastal areas of Europe. They feed primarily on grasses and sedges, forming large, noisy flocks during migration. A fun fact is that their name originated from a medieval myth claiming they hatched from barnacles.
Barred warbler: The Barred warbler has a distinctive black and white barred back, wings, and tail with a pale eyebrow stripe. It inhabits open woodlands, scrublands, and hedgerows in Europe and Asia during breeding, migrating to sub-Saharan Africa for winter. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, foraging actively in bushes and trees. A fun fact is that its song resembles a rapid "tsee-tsee-tsee" call.
Barrows goldeneye: Male Barrow's goldeneyes have a glossy green head with a white face patch, while females are brown with a pale cheek. They breed in northern freshwater lakes and rivers, migrating to coastal marine waters in winter. Their diet consists of aquatic invertebrates and small fish, and they are skilled divers. A fun fact is their flight has a distinctive bouncing motion during migration.
Bearded reedling: The Bearded reedling has a gray body, yellowish underparts, and a distinctive black facial "beard." It inhabits dense reedbeds in wetlands across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on seeds and insects, often foraging in reed stems while moving in small social groups. Its characteristic chattering call gives it the nickname "chattering tit."
Bearded vulture: This large bird has a pale body with dark wingtips and a distinctive dark facial beard. It inhabits high mountain ranges across Europe, Asia, and Africa, soaring on thermals while feeding primarily on bone marrow. Its unique behavior involves dropping bones from great heights to access marrow, making it one of the few birds that intentionally break bones for food.
Belted kingfisher:
The Belted kingfisher has a blue-gray back, white underparts, and a large head with a crest. Males show a single chest band while females have two bands. It inhabits shorelines of rivers, lakes, and coastal areas.

It primarily eats fish but also consumes insects and small amphibians. It hunts by hovering above water before diving headfirst to catch prey.

It can rotate its head nearly 180 degrees to view prey underwater.
Berthelots pipit: Berthelots pipit has brown streaked upperparts and a pale throat with a dark crown stripe. It inhabits open grasslands and cultivated areas in the Canary Islands and Cape Verde. It feeds on insects and seeds, foraging on the ground and flying short distances with a characteristic fluttering flight. A fun fact is that it is one of the few bird species that breeds year-round on the Canary Islands without migrating.
Bimaculated lark: The Bimaculated lark has a brown back, white throat, and distinctive black and white facial markings including two white spots above the eyes. It inhabits dry grasslands and open savannas across eastern Africa. Its diet consists of insects and seeds foraged from the ground, and it exhibits short, low flights with minimal singing. A fun fact is that it uses a soft ticking alarm call to warn others of danger while foraging on the ground.
Black francolin: The Black francolin has dark brown plumage with white spots on its wings and a distinctive white throat patch. It inhabits grasslands, agricultural fields, and scrublands across South Asia. Its diet consists of seeds, insects, and plant matter, and it is a ground-dwelling bird that forms pairs and calls loudly at dawn. A fun fact is that its loud, repeated call sounds like "franklin," giving the bird its common name.
Black grouse: Male Black grouse have black plumage with white wing patches and a prominent neck ruff. They inhabit boreal forests, moorlands, and open woodlands across northern Europe and Asia. Their diet consists of plants, leaves, berries, and insects, especially for chicks, and they gather in leks for competitive mating displays. Males produce a loud wing-clapping sound during courtship to attract females.
Black guillemot: Black guillemots have dark plumage with a white wing patch in summer and a paler appearance in winter. They inhabit rocky coastlines and islands across the northern Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Their diet consists mainly of fish and marine invertebrates, and they are skilled divers that forage underwater. They use their wings to propel themselves while swimming underwater like flying.
Black kite: Black kites have dark brown plumage, a pale head, and a deeply forked tail. They inhabit open country including grasslands, wetlands, and urban areas across Africa, Asia, and Europe. They are opportunistic feeders consuming carrion, insects, and small vertebrates, often soaring in thermals or scavenging near humans. They are known to follow agricultural machinery to catch insects disturbed by plowing.
Black lark: The Black lark has dark brown upperparts with a pale eyebrow and a pale throat. It inhabits open grasslands and steppes across central Asia. Its diet consists of insects and seeds, and it forages on the ground while often singing from a low perch. A fun fact is that it performs an impressive song flight, ascending while singing and then parachuting down to the ground.
Black redstart: The Black redstart has dark grey or black plumage with a prominent red tail in males, while females are browner. It inhabits urban areas like cities and towns, nesting on buildings and foraging on streets. Its diet consists mainly of insects and spiders, and it is active, often hopping on the ground. A fun fact is that it readily nests on buildings, making it a common sight in European city centers.
Black scoter: Black scoters are dark ducks with a distinctive yellow bill and patch. They inhabit coastal waters, estuaries, and bays across northern regions. Their diet consists mainly of shellfish and marine invertebrates, and they dive for food in large groups. A fun fact is they produce loud, frog-like calls during courtship displays.
Black stork:
The Black stork has all-black plumage with white underparts and a long red bill. It inhabits forests near wetlands across Europe and Asia, nesting in tall trees. It feeds primarily on fish, amphibians, and small mammals, often foraging alone in shallow water.  
Black storks are known for their silent flight and strong migratory patterns, avoiding human settlements.  
A fun fact is that in some European cultures, spotting a Black stork is considered a sign of good luck.
Black tern: Black terns have a dark gray back, white underparts, and a black cap in summer. They nest in freshwater marshes and wetlands across North America and Eurasia. Their diet consists of insects and small fish caught in mid-air during agile flight. They perform aerial courtship displays with rapid dives and twists.
Black wheatear: This small bird has black plumage with distinctive white wing patches and inhabits dry rocky slopes across North Africa and the Middle East. It primarily feeds on insects, foraging actively on the ground while perching on rocks to scan for prey. Its name originates from its loud, repetitive call that sounds like "wheatear."
Black woodpecker: The Black woodpecker is a large black bird with white wing patches and a red crown in males. It inhabits mature forests across Europe and Asia, preferring dead or decaying trees. Its diet consists mainly of wood-boring insects, and it is known for powerful drumming on trees to communicate. Its drumming can be heard over a kilometer away.
Black-bellied sandgrouse: The Black-bellied sandgrouse has a gray-brown body with a distinctive dark patch on its belly. It inhabits dry, open country including deserts and steppes across Africa and Asia. Its diet consists mainly of seeds, and it is known for long flights to drinking water sources. Males carry water in specialized belly feathers to feed their chicks.
Black-billed cuckoo: The Black-billed cuckoo has a grayish-brown back, pale underparts, a black bill, and a distinctive white throat patch. It inhabits deciduous and mixed forests across eastern North America, often in dense thickets near water. Its diet primarily consists of insects, especially caterpillars, which it forages for in trees and shrubs, and it is known for its secretive behavior and loud, repetitive calls. It can consume hairy caterpillars that other birds avoid due to their defenses.
Black-browed albatross: The Black-browed albatross has dark brown upperparts, a white face and underparts, and a distinctive black eyebrow stripe. It breeds on remote sub-Antarctic islands and spends most of its life soaring over the open Southern Ocean. Its diet consists of fish, squid, and krill, and it is a strong, efficient glider that often follows ships. These birds form long-lasting pair bonds and can live over fifty years.
Black-crowned night heron: This bird has a stocky body, a dark gray back, a distinctive black crown, and white underparts. It inhabits freshwater and coastal wetlands worldwide, nesting in trees or shrubs near water. It feeds primarily on fish, amphibians, and insects, hunting at night or dusk from a perch. Its loud, harsh call resembles a duck's quack.
Black-crowned sparrow-lark: The Black-crowned sparrow-lark has a brown back, pale underparts, and a distinctive black crown on its head. It inhabits dry, open scrublands and grasslands across North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. It feeds mainly on insects and seeds while foraging on the ground, often singing from a low perch. Its song resembles a loud, repetitive "chirp-chirp" call.
Black-crowned tchagra: The Black-crowned tchagra has a black crown, gray back, and white underparts with dark streaking. It inhabits dense thickets and woodlands across sub-Saharan Africa, often near acacia trees. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, being shy and territorial, usually seen in pairs. Its distinctive call sounds like "tchagga" giving the bird its common name.
Black-headed bunting: Male Black-headed buntings have a striking black head and neck in breeding plumage with a bright yellow chest. They inhabit open grasslands, farmlands, and shrubby areas across temperate Eurasia. They eat seeds and insects, often feeding in flocks and singing from perches. Their melodious song is a characteristic sound in their breeding grounds.
Black-headed gull: The Black-headed gull has a brownish head in summer, pale grey back, and white underparts. It inhabits coastal areas, lakes, and rivers across Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects, fish, and scraps, often gathering in large noisy flocks. Its distinctive call sounds like "kree-ee" and it is known for stealing food from other birds.
Black-legged kittiwake: Black-legged kittiwakes have white bodies, gray backs, and black legs. They nest on coastal cliffs and forage over open oceans. They eat fish caught by plunge-diving and feed while flying in large colonies. Their name comes from their loud, distinctive call.
Black-necked grebe: The Black-necked grebe has a dark neck and chest in breeding plumage, contrasting with its pale head and body. It inhabits shallow freshwater lakes and ponds across Europe and Asia. It feeds on aquatic insects, crustaceans, and small fish, diving expertly and performing complex courtship displays. A fun fact is that it can swim underwater using its wings like a penguin.
Black-tailed godwit: The Black-tailed godwit has long legs, a long curved bill, and distinctive black tail feathers during breeding season. It inhabits wet grasslands and marshes in summer, migrating to coastal mudflats and estuaries in winter. Its diet consists of invertebrates like worms and insects, and it feeds by probing mud while often moving in noisy flocks. A fun fact is that its loud, distinctive call sounds like "kree-ee" and can be heard over long distances.
Black-throated accentor: This bird has a dark throat patch, brown back, and pale underparts, found in rocky mountain habitats across Asia. It feeds on insects and seeds while foraging on the ground, often alone. Its song resembles 'chick-a-dee' calls.
Black-throated loon: The Black-throated loon has a black throat patch, gray back, and white underparts in breeding plumage. It breeds on Arctic tundra lakes and winters along coastal oceans. It dives for fish, its primary diet, and is typically solitary and wary. Its haunting series of wailing calls is often heard across northern waters at night.
Black-winged kite: This small raptor has gray upperparts, white underparts, and distinctive black wing patches. It inhabits open grasslands and wetlands, hunting rodents and insects while hovering motionless. A fun fact is that it can hover for extended periods to spot prey.
Black-winged pratincole: The Black-winged pratincole has dark wings and a white body with a dark patch on its forehead. It inhabits open wetlands, grasslands, and floodplains across Africa and Asia. It feeds on flying insects caught in swift, agile flight while foraging in flocks. Its name comes from the French word for grasshopper catcher, reflecting its diet.
Black-winged stilt: The Black-winged stilt has long pink legs, a black-and-white body, and a long thin bill. It inhabits shallow freshwater wetlands, lakes, and mudflats globally. It feeds on aquatic insects and small invertebrates, foraging by wading and pecking. Its exceptionally long legs allow it to stand in deeper water than most other waders.
Blue rock thrush: Male Blue rock thrushes display vibrant blue plumage with a white throat, while females are brown-streaked. They inhabit rocky cliffs, mountains, and outcrops across Europe, Asia, and Africa. They eat insects and small invertebrates, often hunting from perches and defending territories with loud songs. A fun fact is that they frequently nest in rock crevices high above the ground, sometimes even on man-made structures like old buildings.
Blue-cheeked bee-eater: The Blue-cheeked bee-eater has bright green upperparts, a blue cheek patch, and a long tail. It inhabits open woodlands and savannas across sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia. It feeds primarily on bees and wasps caught in flight, often hunting from a perch and exhibiting cooperative breeding behavior. These birds remove stingers from prey by beating them against a branch before eating.
Blue-winged teal: Blue-winged teals have distinctive blue wing patches in males, brown bodies, and white eye stripes. They inhabit shallow freshwater wetlands, marshes, and ponds across North America. Their diet includes aquatic plants, seeds, and small invertebrates, and they form large social flocks during migration. They are among the earliest migrating ducks to arrive on breeding grounds each spring.
Bluethroat: Male Bluethroats feature a striking blue throat patch on a dark brown body, with females being more streaked and brown. They breed in wetland reed beds across Eurasia and migrate to tropical regions, feeding mainly on insects caught in vegetation. A fun fact is that they can mimic other bird species' calls.
Blyths pipit: Blyth's pipit has a brown streaked back, pale underparts, and a pale eyebrow stripe. It inhabits open grasslands, agricultural fields, and steppe regions across Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and seeds, foraging actively on the ground with short flights. Its distinctive high-pitched song helps distinguish it from similar pipits.
Blyths reed warbler: Blyth's reed warbler has dull brown upperparts and pale underparts with a pale eyebrow. It inhabits reedbeds and wetlands across Asia during breeding. Its diet consists of insects and spiders, and it sings loudly from reed tops. It is known for its loud, repetitive song often heard during migration.
Bohemian waxwing: Bohemian waxwings have grayish-brown bodies, a distinctive crest, a black mask, and waxy red tips on their wing feathers. They inhabit coniferous forests across northern regions and migrate south to feed on berries in orchards and hedgerows. Their diet is primarily fruit, supplemented by insects in summer, and they move in noisy, social flocks. Their name reflects their nomadic nature, as they wander widely in search of fruit.
Bonapartes gull: Bonaparte's gull has a distinctive black head with a white eyering in breeding plumage, gray back, and white underparts. It inhabits coastal areas, estuaries, and inland lakes during breeding, migrating to marine waters and coastal bays in winter. Its diet includes insects, small fish, and crustaceans, and it exhibits agile, buoyant flight while often scavenging. A fun fact is that it is one of the few gull species that regularly migrates to the southern hemisphere for winter.
Bonellis eagle: Bonelli's eagle has dark brown plumage with a pale neck and distinctive white patches on its wings. It inhabits mountainous regions, forests, and rocky areas across southern Europe, Africa, and Asia. It hunts birds and small mammals, often soaring and gliding from perches. A fun fact is that it frequently nests on cliff faces or large trees, sometimes reusing the same site for many years.
Booted eagle: Booted eagles have dark brown upperparts and pale streaked underparts. They inhabit open woodlands, grasslands, and agricultural areas across Europe, Africa, and Asia. They hunt small mammals, reptiles, and birds using agile flight and perching. They can migrate long distances, sometimes crossing the Sahara Desert during seasonal movements.
Booted warbler: The Booted Warbler has brown upperparts, pale buff underparts, and a distinctive white eye ring. It inhabits reedbeds and wet grasslands in Europe and Asia during breeding. It feeds primarily on insects gleaned from vegetation and is typically shy and active within dense cover. Its name comes from dark feather tufts resembling boots on its legs.
Boreal owl: The Boreal owl has brown and white streaked plumage with a pale face and large yellow eyes. It inhabits dense coniferous and mixed forests across northern North America and Eurasia. Its diet primarily consists of small mammals like voles, and it is a nocturnal hunter that defends its territory with calls. A fun fact is that its distinctive call sounds like a bouncing ball.
Brambling: Brambling has a distinctive appearance with a bright orange-red breast and crown in summer, fading to brownish-gray in winter. It breeds in coniferous forests across northern Europe and Asia, migrating to temperate regions for winter where it feeds primarily on seeds, especially birch and alder. Brambling is highly social, forming large flocks during migration and winter. A fun fact is that Brambling flocks sometimes descend on urban parks in winter, feeding on seeds from ornamental trees.
Brant: Brant geese have dark brown bodies, white necks, and black heads with a distinctive white face patch. They breed in Arctic tundra and migrate to coastal salt marshes and estuaries in winter. Their diet consists of grasses, seaweed, and aquatic plants, and they travel in noisy, V-shaped flocks during migration. A fun fact is that the name "Brant" comes from the bird's loud, braying call.
Bridled tern: The Bridled tern has a white body, gray back, black crown, and a distinctive dark band across its eyes. It inhabits tropical and subtropical oceans, nesting on sandy or rocky islands and foraging over open seas. Its diet consists of small fish and plankton, caught by plunge-diving or surface-seizing, and it nests colonially with synchronized aerial displays. A fun fact is that they often ride ocean swells while flying, using the wave motion to conserve energy.
Broad-billed sandpiper: The Broad-billed sandpiper has a short broad bill, brown streaked upperparts, and a pale breast. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters in wetlands across Africa and Asia. Its diet consists of insects and small invertebrates, foraging actively in shallow water. A fun fact is that its call sounds like a rapid "peep-peep."
Brown booby: Brown boobies have dark brown plumage with a pale head and white underparts. They inhabit tropical and subtropical oceans, nesting on remote islands. They feed primarily on fish caught by plunge-diving and are social, nesting in colonies. Their clumsy landings on water often cause them to splash.
Brown fish owl: Brown fish owls have brown and streaked plumage with large yellow eyes and a rounded head. They inhabit forests and woodlands near rivers, lakes, and wetlands across South and Southeast Asia. Their diet primarily consists of fish caught by swooping from perches, and they are solitary nocturnal hunters. They can rotate their heads nearly 270 degrees to scan for prey.
Brown shrike: The Brown shrike has brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a dark mask across its eyes. It inhabits open woodlands, scrublands, and farmlands across temperate Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and small vertebrates, often impaling prey on thorns. This behavior earned it the nickname "butcher bird."
Brown-necked raven: Brown-necked ravens are large all-black birds with a distinctive brown neck patch, found in arid and semi-arid habitats across North Africa and the Middle East. They eat a varied diet including carrion, insects, fruits, and human food scraps, often foraging in groups with noisy, social behavior. A fun fact is that they are known to steal food from campers and livestock, showing remarkable boldness and intelligence.
Buff-bellied pipit: The Buff-bellied pipit has a pale buff belly, streaked brown back, and a pale eyebrow. It inhabits open grasslands, meadows, and agricultural fields across Asia and Europe. Its diet consists mainly of insects and seeds, and it forages on the ground, often running and making short flights. This bird is known for its loud, melodious song sung from an elevated perch.
Buff-breasted sandpiper: The Buff-breasted sandpiper has a buff-colored breast, streaked brown back, and short dark bill. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters on grasslands in South America. It feeds on insects and invertebrates by probing and pecking while foraging in open areas. This species undertakes one of the longest migrations among shorebirds, traveling over 12,000 miles annually.
Bufflehead: Buffleheads have striking black and white plumage with a large white patch on the male's head. They breed in forested lakes and winter along coastlines, diving for aquatic invertebrates like insects and crustaceans. They nest in tree cavities and form small flocks, with a fun fact being they are the smallest diving duck in North America.
Bulwers petrel: Bulwer's petrel has a greyish-brown back and wings with a dark cap, pale underparts, and a pale face. It breeds on remote oceanic islands in the Atlantic and Indian Oceans and spends most of its life far from land. Its diet consists of small fish and squid caught by surface dipping, and it is nocturnal at breeding colonies. A fun fact is that its name comes from the distinctive "bul-ler" call it makes.
Cackling goose:
Cackling geese are small, stocky waterfowl with short necks, dark heads, and light underbellies. They form tight family groups and produce loud, high-pitched calls.  
They breed in Arctic tundra regions and migrate to grasslands and agricultural fields in temperate zones, feeding primarily on grasses, grains, and seeds.  
Their distinctive call is much higher-pitched and shorter than the Canada goose's honk.
Calandra lark: Calandra larks have brown streaked upperparts, a pale eyebrow, and a white throat. They inhabit open farmlands, grasslands, and steppe regions across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists of seeds and insects, and they forage on the ground while singing loudly from elevated perches. A fun fact is that their loud, distinctive song can often be heard from over a kilometer away during the breeding season.
Canada goose: Canada geese have brown bodies, white facial markings, and dark necks. They inhabit wetlands, parks, and agricultural areas across North America, feeding on grasses and grains while forming strong family groups. A fun fact is that they fly in V-formations to conserve energy during migration.
Canary Islands chiffchaff: This bird has a dull olive-brown upper body, pale eyebrow, and yellowish underparts, inhabiting laurel forests in the Canary Islands. It primarily eats insects and spiders, foraging actively in dense vegetation with a characteristic repetitive call. A fun fact is that its song was long mistaken for the common chiffchaff before genetic studies confirmed it as a distinct subspecies.
Canary Islands stonechat: The Canary Islands stonechat has a brown back, pale breast, and males display a black facial mask. It inhabits open scrublands and coastal areas across the Canary Islands, feeding primarily on insects caught in flight. Its name comes from its distinctive sharp "stone-chat" call.
Canvasback: Canvasbacks have a distinctive sloping forehead, red head, and black chest with a white back. They nest in freshwater marshes and migrate to large lakes and coastal bays. Their diet consists mainly of aquatic plants and invertebrates, and they are social birds forming large flocks. A fun fact is that their common name comes from the white, canvas-like appearance of their breast feathers.
Carrion crow: Carrion crows are entirely black birds with a glossy sheen and strong, straight bills. They inhabit diverse environments including forests, farmlands, and urban areas across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists of carrion, insects, grains, and human food waste, and they are highly intelligent, social birds known for complex vocalizations. A fun fact is that they can recognize individual human faces and remember negative encounters.
Caspian gull: The Caspian gull has pale grey wings, a white head, and a pale yellow eye. It breeds near coastal areas and large inland lakes across Eurasia, migrating to coastal regions in winter. Its diet includes fish, insects, and scavenged food, and it often feeds in noisy colonies. It is known for stealing food from other birds.
Caspian plover: The Caspian plover has a pale brown back, white underparts, and a distinct dark eye stripe. It breeds in open grasslands and steppes near water in Central Asia and winters in Africa and South Asia. It feeds on insects and small invertebrates by running and probing the ground. It can run very fast to catch prey on foot.
Caspian snowcock: The Caspian snowcock has gray-brown plumage with distinctive white facial stripes and a white throat patch. It inhabits high mountain slopes above 3000 meters in the Tian Shan and Pamir ranges, feeding mainly on grasses and seeds. These birds form flocks and are known for loud calls, and they can run swiftly across steep rocky terrain to evade predators.
Caspian tern: The Caspian tern has a pale gray back, black cap, and a long bright red bill. It inhabits coastal areas, lakes, and rivers worldwide, often nesting in colonies on sandy or gravelly shores. It feeds primarily on fish caught by plunge-diving and exhibits strong, direct flight. Its bill is the longest relative to body size among all tern species.
Cattle egret: Cattle egrets are small white birds with yellow legs and bill, developing a plume on the back during breeding. They inhabit grasslands, pastures, and wetlands worldwide, often following large grazing animals. They eat insects, frogs, and small fish, foraging by walking slowly and catching prey disturbed by livestock. A fun fact is that they expanded their range dramatically from Africa to colonize the Americas in the 20th century.
Caucasian grouse: The Caucasian grouse has a dark black plumage with white wing patches in males, while females are brown and streaked. It inhabits coniferous and mixed forests at high elevations across the Caucasus Mountains. Its diet consists mainly of plant material including berries, leaves, and seeds, and it exhibits lekking behavior where males display on open grounds. A fun fact is that males perform intricate aerial displays during courtship, involving rapid wing beats and loud calls.
Caucasian snowcock: The Caucasian snowcock has gray plumage with white underparts and a black throat patch. It inhabits high alpine rocky slopes and meadows above the tree line in the Caucasus Mountains. Its diet consists of grasses, seeds, and vegetation, and it is a social ground-dwelling bird that moves in flocks. It can run swiftly across steep rocky terrain to evade predators.
Chestnut bunting: The Chestnut bunting has chestnut-brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a black face mask in males. It inhabits open grasslands, scrublands, and agricultural areas across Asia, migrating to warmer regions in winter. Its diet consists mainly of seeds, foraging on the ground in flocks during non-breeding seasons. A fun fact is that its distinctive call sounds like a small, ringing bell.
Chukar partridge: Chukar partridges have a grey head with a black neck band, brownish body, and white underparts. They inhabit rocky, mountainous slopes across Asia and the Middle East. They eat seeds, insects, and vegetation while living in coveys on the ground. Chukars were successfully introduced to North America for hunting purposes.
Cinereous bunting: The Cinereous bunting has grey plumage with dark streaks on its back and a pale eyebrow. It inhabits open grasslands, steppes, and cultivated fields across central Asia. It feeds mainly on seeds and insects, foraging on the ground in flocks and often seen in pairs or small groups. Its loud, clear whistled song is distinctive and often heard during the breeding season.
Cinereous vulture: The Cinereous vulture has dark gray-brown plumage with a pale head and neck ruff, often seen soaring over open grasslands and mountainous regions across Europe and Asia. It primarily feeds on carrion, relying on keen eyesight to locate dead animals and spending much time soaring on thermals. A fun fact is that it drinks water by scooping it into its beak and tilting its head back to swallow.
Cirl bunting: The Cirl bunting has a streaked brown back, pale breast, and a distinctive yellow and black head pattern in males. It inhabits farmland with hedgerows and scrub across southern Europe. Its diet consists mainly of seeds and insects, foraging on the ground in small groups. A fun fact is that it was successfully reintroduced to parts of Britain through conservation programs supporting traditional farming methods.
Citril finch: The Citril finch has yellowish-brown plumage with a pale eyebrow and an orange bill. It inhabits mountainous pine forests across the Alps and Pyrenees. Its diet consists mainly of seeds and insects, and it forms noisy social flocks. It is known for its loud, distinctive calls that carry through mountain valleys.
Clamorous reed warbler: This warbler has brown-streaked upperparts and pale underparts with a distinct pale eyebrow stripe. It inhabits dense reed beds and wetlands across Asia, feeding primarily on insects and spiders while remaining secretive and vocal. Its loud, repetitive song is the origin of its common name "clamorous."
Coal tit: The Coal tit has a black cap, white cheeks, and a grey back with white underparts. It inhabits woodlands, parks, and gardens, often in coniferous forests. It feeds on insects, seeds, and nuts, foraging actively in trees and sometimes hanging upside down. Coal tits cache food in tree bark crevices for later retrieval.
Collared flycatcher:
Male collared flycatchers have black heads and bodies with a white collar and wing patches. Females are browner with less distinct markings. They breed in deciduous forests across Europe and Asia, nesting in tree cavities.

They feed primarily on flying insects caught in mid-air. Males defend territories aggressively during the breeding season.

Their loud, repetitive call sounds like "tsee-tsee" or "chick-a-dee-dee."
Collared pratincole:
This bird has a pale grey back, white underparts, and a distinct dark collar around its neck. It inhabits open grasslands, wetlands, and riverbanks across Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects caught mid-flight while flying in flocks, often foraging over water.  
It can drink water while flying during migration.
Common blackbird: Male Common blackbirds are glossy black with a yellow beak and eye ring. They inhabit gardens, woodlands, and parks across Europe and Asia. Their diet includes insects, worms, and berries, and they sing loudly from perches while defending territories. A fun fact is that their song is often heard at dawn and dusk.
Common bulbul:
The Common bulbul has brownish upperparts, a pale throat, and a small crest. It inhabits gardens, forests, and urban areas across South and Southeast Asia. Its diet includes fruits, insects, and nectar, and it is often seen in noisy, social groups.  
This bird is known for its loud, repetitive call that sounds like "bulbul," giving the species its common name.
Common buzzard: The Common buzzard has brownish plumage with a broad wingspan and a characteristic flight pattern showing a distinct 'V' shape. It inhabits diverse landscapes including woodlands, farmlands, and open countryside across Europe and Asia. It primarily hunts small mammals like rodents and insects, often soaring or perching to spot prey. A fun fact is that its plumage color varies significantly, with pale and dark morphs existing within the same population.
Common chaffinch:
Male chaffinches have blue-grey caps and pink breasts with brown wings. Females are duller grey-brown. They inhabit woodlands, parks, and gardens across Europe and Asia.  
Their diet is mainly seeds and insects, especially caterpillars for their young. They are social birds, often seen in flocks and known for their cheerful song.  
Chaffinches have regional song dialects that change as birds move to new areas.
Common chiffchaff: The Common chiffchaff has olive-green upperparts and pale yellow underparts with a distinct pale eye ring. It inhabits woodlands, gardens, and scrub across Europe and Asia, migrating to southern Europe and Africa for winter. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders gleaned from foliage, known for its energetic foraging and characteristic "chiff-chaff" call. Its name directly imitates this repeated song, making it one of the first warblers to return to breeding grounds in spring.
Common crane:
The Common crane has gray plumage, a red crown, and a black neck. It inhabits wetlands across Europe and Asia, migrating to Africa and South Asia for winter. It eats plants, insects, and small animals, and performs elaborate courtship dances.  
Common cranes fly in V-formations at very high altitudes during migration.
Common cuckoo: The Common cuckoo has a grayish back and barred breast in males, while females are brown with similar barring. It inhabits open woodlands, farmlands, and gardens across Europe, Asia, and parts of Africa. Its diet consists mainly of insects, especially caterpillars, and it practices brood parasitism, laying eggs in other birds' nests. A fun fact is that the cuckoo's call inspired the name for the sound of a clock striking the hour.
Common eider: The Common eider has a distinctive black and white plumage in males with a green head, while females are brown. It inhabits coastal marine areas, nesting on islands and rocky shores across the northern hemisphere. Its diet consists mainly of mollusks and crustaceans, and it forms large flocks while swimming strongly. Its down feathers are highly valued for insulation.
Common firecrest:
The Common firecrest has a bright orange crown patch, green upperparts, and white eye stripes. It inhabits mixed forests with conifers and broadleaves across Europe and western Asia. It feeds on small insects like aphids and spiders, foraging acrobatically in tree canopies.  
A fun fact is that it is Europe's smallest warbler.
Common goldeneye: Male Common goldeneyes have a striking black and white head with a bright yellow eye and a green sheen on the crown. They inhabit freshwater lakes and rivers in forested regions across North America and Eurasia, nesting in tree cavities. They dive to feed on fish, insects, and crustaceans, often forming large flocks during migration. Males perform a unique head-pumping display during courtship.
Common grasshopper warbler: This small brown bird has a pale eyebrow stripe and blends into dense vegetation. It lives in wet grasslands, reedbeds, and scrub areas across Europe and Asia. It eats insects like grasshoppers and spiders, staying hidden while singing a loud buzzing song from the ground. Its song mimics a grasshopper's buzz, hence its common name.
Common greenshank: The Common greenshank has greenish legs, a long slightly curved bill, and gray-brown plumage. It breeds in wetlands across northern Europe and Asia and winters in coastal areas of Africa and Southeast Asia. It feeds on invertebrates by probing mudflats and is often seen in flocks during migration. Its name comes from its loud distinctive call sounding like "green-shank."
Common gull: Common gulls have a grey back, white head and underparts, and black-tipped wings. They inhabit coastal areas, lakes, rivers, and urban sites across Europe and Asia. Their diet includes fish, insects, and human food scraps, and they are known for scavenging and agile flight. They often gather in large numbers at landfills.
Common house martin: The Common house martin has a dark blue back, white underparts, and a white rump. It nests under eaves on buildings in urban and rural areas across Europe and Asia. It feeds on flying insects caught in flight, often in large, noisy groups. Its mud nests are reused for multiple broods each season.
Common kestrel: The Common kestrel has a brown back, barred tail, and distinctive dark eye stripes. It inhabits open country including farmland, grasslands, and urban areas across Europe, Asia, and Africa. It hunts by hovering to spot small mammals and insects before diving. Kestrels can see ultraviolet light to track mouse urine trails.
Common kingfisher: The Common kingfisher has bright blue upperparts and orange underparts with a long pointed bill. It inhabits freshwater habitats like rivers and ponds across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on small fish, catching them by diving from perches, and is known for its territorial behavior. A fun fact is that it can see fish underwater by compensating for light refraction.
Common linnet: The Common linnet has streaked brown upperparts and a pinkish breast in males, with both sexes showing pale streaking. It inhabits open farmland, hedgerows, and scrubland across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists mainly of seeds, and it forages in flocks, often singing from exposed perches. A fun fact is that linnets were once kept for singing competitions in Europe.
Common loon:
Common loons have black-and-white spotted backs, white chests, and red eyes. They inhabit freshwater lakes and ponds in northern North America and Eurasia.  
Their diet consists mainly of fish, frogs, and insects, and they are territorial divers known for loud calls.  
A fun fact is that their haunting wail call can be heard over several kilometers across calm lake surfaces.
Common merganser:
Male Common mergansers have reddish heads and white bodies with black wings. Females are brown with a distinctive crest. They inhabit freshwater lakes, rivers, and coastal waters across northern continents.

They primarily eat fish, using their serrated bills to grip slippery prey. They dive underwater to hunt and often form large groups outside breeding season.

Their serrated bill edges help them hold onto fish, making them efficient underwater hunters.
Common moorhen: The Common moorhen has dark brown plumage, a red bill, and a distinctive white flank stripe. It inhabits freshwater wetlands including ponds, lakes, and marshes across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists of aquatic plants, insects, and small invertebrates, and it is typically shy and secretive. It can swim and dive underwater to escape danger.
Common murre: The Common murre has black upperparts and a white underbelly with a long, pointed bill. It nests on steep rocky cliffs across the North Atlantic and Pacific coasts and spends most of its life at sea. It feeds primarily on small fish like herring and capelin by diving underwater, often forming large breeding colonies. This bird can dive to depths of 180 meters to catch prey.
Common nighthawk: Common nighthawks have gray-brown plumage with white wing patches visible in flight. They inhabit open areas like grasslands, parks, and urban landscapes, often nesting on bare ground or gravel roofs. Their diet consists of flying insects caught mid-air during crepuscular activity. A fun fact is that males produce a distinctive booming sound during courtship dives using specialized wing feathers.
Common nightingale: The Common nightingale has brown upperparts, a pale breast, and a distinctive pale eyebrow stripe. It inhabits dense thickets, woodlands, and gardens across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and worms, and is renowned for its powerful, complex nocturnal song during the breeding season. Its song inspired countless poems and musical compositions.
Common pheasant: Male Common pheasants display vibrant plumage with iridescent necks and long tails. Females are brown and streaked for camouflage. They inhabit grasslands, farmlands, and forest edges across Europe and Asia, feeding on seeds, insects, and grains while foraging on the ground. Males perform loud calls and elaborate displays during breeding season. They were introduced to North America and are now a common game bird there.
Common pochard:
Male Common Pochards have a distinctive chestnut head and red eyes. Females are brown with a paler face. They inhabit freshwater lakes and ponds across Europe and Asia.  
They dive for aquatic plants, invertebrates, and small fish. They are social in winter but often solitary during breeding.  
A fun fact is that their population has declined significantly due to habitat loss and pollution.
Common quail: The Common quail is a small brown bird with black and white streaked head markings and a distinctive call. It inhabits grasslands, farmlands, and hedgerows across Europe, Asia, and Africa. Its diet consists mainly of seeds and insects, and it is shy, ground-dwelling, and secretive. A fun fact is its call sounds like "wet my whistle" to human ears.
Common raven: This large all-black bird has a wedge-shaped tail and a deep croaking call. It inhabits diverse environments from forests to cities across the Northern Hemisphere and feeds on carrion, insects, and small animals. Ravens are highly intelligent, using tools and solving complex problems, and they can mimic sounds including human speech.
Common redpoll: The Common redpoll has a small, stocky body with a distinctive red forehead patch, streaked brown breast, and pale underparts. It inhabits boreal forests and tundra in summer, moving to open woodlands and gardens in winter. Its diet consists mainly of seeds from birches, alders, and weeds, and it forages actively in flocks, often hanging upside down. It can eat snow to obtain water during cold weather.
Common redshank: The Common redshank has long red legs, a brown-streaked back, and a pale belly. It inhabits wetlands, mudflats, and coastal marshes across Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects, worms, and small crustaceans, foraging actively by probing mud with its bill and giving loud alarm calls. Its distinctive ringing "tchink" call is often heard before the bird is seen.
Common redstart:
Male Common redstarts have black heads, wings, and tails with bright orange-red lower backs and flanks. Females are browner with less red. They inhabit deciduous woodlands, parks, and gardens across Europe and Asia.  
They feed primarily on insects caught in flight or gleaned from trees, often flicking their tails while foraging.  
Males use their bright tail to distract predators during aerial displays.
Common reed bunting: This bird has a streaked brown back and a yellowish throat in males during breeding. It lives in reedbeds and wet meadows across Europe and Asia. Its diet includes seeds and insects, and it forages on the ground while singing from reed tops. Its distinctive call sounds like "chink-chink-chink."
Common reed warbler: This small brown bird has a streaked back and pale breast. It inhabits reed beds and wetlands across Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects and spiders while being secretive and vocal in dense vegetation. Its fun fact is that it undertakes one of the longest migratory journeys of any small bird, traveling over 5,000 kilometers each way.
Common ringed plover: This small shorebird has brown upperparts, white underparts, a black breast band, and a yellow eye ring. It nests on sandy beaches and mudflats across Europe and Asia. It feeds on small invertebrates like insects and worms by probing sand while running and stopping during foraging. Its distraction display involves feigning a broken wing to lead predators away from nests.
Common rock thrush: Adult males have gray-blue plumage with a white throat, while females are browner. They inhabit rocky cliffs and mountainsides across Eurasia, feeding on insects caught in flight or gleaned from rocks. This bird is known to mimic the calls of other species.
Common rosefinch:
Male Common rosefinches have striking pink or rose-colored heads and chests with brown backs. Females are duller brown with streaks. They inhabit temperate forests, gardens, and parks across Europe and Asia.  
Their diet consists mainly of seeds and insects, especially during breeding season. They are social birds often seen in small flocks.  
A fun fact is that their vibrant pink coloration in males inspired the common name of this bird.
Common sandpiper: The Common sandpiper has a brown back, white underparts, and a distinctive head-bobbing walk. It inhabits shallow freshwater and coastal areas, feeding on insects and small invertebrates. It exhibits a characteristic run-stop feeding motion and is known for its loud, ringing call during flight. A fun fact is that it often forages along water edges with a rapid, jerky movement, earning its common name.
Common scoter: Male Common scoters are entirely black with a distinctive yellow patch on the bill. They nest in boreal forests near water and spend winters on coastal marine waters. They dive for shellfish and other invertebrates, often forming large flocks during migration. Their call resembles a soft "whoo" sound, unusual for ducks.
Common shelduck: Common shelducks have striking black and white plumage with a chestnut back and a pale head. They inhabit coastal areas, estuaries, and wetlands across Europe and Asia, nesting in burrows. Their diet consists of aquatic plants, mollusks, and insects, and they are highly social, forming noisy groups. Their loud honking calls are so distinctive they gave the species its common name.
Common snipe:
The Common snipe has mottled brown and black plumage for camouflage and a long, straight bill. It inhabits wet meadows, marshes, and grassy fields across Europe and Asia.  
It feeds on insects, worms, and small invertebrates by probing mud with its bill.  
Its distinctive winnowing display during flight creates a loud, vibrating sound often mistaken for a ghostly noise.
Common starling: Common starlings have glossy black plumage with white speckles in winter and iridescent purple-green sheen in summer. They inhabit urban areas, farmlands, and woodlands across Europe and introduced regions worldwide. Their diet includes insects, fruits, and human food scraps, and they form large noisy flocks that forage together. They are famous for mimicking car alarms and other sounds.
Common swift: Common swifts have dark brown plumage, long swept-back wings, and a deeply forked tail. They nest in cliffs or buildings across Europe and Asia, migrating to Africa for winter. They eat flying insects caught mid-air, spending almost their entire lives in flight. They can sleep while flying.
Common tern: Common terns have gray backs, white fronts, black caps in summer, and slender red bills. They nest on coastal beaches and islands, migrating long distances to winter along tropical coasts. They feed primarily on small fish caught by plunge-diving and exhibit colonial nesting behavior. A fun fact is that some individuals migrate over twenty thousand miles annually between breeding and wintering grounds.
Common whitethroat: The Common whitethroat has brown upperparts, pale grey underparts, and a distinctive white throat patch. It inhabits scrublands, hedgerows, and bushy areas across Europe and Asia. It feeds mainly on insects in summer and berries in winter, often foraging actively in dense vegetation while singing a rapid, buzzy song. A fun fact is that its loud, repetitive song sounds like "wheet-wheet" and is often heard before the bird is seen.
Common wood pigeon: The Common wood pigeon is a large gray bird with a white neck patch and black tail bars. It inhabits woodlands, parks, and urban areas across Europe and Asia, feeding primarily on seeds, fruits, and crops. It is social and noisy, often seen in flocks, and known for its distinctive cooing call. A fun fact is that it is one of the most common birds in British gardens, sometimes considered a pest due to its crop damage.
Corn bunting: The Corn bunting is a brownish bird with streaked upperparts and a pale breast. It inhabits open farmland, grasslands, and cereal fields, especially during breeding. Its diet consists mainly of seeds and insects, and it forages on the ground while singing loudly from a perch. A fun fact is that its loud, repetitive song sounds like "corn, corn" which gave the bird its common name.
Corn crake: This brown bird with dark streaks blends into wet grasslands and cereal fields across Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects and plants, being secretive and active at night. Its loud 'crex crex' call, heard at dawn, gave it its common name.
Corsican finch:
The Corsican finch has a brown body with streaked back and a pale face. It inhabits open woodlands and scrublands on Corsica. Its diet includes seeds and insects, and it often forages in small flocks.  
A fun fact is that this bird was once classified as a subspecies of the common chaffinch.
Corsican nuthatch: This bird has a gray back, white underparts, and a black eye stripe. It lives exclusively in Corsica's mature pine forests, feeding on insects and pine seeds while climbing tree trunks. A fun fact is that it is the only nuthatch species endemic to a single island.
Corys shearwater: Cory's shearwater has dark brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a distinctive dark patch over the eye. It breeds on remote oceanic islands and spends most of its life far out at sea in the Atlantic and Mediterranean. It feeds primarily on fish and squid, often catching prey by surface seizing and occasionally diving deep. A fun fact is that it can dive underwater to catch prey, reaching depths of up to ten meters.
Cream-colored courser: The Cream-colored courser has pale sandy plumage with a white eye stripe and long legs for running. It inhabits arid deserts and dry grasslands across North Africa and the Middle East. It feeds primarily on insects and small invertebrates while moving swiftly on the ground. Its soft chuckle-like call is a distinctive feature heard at dawn and dusk.
Crested honey buzzard: The Crested honey buzzard has a brownish body with a distinctive dark crest, pale streaked throat, and broad wings. It inhabits forested regions across Asia, including India and Southeast Asia, often soaring high on thermals. Its diet primarily consists of wasp and bee larvae, which it locates by probing nests, and it exhibits solitary behavior except during breeding. A fun fact is that it can safely consume stinging insects due to its dense feathering and specialized feeding techniques.
Crested lark: Crested larks have a brown and streaky back, a pale eyebrow, and a distinctive short crest on their head. They inhabit open grasslands, farmlands, and dry fields across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists of seeds and insects, and they forage on the ground while singing loudly from perches. Their melodious song can often be heard from a considerable distance.
Crested tit: Crested tits have a black crest, white cheeks, and a black eye stripe on a grey body. They inhabit coniferous forests across Europe and Asia. Their diet includes insects, seeds, and berries, and they are active, often joining mixed-species flocks. They can mimic the calls of other birds.
Crowned sandgrouse: The Crowned sandgrouse has a distinctive dark crown and brown body with white streaks, blending into its dry habitat. It lives in arid savannas and semi-deserts across Africa, feeding mainly on seeds and occasionally insects. It travels daily to waterholes at dawn and dusk, and males carry water in specialized belly feathers to hydrate their chicks.
Curlew sandpiper: Curlew sandpipers have a slender build, long curved bill, and brownish streaked plumage in summer with white underparts. They breed on Arctic tundra and migrate to coastal mudflats worldwide. Their diet consists of small invertebrates found by probing in wet sand or mud, and they often feed in large flocks. They undertake one of the longest migrations of any shorebird, traveling up to ten thousand miles annually.
Cyprus scops owl: The Cyprus scops owl has brown plumage with distinctive ear tufts and a pale facial disc. It inhabits wooded areas, particularly pine forests, across the island of Cyprus. It hunts insects and small vertebrates at night, being solitary and territorial. This owl is the only breeding owl species endemic to Cyprus.
Cyprus warbler: The Cyprus warbler has grayish-brown upperparts, a pale eyebrow, and a white throat. It inhabits scrublands and woodlands across Cyprus. It feeds primarily on insects while foraging in dense vegetation. A fun fact is that it was previously classified as a subspecies of the lesser whitethroat.
Cyprus wheatear: The Cyprus wheatear has a gray back, white rump, and black wings. It inhabits dry, open scrublands and rocky hillsides across Cyprus. It feeds mainly on insects and spiders, often foraging on the ground and perching on rocks. Its melodious song is notably varied and pleasant for a wheatear.
Dalmatian pelican: Dalmatian pelicans have white bodies, black wings, and a pale head with an orange throat pouch. They inhabit shallow freshwater wetlands across Europe and Asia. They eat fish by scooping them with their large pouches and often feed in groups. Their necks are the longest among pelican species.
Dark chanting goshawk: Dark chanting goshawks have dark gray upperparts, pale throats, and white underparts with fine barring. They inhabit open woodlands, savannas, and bushlands across sub-Saharan Africa. They hunt small vertebrates and insects from perches, often displaying aggressive territorial behavior. Their distinctive loud, repeated "ch-ch-ch" calls give the species its common name.
Dartford warbler: The Dartford warbler has grey-brown upperparts, a pale throat, and a dark eye stripe. It inhabits lowland heathlands and scrubby areas, particularly in southern England and western Europe. It feeds mainly on insects and spiders, is highly territorial, and sings a loud, repetitive song. A fun fact is that this species has expanded its range northwards in Britain due to climate change and improved habitat management.
Demoiselle crane: The Demoiselle crane has gray plumage with white head markings and long legs, breeding in open grasslands across Asia and Europe. It eats insects, seeds, and small animals while forming large migratory flocks that perform elaborate courtship displays. They are known to migrate over the Himalayas at high altitudes.
Desert lark: The Desert lark has brown and buff plumage with streaked patterns for camouflage in sandy deserts. It inhabits arid regions like the Sahara, foraging on the ground for insects and seeds. Its behavior includes singing from low perches and forming small flocks. A fun fact is that its song sounds like a series of high-pitched, bubbling notes.
Desert sparrow: This small bird has brown streaked plumage and lives in hot, dry desert areas. It eats mostly seeds and insects, foraging in groups with loud calls. Fun fact: It can survive without drinking water by getting moisture from its food.
Desert wheatear: The Desert wheatear has a brownish back, white underparts, and a black mask around the eyes. It inhabits arid deserts and dry scrublands across North Africa and the Middle East. It feeds primarily on insects, foraging on the ground and perching on rocks or low shrubs. It can obtain sufficient moisture from its insect diet, eliminating the need for drinking water.
Double-spurred spurfowl: The Double-spurred spurfowl has brown plumage with white barring and distinctive double spurs on its legs. It inhabits dry savannas and grasslands across eastern Africa, feeding primarily on seeds, insects, and small fruits. It is a ground-dwelling bird that moves in small groups and is known for its loud, distinctive call. A fun fact is that its common name directly references the two spurs on its legs, which it uses during territorial disputes.
Dunlin: The Dunlin has a brownish back with black spots in summer, paler below, and breeds in Arctic tundra before migrating to coastal beaches. It feeds on invertebrates like worms and crustaceans by probing mudflats while foraging in flocks. Its distinctive call gives the species its name.
Dunnock: The dunnock is a small brown bird with a pale breast and streaked back, commonly found in gardens, woodlands, and hedgerows across Europe and Asia. It feeds mainly on insects and seeds, foraging quietly on the ground while often remaining hidden. Dunnocks are known for complex mating systems where males may mate with multiple females, and they have a distinctive soft, warbling song. A fun fact is that dunnocks are among the most promiscuous birds, with males frequently attempting to mate with females beyond their primary partner.
Duponts lark: Dupont's lark has pale brown streaked upperparts, a pale throat, and a distinct white eye stripe. It inhabits dry grasslands and agricultural fields across southern Europe and North Africa. Its diet includes insects and seeds, and it forages on the ground while singing loudly from perches. A fun fact is that its song is unusually loud for such a small bird.
Dusky thrush: The Dusky thrush has dark brown upperparts, a pale breast with dark streaks, and a prominent white eye-ring. It breeds in coniferous forests across northern Asia and winters in open woodlands and gardens. Its diet consists of insects, berries, and fruits, and it forages actively on the ground. This bird is noted for its melodious, flute-like song during the breeding season.
Dusky warbler: The Dusky warbler has dark brown upperparts, pale gray underparts, and a distinct pale eye ring. It inhabits dense shrubs and forests in eastern Asia during breeding, migrating to Southeast Asia for winter. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, moving restlessly through foliage while foraging. A fun fact is that it is one of the earliest warblers to return to its breeding grounds in spring.
Eastern Orphean warbler: The Eastern Orphean warbler has plain brown upperparts and a pale buff breast. It inhabits dry scrublands, open woodlands, and forest edges across southern Europe and western Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and is active, often flitting through dense vegetation while foraging. This species undertakes an impressive long-distance migration each year, traveling from Europe to sub-Saharan Africa.
Eastern black-eared wheatear: The Eastern black-eared wheatear has a pale brown upper body with a distinctive black patch behind each eye. It inhabits open, rocky, and arid landscapes across parts of Asia and Africa. It feeds primarily on insects caught on the ground and is often seen perching prominently on rocks or shrubs. This bird undertakes impressive long-distance migrations to wintering grounds in Africa.
Eastern imperial eagle: The Eastern imperial eagle has dark brown plumage with a pale neck patch and yellow eyes. It inhabits open woodlands, steppes, and grasslands across Eurasia, avoiding dense forests. It hunts mammals like rodents and hares by soaring and diving, often remaining solitary except during breeding. A fun fact is that it migrates long distances, sometimes crossing the Himalayas.
Eastern olivaceous warbler:
This small warbler has olive-green upperparts and pale yellow underparts. It inhabits scrublands, forests, and gardens across eastern Europe and western Asia. It feeds primarily on insects gleaned from foliage and is active in the canopy during migration.

Its loud, repetitive song is a key identification feature in its breeding range.
Eastern rock nuthatch:
It has gray upperparts, a pale breast, and a distinct black eye stripe.  
It inhabits rocky cliffs and mountainous regions across Asia, feeding on insects and seeds while moving headfirst down rock faces.  
Fun fact: It can climb down vertical surfaces headfirst without slipping, a rare skill among birds.
Eastern yellow wagtail: It has bright yellow underparts and olive-green upperparts, constantly wagging its tail while foraging. It breeds in wet meadows and rice paddies across northern Asia, feeding primarily on insects caught on the ground or in flight. A fun fact is that its distinctive call sounds like a sharp repeated "wheet."
Egyptian goose: Egyptian geese have brown bodies with white faces, necks, and chest patches, and distinctive black-and-white wing feathers. They inhabit wetlands, rivers, and lakes across Africa and introduced regions like Europe, feeding on grasses, seeds, and insects. Known for strong pair bonds and loud calls, they often form large flocks outside breeding season. A fun fact is that they were introduced to the United Kingdom in the 18th century and now have a thriving wild population.
Egyptian nightjar: The Egyptian nightjar has mottled brown and gray plumage that provides excellent camouflage on the ground. It inhabits open savannas, deserts, and grasslands across Africa and southwestern Asia. It feeds primarily on flying insects at dusk and night, nesting directly on the ground with minimal cover. Its cryptic resting posture often makes it appear like a pile of leaves.
Egyptian vulture: The Egyptian vulture has pale yellowish plumage, a white head, and dark flight feathers. It inhabits open grasslands, savannas, and agricultural areas across Africa, Europe, and Asia. It primarily feeds on carrion but also eats eggs and insects, often foraging in groups. A fun fact is that it is one of the few bird species known to use tools, such as dropping stones to break ostrich eggs.
Eleonoras falcon: This falcon has dark brown upperparts and pale underparts with a distinctive white head patch. It nests on rocky cliffs across the Mediterranean Sea and hunts insects and small birds in mid-air. A fun fact is that it times its breeding to coincide with the autumn migration of songbirds, providing abundant food for chicks.
Eurasian blackcap: The Eurasian blackcap has a dark cap on males and a brown cap on females, with olive-brown upperparts and a pale underbelly. It inhabits woodlands, gardens, and shrubby areas across Europe and Asia, migrating to sub-Saharan Africa for winter. It feeds on insects, berries, and fruits, often singing from high perches during the breeding season. A fun fact is that blackcaps can sing at night while migrating, possibly to navigate or avoid predators.
Eurasian blue tit: The Eurasian blue tit has a distinctive blue cap, white cheeks, and a black eye stripe against a yellow breast. It inhabits woodlands, gardens, and parks across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on insects, seeds, and berries, displaying active and acrobatic foraging behavior. This bird can recognize human faces and remember food locations for months.
Eurasian bullfinch: The Eurasian bullfinch has a short tail and a chunky body with a distinctive pink breast in males and a duller brownish appearance in females. It inhabits woodlands, parks, and gardens across Europe and Asia, feeding mainly on seeds and tree buds. It is a shy bird often seen in small flocks, known for its strong beak used to crack seeds. A fun fact is that bullfinches can eat seeds with hard shells that other birds cannot open.
Eurasian collared dove: The Eurasian collared dove has a pale gray body, pink legs, and a distinctive black collar around its neck. It inhabits urban areas, parks, and farmlands across Europe, Asia, and North America. It feeds mainly on seeds and grains and is often seen in pairs or small groups, making soft cooing calls. This species rapidly expanded its range in North America after being introduced in the 1980s.
Eurasian coot: The Eurasian coot is a dark grey-black waterbird with a prominent white shield on its forehead. It inhabits freshwater ponds, lakes, and marshes across Europe and Asia, feeding primarily on aquatic plants and small invertebrates. It is highly aquatic, diving for food and displaying strong territorial behavior during breeding. A fun fact is that coots create distinctive mud footprints when walking on soft shores.
Eurasian crag martin: This small bird has gray-brown upperparts, a pale throat, and a slightly forked tail. It nests on cliffs and buildings across Europe and Asia. It feeds on flying insects while foraging in flight, often in small groups. Its mud nests are remarkably sturdy and sometimes reused for multiple broods.
Eurasian curlew: The Eurasian curlew has a long curved bill, brown streaked plumage, and a distinctive long neck. It inhabits wetlands, grasslands, and coastal mudflats across Europe and Asia, migrating to coastal areas in winter.
