It feeds on invertebrates like worms and insects by probing mud, and is known for its loud, far-carrying call. Its call is so loud it can be heard over two kilometers away.
Eurasian dotterel: The Eurasian dotterel has black-and-white head markings and streaked brown breast feathers. It breeds in open tundra and moorlands across northern Europe and Asia, migrating to southern Europe and Africa for winter. It feeds primarily on insects and invertebrates found on the ground, displaying lekking behavior where males compete for females. A fun fact is that its name comes from the Middle English word for "little dotter," describing the spotted pattern on its breast.
Eurasian eagle-owl: The Eurasian eagle-owl has a large size, dark brown plumage with white markings, prominent ear tufts, and yellow eyes. It inhabits forests, rocky areas, and sometimes urban outskirts across Europe and Asia. It hunts primarily mammals like rodents and rabbits at night, is solitary and territorial, and often perches on high points to observe its territory. Its hearing is so acute it can locate prey under snow or dense foliage.
Eurasian golden oriole: Males have bright yellow plumage with black wings and tail, while females are olive-green; they inhabit deciduous forests across Europe and Asia. They feed on insects, fruits, and nectar, foraging high in tree canopies and known for their loud, flute-like songs during breeding. A fun fact is that their distinctive song inspired the name "oriole" meaning "golden" in some languages.
Eurasian hobby: The Eurasian hobby has a slender body, long pointed wings, and a dark facial mask. It inhabits open landscapes across Europe and Asia, nesting in trees or cliffs. It feeds primarily on insects like dragonflies and swifts, catching them mid-air with agile flight and sharp dives. This bird can reach speeds over 100 kilometers per hour while pursuing prey.
Eurasian hoopoe: The Eurasian hoopoe has a distinctive curved crest of feathers, brown body with white and black wing patterns, and a long bill. It inhabits open woodlands, grasslands, and gardens across Europe, Asia, and North Africa. Its diet consists mainly of insects, spiders, and worms, which it finds by probing the ground with its bill, and it is known for its undulating flight and loud call. A fun fact is that hoopoes have a foul-smelling secretion from a gland near their tail used to deter predators.
Eurasian jay: The Eurasian jay has grey-blue wings, a reddish-brown back, and a black stripe through its eye. It inhabits woodlands, forests, and parks across Europe and Asia. It eats insects, nuts, fruits, and seeds, and caches food for winter while being vocal and somewhat shy. It can mimic the calls of other birds including hawks.
Eurasian magpie: The Eurasian magpie has distinct black and white plumage with glossy green and blue wing feathers. It inhabits woodlands, farmlands, and urban parks across Europe and Asia. It eats insects, small mammals, fruits, and human food scraps, showing high intelligence in problem-solving and social interactions. A fun fact is that magpies can recognize themselves in mirrors, demonstrating self-awareness rare among birds.
Eurasian nuthatch: The Eurasian nuthatch has a blue-gray back, rust-colored flanks, and a black eye stripe. It inhabits mature forests, especially coniferous or mixed woodlands across Europe and Asia. Its diet includes insects, seeds, and nuts, and it uniquely climbs tree trunks headfirst. It caches food in bark crevices for later retrieval.
Eurasian oystercatcher: The Eurasian oystercatcher has black upperparts, white underparts, a long red bill, and red legs. It inhabits coastal shores, nesting on sandy or rocky beaches and feeding in intertidal zones. Its diet primarily consists of mollusks, which it probes for and pries open with its bill, often calling loudly while defending territory. A fun fact is that it sometimes uses tools like stones to break open shellfish.
Eurasian penduline tit: The Eurasian penduline tit has a black and white head pattern, a pale yellow breast, and greyish upperparts. It inhabits reedbeds and willow thickets near freshwater wetlands across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists mainly of insects and spiders, and it builds distinctive hanging nests suspended from branches. It is the only European bird that builds such pendulous nests.
Eurasian pygmy owl: This small owl has brown mottled plumage with white streaks and a rounded head. It inhabits coniferous and mixed forests across Europe and Asia. It hunts small mammals, insects, and birds at dawn and dusk from a perch, being solitary and territorial. A fun fact is that it can rotate its head nearly 180 degrees to scan for prey.
Eurasian scops owl: The Eurasian scops owl has mottled brown plumage with ear tufts and large eyes for camouflage in trees. It inhabits open woodlands, forests, and gardens across Europe and Asia, nesting in tree cavities. It hunts insects like moths and beetles at night, being mostly silent and elusive during the day. Its mottled brown feathers make it nearly invisible against tree bark.
Eurasian siskin: Eurasian siskins have greenish-yellow bodies, black and white wing bars, and a bright yellow rump. They inhabit coniferous and mixed forests across Europe and Asia, often moving to lower elevations in winter. Their diet consists mainly of tree seeds, and they feed acrobatically in flocks. They readily visit bird feeders offering sunflower seeds.
Eurasian skylark: The Eurasian skylark has brown streaked plumage for camouflage in open ground. It inhabits grasslands, farmlands, and meadows across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists of seeds and insects, and it is renowned for its soaring flight display while singing loudly from high altitudes. A fun fact is that it can sing continuously for several minutes while ascending to great heights.
Eurasian sparrowhawk: The Eurasian sparrowhawk has a slender body with short rounded wings, reddish barring on the chest in males, and brown upperparts in females. It inhabits woodlands, forests, and sometimes gardens across Europe and Asia. It hunts small birds primarily, using explosive short flights from cover, and is highly territorial. A fun fact is that females often hunt larger prey than males due to their greater size.
Eurasian spoonbill: The Eurasian spoonbill has a distinctive white plumage and a long, flattened, spoon-shaped bill. It inhabits shallow wetlands, estuaries, and marshes across Europe and Asia, feeding on small fish and aquatic invertebrates by sweeping its bill side-to-side. It nests colonially in trees or reeds and is migratory. Fun fact: Its unique bill shape allows it to efficiently filter food from water while moving slowly through shallow areas.
Eurasian stone-curlew: The Eurasian stone-curlew has sandy-brown plumage with white underparts and large yellow eyes. It inhabits open, dry grasslands, steppes, and cultivated fields across Europe and Asia. It feeds mainly on insects and other invertebrates at night, being largely nocturnal and secretive during the day. Its loud, distinctive call resembling a curlew gives the species its common name.
Eurasian teal:
Male Eurasian teals have a distinctive green head patch and chestnut flanks. Females are brown with a pale face stripe. They inhabit freshwater wetlands across Europe and Asia.  
They feed on aquatic plants, insects, and small crustaceans by dabbling in shallow water. They form large flocks during migration and breeding.  
Their rapid, low flight is among the fastest of all ducks.
Eurasian three-toed woodpecker:
This woodpecker has black and white barred plumage with a red crown patch. It inhabits mature coniferous forests across northern Europe and Asia. Its diet consists of wood-boring insects, and it forages by climbing tree trunks, drumming loudly to communicate.  
A fun fact is that it uniquely has three toes on each foot, unlike most woodpeckers which have four.
Eurasian tree sparrow: The Eurasian tree sparrow has a chestnut crown, gray face, and a black throat patch. It inhabits human settlements, farmlands, and parks across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists of seeds and insects, and it often forages in flocks, nesting in tree cavities or building crevices. A fun fact is that it readily adapts to urban environments, frequently seen near buildings and feeders.
Eurasian treecreeper: Eurasian treecreepers have brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a long curved bill. They inhabit mature woodlands and forests, foraging on tree trunks for insects and spiders by climbing in a spiral pattern. They often follow woodpeckers to catch disturbed prey. A fun fact is they can climb headfirst down tree trunks.
Eurasian whimbrel: The Eurasian whimbrel has a brownish back with dark streaks, a long curved bill, and a white underbelly. It inhabits wetlands and tundra breeding grounds across northern Europe and Asia, migrating to coastal areas in Africa and South Asia for winter. Its diet consists of invertebrates like worms and insects, and it forages by probing mudflats with its distinctive bill. This bird holds the record for the longest non-stop flight of any shorebird, covering over 5,000 kilometers during migration.
Eurasian wigeon: Eurasian wigeon males have a chestnut head, white forehead, and a green patch on the crown. They inhabit shallow freshwater wetlands, ponds, and marshes across Europe and Asia. They feed primarily on aquatic vegetation and grasses, often grazing in flocks and being vocal during migration. A fun fact is that they are sometimes called 'baldpates' due to the white patch on the male's head.
Eurasian woodcock: The Eurasian woodcock has cryptic brown and black mottled plumage for forest camouflage and a long straight bill for probing soil. It inhabits damp woodlands and forests, feeding primarily on earthworms and insects during twilight. Its courtship display involves a spiraling flight with a distinctive buzzing sound produced by wing beats.
Eurasian wren: The Eurasian wren is a small brown bird with a short tail and a pale eyebrow stripe. It inhabits woodlands, gardens, and dense hedgerows across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, exhibiting energetic foraging and a loud, complex song despite its tiny size. Its song is remarkably loud for its body size, often heard before the bird is seen.
Eurasian wryneck: The Eurasian wryneck has brown and gray barred plumage with a pale throat and short tail. It inhabits open woodlands and farmlands across Europe and Asia, nesting in tree cavities and migrating to Africa for winter. Its diet consists mainly of ants and other insects, and it is known for twisting its neck unnaturally. It can mimic the sound of a woodpecker drumming with its beak.
European bee-eater: The European bee-eater has vibrant green and yellow plumage, a reddish head, and long tail streamers. It inhabits open country with sandy banks for nesting, often near meadows or farmland. It feeds exclusively on bees and wasps caught mid-air, displaying social nesting and vocal communication. A fun fact is that it removes stingers from bees before eating them.
European golden plover: It has a golden-brown back and black face mask in summer, fading to grey in winter, and inhabits open grasslands and tundra during breeding. It feeds on insects, worms, and seeds in flocks, running and stopping while foraging. Its distinctive call inspired the common name plover.
European goldfinch: The European goldfinch has a distinctive red face, black and white wings, and a bright yellow wing bar. It inhabits gardens, parks, and open woodlands across Europe and western Asia, feeding mainly on seeds from thistles and other plants. It is highly social, often seen in flocks, and known for its cheerful, complex song. A fun fact is that it was historically popular as a cage bird due to its attractive appearance and pleasant singing.
European green woodpecker: This bird has bright green upperparts, a red crown, and a yellow face patch. It inhabits deciduous and mixed forests across Europe, foraging on the ground for ants. Its diet consists mainly of ants, which it extracts with a long sticky tongue. A fun fact is that it is sometimes called the 'yaffle' due to its loud, laughing call.
European greenfinch: The European greenfinch has green body plumage with yellow wing and tail markings. It inhabits woodlands, gardens, and farmlands across Europe and western Asia. Its diet consists mainly of seeds, and it feeds in noisy, social flocks. A fun fact is that it is a popular bird for captivity in some regions due to its hardiness.
European herring gull: European herring gulls have gray backs, white heads, and yellow bills with a red spot. They nest on coastal cliffs, beaches, and urban areas across northern Europe and North America. Their diet includes fish, insects, carrion, and human food waste, and they are highly vocal scavengers. They can recognize individual human faces and remember them for years.
European honey buzzard: The European honey buzzard has a brownish body with a pale head and distinctive barred underwings. It inhabits woodlands across Europe and migrates to sub-Saharan Africa. Its diet consists primarily of wasp and hornet larvae, which it locates by probing nests, and it soars extensively during migration. A fun fact is that it avoids bee stings by covering its face with feathers while feeding.
European nightjar: The European nightjar has mottled brown and gray plumage that provides excellent camouflage on forest floors. It inhabits open woodlands and heathlands across Europe and Asia, nesting directly on the ground. It feeds on flying insects like moths and beetles, hunting at dusk and night with wide mouths. Its churring call is a common sound in summer evenings. A fun fact is that it can swallow insects whole while flying, and its name 'goatsucker' comes from a now-discredited myth about drinking goat's milk.
European pied flycatcher: Male European pied flycatchers have black and white plumage with a white eyebrow, while females are brownish. They breed in deciduous and mixed forests across Europe, nesting in tree cavities. They feed primarily on insects caught in mid-air, often perching to watch for prey before darting out, and are migratory, spending winters in Africa. A fun fact is that males often sing from prominent perches to attract females and defend territories.
European robin: The European robin has a distinctive red breast, brown back, and white eye stripe. It inhabits woodlands, gardens, and parks across Europe, feeding on insects, worms, and berries while defending territories through song. Its bright red breast made it a popular symbol on British Christmas cards.
European roller: The European roller has vibrant blue and brown plumage with a long tail. It inhabits open woodlands and farmlands across Europe and Africa, migrating seasonally. It feeds primarily on insects caught in aerial acrobatics and nests in tree cavities. A fun fact is that rollers sometimes line their nests with mud to deter predators.
European serin: The European serin has a greenish-yellow body with a pale stripe above its eye. It inhabits open woodlands, farmlands, and gardens across Europe. It feeds primarily on seeds and forages in small social flocks. Its cheerful, high-pitched song is a common sound in its habitat.
European shag: The European shag has dark black plumage with a green sheen, a prominent crest, and a long hooked bill. It inhabits rocky coastlines across Europe, nesting on cliffs and diving for fish in the sea. Its diet consists mainly of fish like herring and sand eels, and it is highly territorial during breeding. A fun fact is that it shakes water from its feathers vigorously after diving, creating a distinctive splashing sound.
European stonechat: The European stonechat has a stocky build with males displaying black upperparts and a chestnut breast. It inhabits open country like heathlands, coastal scrub, and farmland across Europe and western Asia. Its diet consists of insects and spiders, and it perches prominently on low bushes or rocks while calling loudly. A fun fact is that stonechats often flick their wings while perched, a behavior thought to signal territory or attract mates.
European storm petrel: The European storm petrel has a dark brown body, white rump, and long wings. It inhabits the North Atlantic and Mediterranean seas, nesting on remote offshore islands. It feeds on plankton and small fish by skimming the ocean surface, often flying low and erratically. Its name comes from sailors' belief that it heralds storms, though it actually thrives in rough seas.
European turtle dove: The European turtle dove has a gray-brown back, pale pink breast, and a black-and-white neck ring. It inhabits open woodlands, farmlands, and gardens across Europe and parts of Asia. It feeds mainly on seeds and berries, forming long-term monogamous pairs that coo softly while nesting in trees. Its soft, repetitive cooing call inspired its common name.
Eyebrowed thrush: The Eyebrowed thrush has a brown back, a distinct white eyebrow, and pale underparts, inhabiting forested mountain areas across East Asia. It forages on the ground for insects and berries, often in small groups during migration. Its melodious song is a notable feature heard during its long seasonal movements.
Feral pigeon: Feral pigeons are typically gray with a white rump and iridescent neck feathers, often with dark wing bars. They live in urban areas, nesting on buildings and feeding on seeds, grains, and human food waste. They are social birds that forage in flocks and can navigate using Earth's magnetic field. A fun fact is that they can recognize themselves in mirrors, indicating self-awareness.
Ferruginous duck: Males have a rich reddish-brown body and dark head with a white eye patch, while females are mottled brown. They inhabit freshwater wetlands, lakes, and ponds across Eurasia, feeding primarily on aquatic plants and small invertebrates. They are shy divers often seen alone or in small groups, and a fun fact is that they produce a distinctive soft 'whoo' call.
Fieldfare: Fieldfare has a brown back, speckled breast, and an orange face patch. It inhabits woodlands, parks, and farmlands across Europe, especially in winter. Its diet includes berries, insects, and worms, and it is highly social, forming noisy flocks. They form noisy winter flocks that can number in the hundreds.
Finschs wheatear: Finschs wheatear has a gray head and back, white throat, and brown wings, favoring dry rocky habitats across East Africa. It feeds on insects found on the ground, often perching upright on rocks to scan for prey. A fun fact is that its name stems from a historical misunderstanding about eating wheat, though it primarily consumes insects.
Forsters tern: Forster's tern has a white body, gray back, and black head cap in breeding season with a red bill. It nests in colonies on wetlands and coastal areas, feeding on small fish and insects by plunge-diving. It frequently steals food from other birds through kleptoparasitism.
Franklins gull: Franklin's gull has a gray back, white head with a black cap in summer, and red legs. It breeds in prairie wetlands and grasslands across North America, migrating to coastal areas and large lakes in winter. Its diet includes insects, fish, and small invertebrates, and it feeds by skimming water or diving while in large, noisy flocks. A fun fact is that it is one of the few gulls known to catch insects while flying.
Fulvous babbler: The Fulvous babbler has a buffy-brown body with a pale throat and dark eye stripe. It inhabits subtropical and tropical forests in Southeast Asia, often foraging in dense undergrowth. It feeds mainly on insects and small invertebrates while moving in noisy, social groups. Its loud, chattering calls resemble a group of people talking.
Gadwall: Gadwall males have gray bodies with black tails and white wing patches, while females are brownish. They inhabit freshwater wetlands, ponds, and marshes across Europe and North America. They feed on aquatic plants, seeds, and small invertebrates by dabbling on the water surface. Gadwalls are known for their unusually quiet flight compared to other ducks.
Garden warbler: Garden warblers are small brown birds with a pale eyebrow stripe and a pale throat. They inhabit woodlands, gardens, and hedgerows across Europe, migrating to sub-Saharan Africa for winter. They eat insects and berries, often foraging in dense foliage and singing a loud, repetitive song. A fun fact is that their song sounds remarkably like the word "garden" when heard clearly.
Garganey: Male Garganeys have a distinctive green head with a white stripe and brown back while females are brownish. They breed in shallow wetlands across Europe and Asia and migrate to Africa and South Asia. They feed on aquatic plants and small invertebrates by dabbling in water. A fun fact is that the name Garganey comes from an old word for a type of duck.
Glaucous gull: Glaucous gulls have pale gray backs and wings with white underparts and pale yellow eyes. They inhabit Arctic regions breeding on tundra coasts and migrate to northern coastal areas in winter. They eat fish, carrion, and scavenge human food, often displaying bold and aggressive feeding behavior. A fun fact is they frequently steal food from other seabirds through kleptoparasitism.
Glossy ibis: The Glossy ibis has dark iridescent plumage showing green and purple sheen, a long curved bill, and reddish legs. It inhabits wetlands, marshes, and coastal areas, feeding on insects, small fish, and amphibians by probing mud. It often forages in groups and nests colonially in trees or reeds. A fun fact is its feathers display a metallic sheen that shifts color with the light angle.
Goldcrest: Goldcrests have greenish upperparts, pale underparts, and a distinctive bright yellow or orange crown stripe. They inhabit coniferous forests across Europe and Asia, often foraging in the upper branches of trees. Their diet consists mainly of small insects and spiders, and they are highly active, constantly moving through foliage. Goldcrests are Europe's smallest bird species and undertake long migratory journeys.
Golden eagle: Golden eagles have dark brown bodies with distinctive golden-brown feathers on their heads and necks. They inhabit mountainous regions across North America, Europe, and Asia, preferring open or forested areas. They primarily hunt mammals like rabbits and ground squirrels, using powerful flight and keen eyesight to hunt alone. They can spot prey from over a kilometer away.
Golden pheasant:
Male Golden pheasants display vivid orange and gold plumage with red crests and black patterns. Females are brown and streaked for camouflage. They inhabit mountainous coniferous and mixed forests in central China.  
Their diet includes seeds, fruits, insects, and plant matter foraged on the forest floor. They are shy, ground-dwelling birds that move quietly through dense undergrowth.  
A fun fact is that their striking feathers were historically used in Chinese imperial robes for ceremonial purposes.
Graceful prinia: The Graceful Prinia is a small brown bird with a pale breast and a long tail found in grasslands and scrub habitats across South Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, foraging actively in dense vegetation while constantly flicking its tail. Its name originates from its repetitive call that sounds like 'prinia-prinia'.
Gray-cheeked thrush: This thrush has a gray face, brown back, and a spotted white breast. It breeds in boreal forests, eats insects and berries, and forages quietly on the forest floor. It makes nonstop flights across the Gulf of Mexico during migration.
Great bittern: The Great bittern has brown and buff plumage with dark streaks, blending perfectly into reed beds. It inhabits freshwater wetlands across Europe and Asia, preferring dense reed growth. It feeds primarily on fish, amphibians, and insects, often standing motionless before striking. Its booming call, heard during spring, sounds like a deep "bonk" and can carry over long distances.
Great black-backed gull: The Great black-backed gull has a dark gray back, white head and underparts, yellow bill with a red spot, and powerful wings. It inhabits coastal areas across North America and Europe, nesting on cliffs or beaches and foraging along shorelines. Its diet includes fish, crustaceans, eggs, carrion, and it is known for aggressive feeding and stealing food from other birds. A fun fact is that it regularly steals fish from cormorants and other seabirds.
Great bustard: The Great bustard is a large bird with males featuring a pale breast, dark neck ruff, and significantly larger size than females. It inhabits open grasslands and steppes across Europe and Asia, avoiding dense forests. Its diet consists mainly of plants, seeds, and insects, and it exhibits lekking behavior where males display for females. Males can weigh up to twenty kilograms making them among the heaviest flying birds.
Great cormorant: Great cormorants are large dark birds with a hooked bill and bare facial skin. They inhabit coastal waters, lakes, and rivers worldwide. They dive for fish, their primary diet, and often gather in large colonies. They can swallow fish whole without regurgitating bones.
Great crested grebe: The Great crested grebe has a striking breeding plumage with a prominent orange crest, a reddish neck, and black-and-white facial markings. It inhabits freshwater lakes and ponds with abundant vegetation across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on fish and aquatic invertebrates, performing elaborate courtship displays including synchronized head-throwing. A fun fact is that it performs a 'weed dance' during mating, where pairs carry aquatic plants while swimming side by side.
Great egret: The Great egret is a large, all-white heron with a long neck, dark legs, and a dagger-like bill. It inhabits wetlands including marshes, ponds, and shorelines across North America. It feeds primarily on fish, amphibians, and insects, often standing motionless to ambush prey. Its historical near extinction due to plume hunting in the early 1900s helped spur the American conservation movement.
Great grey owl: The Great grey owl has pale gray plumage with dark streaks and a large facial disc. It inhabits dense coniferous forests across northern North America and Eurasia. It primarily hunts small mammals like voles by listening for movement under snow, often perching silently for long periods. Its feathers are exceptionally soft, making its flight nearly silent.
Great grey shrike: The Great grey shrike has a grey body with black wings and a distinct dark facial mask. It inhabits open woodlands, tundra, and scrublands across northern Eurasia and North America. It hunts insects and small vertebrates, often impaling prey on thorns to store for later. A fun fact is that it mimics the calls of other birds to attract prey or confuse rivals.
Great reed warbler: The Great reed warbler has brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a pale eyebrow stripe. It inhabits reedbeds and wetlands across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists of insects and spiders, and it sings loudly from reed stems while being shy and secretive. It is known for its complex, varied song that can include mimicry of other birds.
Great shearwater: Great shearwaters have dark brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a prominent white rump. They inhabit the open ocean year-round, breeding on remote subantarctic islands. Their diet consists of fish, squid, and crustaceans, and they exhibit long-distance migration with dynamic, banking flight. They are known to be attracted to artificial lights at night, sometimes causing mass beach strandings.
Great skua: The Great skua is a large, dark brown seabird with a robust build and distinctive pale markings on its wings. It breeds on rocky coasts and islands across northern Europe and North America, then migrates widely over open ocean. It is an aggressive predator and kleptoparasite, stealing food from other birds and eating fish, squid, and small seals. Fun fact: It is known to harass much larger birds like gulls and eagles to steal their catches.
Great snipe: The Great snipe has brown and black streaked plumage with a pale face and a white eye stripe. It inhabits wet grasslands, marshes, and tundra breeding grounds across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists of insects, worms, and seeds, and it displays lekking behavior where males perform aerial courtship flights. A fun fact is that Great snipes are among the fastest migrating birds, reaching speeds over 100 kilometers per hour during their long journeys.
Great spotted cuckoo: The Great spotted cuckoo has a dark grey back, white underparts, and distinctive black and white wing patterns. It inhabits woodlands, parks, and open countryside across Europe and western Asia. It eats insects like caterpillars and beetles and is a brood parasite, laying eggs in other birds' nests. Its loud, laughing call is a common sound in its habitat.
Great spotted woodpecker: The Great spotted woodpecker has black and white plumage with a bright red patch on the male's head. It inhabits woodlands, parks, and gardens across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on insects like wood-boring beetles, foraging by pecking bark and drumming on trees. Its drumming pattern is loud and rapid, often heard before the bird is seen.
Great tit: The Great tit has a distinctive black head with white cheeks, a yellow breast, and greenish back. It inhabits woodlands, gardens, and parks across Europe and Asia. It eats insects, seeds, and berries, and is known for its bold, adaptable behavior including hanging upside down. Great tits can recognize and remember human faces.
Great white pelican: The Great white pelican is a large white bird with pinkish legs and a massive yellow bill. It inhabits shallow wetlands across Africa, Europe, and Asia, often nesting colonially on islands. It feeds primarily on fish, using cooperative techniques to herd prey into shallow water. A fun fact is that these birds can fly long distances, sometimes over 100 kilometers in a single day.
Greater flamingo: Greater flamingos have long pink legs, a curved neck, and pink plumage that deepens with age. They inhabit shallow coastal lagoons, salt flats, and mudflats across Africa, Asia, and Europe. Their diet consists of brine shrimp, algae, and small invertebrates filtered through their specialized beaks, and they often feed in large, noisy groups. Their pink coloration comes from carotenoid pigments in their food.
Greater hoopoe-lark: The Greater hoopoe-lark has a brownish body with a distinct short crest and pale underparts. It inhabits dry grasslands, deserts, and open scrublands across southern Asia. It feeds on insects and seeds while foraging on the ground, often bobbing its head and singing loudly. Its repetitive call sounds like "hoopoe-hoopoe" giving it its common name.
Greater painted-snipe: The Greater painted-snipe has bold chestnut and black plumage with white markings on the wings, particularly noticeable in males. It inhabits shallow freshwater wetlands, marshes, and rice paddies across Asia and Africa. It feeds on insects, worms, and small crustaceans, foraging alone or in pairs at dawn and dusk. Females are larger and more brightly colored than males.
Greater sand plover: The Greater sand plover has a brownish back, white underparts, and a dark eye stripe in breeding plumage. It inhabits sandy beaches, mudflats, and coastal areas across Asia and Africa, migrating long distances. Its diet consists of insects, worms, and small crustaceans, which it finds by running and probing the ground. A fun fact is that it undertakes one of the longest annual migrations of any shorebird, traveling up to 10,000 kilometers between breeding and wintering grounds.
Greater scaup:
Male Greater scaups have a glossy green head, black breast, and white body. Females are brown with a pale face. They inhabit northern freshwater lakes in summer and coastal marine waters in winter.

They dive for aquatic invertebrates and plants like mollusks and aquatic vegetation. They are social, forming large flocks during migration and winter.

Their name comes from the Old English word for "duck," meaning "scaup" refers to their diving habit.
Greater short-toed lark: The Greater short-toed lark has brown-streaked upperparts, pale underparts, and a short bill. It inhabits open grasslands, agricultural fields, and dry steppes across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on seeds and insects, foraging on the ground and performing distinctive singing flights. Its song, delivered while ascending in a spiral, is a notable behavior.
Greater spotted eagle: The Greater spotted eagle has dark brown plumage with prominent white patches on its wings and a paler head. It inhabits wetlands, grasslands, and open woodlands across Asia and Europe, often near water. It hunts small mammals, birds, and insects, typically soaring high before diving. It undertakes long migrations, traveling thousands of kilometers from breeding grounds to wintering areas in Africa and South Asia.
Greater white-fronted goose: The Greater white-fronted goose has a brown body, white face patch, and pink bill. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters in grasslands and agricultural fields across temperate zones. Its diet consists of grasses, grains, and aquatic plants, and it forms large, noisy flocks during migration. Its loud, honking calls are often heard for miles during flight.
Greater yellowlegs: Greater yellowlegs have long yellow legs, brown upperparts, and white underparts streaked with dark markings. They inhabit wetlands, shorelines, and mudflats year-round, foraging for insects, fish, and crustaceans by stalking through shallow water. They are among the fastest migrating shorebirds, capable of sustained flight speeds over fifty miles per hour.
Green sandpiper: Green sandpipers have greenish-brown upperparts, a pale breast with dark streaks, and a short, straight bill. They forage rapidly in shallow water, probing mud for insects and small invertebrates. They breed in wetlands across northern Europe and Asia, migrating to Africa and southern Asia for winter. Their distinctive high-pitched "wheet" call is often heard before the bird is seen.
Greenish warbler: This small warbler has greenish upperparts and yellowish underparts. It breeds in coniferous forests across Eurasia and feeds primarily on insects. It forages actively in trees and sings a thin song from perches. A fun fact is that its population forms a nearly complete ring around the Tibetan Plateau, with different subspecies meeting only at the ends of the ring.
Grey heron: The Grey heron has grey plumage, a long neck, and a yellow bill. It inhabits wetlands, rivers, and lakes across Europe and Asia. It hunts fish, amphibians, and small mammals by standing motionless for long periods. A fun fact is that it moves with remarkable slowness while hunting.
Grey hypocolius: The Grey hypocolius has gray plumage with a pale face and dark eyes. It inhabits arid scrublands and gardens across the Middle East and North Africa. Its diet consists of berries and insects, and it is often seen in small flocks. A fun fact is that its name comes from its distinctive call, which sounds like "hypo".
Grey partridge: The Grey partridge has a plump body with grey-brown plumage, a pale face, and a black band across the throat. It inhabits farmland with crops and hedgerows across Europe and Asia. Its diet includes seeds, insects, and vegetation, and it forms coveys while foraging on the ground. It is a traditional symbol of the British countryside, often associated with rural landscapes and hunting.
Grey plover: The Grey plover has grey upperparts, white underparts, and a distinctive black breast band in summer. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters on coastal mudflats and beaches worldwide. It feeds on invertebrates like insects and crustaceans by probing and running along shorelines. A fun fact is that it undertakes some of the longest non-stop migrations of any bird, covering over 10,000 kilometers.
Grey wagtail: The Grey wagtail has a grey back, bright yellow underparts, and constantly wags its long tail while perched. It inhabits rivers, streams, and wetlands across Europe and Asia, feeding primarily on insects caught in flight or picked from water surfaces. This active bird is often seen hopping on rocks or banks while foraging, and it is known for its distinctive tail-wagging behavior. A fun fact is that its tail-wagging may help startle insects into flight for easier capture.
Grey-headed woodpecker: The Grey-headed woodpecker has a grey head and neck, black wings with white spots, and a red crown patch on males. It inhabits mature deciduous and mixed forests across Europe and Asia, preferring old trees for foraging. Its diet consists mainly of wood-boring insects, and it exhibits quiet drumming behavior rather than loud calls. A fun fact is that it often forages alone in the forest canopy, rarely joining mixed-species flocks.
Grey-necked bunting: The Grey-necked bunting has a grey neck patch, brown upperparts, and a pale belly. It inhabits open woodlands, scrublands, and agricultural areas across South and Southeast Asia. It feeds primarily on seeds and insects while foraging in small social groups on the ground. Its repetitive call sounds like 'tink-tink' during the breeding season.
Greylag goose: Greylag geese have gray-brown plumage, a pink bill, and pink legs. They inhabit wetlands, grasslands, and farmlands across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists mainly of grasses and crops, and they form strong family groups that migrate in V-formations. They are the direct wild ancestors of all domestic geese.
Griffon vulture: Griffon vultures have dark brown plumage, a bare featherless head and neck, and a distinctive hood. They inhabit mountainous regions across Europe, Asia, and Africa, nesting on cliffs. They feed exclusively on carrion, soaring for long distances using thermal currents. Their keen sense of smell helps locate food from great distances.
Gull-billed tern: The Gull-billed tern has a gray back, white underparts, a black cap in breeding season, and a yellow bill with a black tip. It inhabits coastal areas, beaches, mudflats, and inland wetlands across multiple continents. Its diet includes insects, small fish, and crustaceans, and it exhibits agile flight while often foraging by diving or snatching prey from water surfaces. It is one of the few terns that regularly catches insects in mid-air like a swallow.
Gyrfalcon: Gyrfalcons have grayish-blue backs, white underparts with dark streaks, and vary in color from light to dark morphs. They inhabit Arctic and subarctic cliffs, migrating southward for winter in open landscapes like tundra and coastal areas. Their diet consists primarily of birds such as pigeons and waterfowl, hunted with powerful aerial dives and high-speed stoops. They are the world's largest falcon species and can reach speeds exceeding 200 kilometers per hour during a dive.
Harlequin duck: Harlequin ducks display striking black and white plumage with chestnut patches on males, while females are browner. They inhabit fast-moving rivers and rocky coastlines in northern North America and Eurasia. Their diet consists of aquatic insects, crustaceans, and mollusks, and they are expert divers. They are known for diving underwater using their wings to propel themselves while foraging.
Hawfinch: Hawfinches have a stocky build, brown upperparts, pale underparts, and distinctive white wing bars. They inhabit mature woodlands and fruit-bearing trees across Europe and Asia. Their strong bills allow them to eat hard seeds and fruits, and they are typically shy, often seen in small flocks. They can crack cherry pits with their powerful beaks.
Hazel grouse: The Hazel grouse has brown and grey mottled plumage for camouflage in forest undergrowth. It inhabits dense deciduous and mixed woodlands, particularly areas with hazel bushes. Its diet includes leaves, berries, and insects, and it is shy, spending most time on the ground rather than flying. A fun fact is that males produce a loud drumming sound by rapidly beating their wings against their bodies during courtship displays.
Helmeted guineafowl: The Helmeted guineafowl has a spotted black and white body, a featherless head with a bony helmet, and red wattles. It inhabits savannas and grasslands across sub-Saharan Africa. It forages on the ground eating seeds, insects, and small vertebrates, often in noisy social groups. Fun fact: Its name originates from the repetitive guinea call it makes.
Hen harrier: Male Hen harriers have grey plumage with a white rump, while females are brown with streaks. They inhabit open grasslands, moorlands, and farmlands across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists mainly of small mammals like voles and birds, and they hunt by flying low over terrain. A fun fact is that males perform spectacular aerial courtship displays involving steep dives and acrobatic flights.
Hermit thrush: The Hermit thrush has a brown back, reddish tail, and a white eye ring with a dark eye stripe. It inhabits coniferous and mixed forests across North America, foraging on the forest floor for insects and berries. Its soft, flute-like song is renowned for its beauty, and it is known for its secretive behavior during the breeding season. Its song is often considered one of the most melodious in North America.
Hooded crow: The Hooded crow has distinct black and gray plumage with a hooded appearance on its head and neck. It inhabits diverse areas including urban centers, farmlands, and woodlands across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists of insects, fruits, carrion, and human food scraps, and it is highly social and intelligent. Hooded crows can recognize individual human faces and remember them for years.
Hooded merganser: Male Hooded mergansers display a distinctive black-and-white crest that they raise and lower. They inhabit wooded freshwater ponds and lakes across North America. They dive for fish, insects, and crustaceans while nesting in tree cavities. Males perform a dramatic head-ducking courtship display.
Hooded wheatear: The Hooded wheatear has a black hood and white underparts in males, while females are brown with pale streaks. It inhabits dry, rocky scrublands and deserts across North Africa and the Middle East. It feeds mainly on insects, foraging by perching on rocks and darting to catch prey. Its loud, repetitive song gives the species its common name.
Horned grebe: The Horned grebe has black-and-white breeding plumage with prominent orange ear tufts. It breeds in shallow freshwater ponds and lakes, migrating to coastal marine waters in winter. Its diet consists of aquatic insects, crustaceans, and small fish, and it dives expertly for food while performing elaborate courtship displays. It can dive to depths of up to ten meters.
Horned lark: Horned larks have a brown and white streaked back, a distinct black crown stripe, and feathered "horns" on their head. They inhabit open grasslands, fields, and beaches, feeding primarily on seeds and insects while foraging on the ground. Their behavior includes singing from elevated perches and a distinctive flight display with fluttering wingbeats; a fun fact is they are one of the few birds that sing while flying upward in a steep arc.
Houbara bustard: The Houbara bustard has sandy-brown plumage with black and white head markings and a distinctive neck pattern. It inhabits arid deserts and steppes across North Africa and Asia. Its diet consists mainly of seeds and vegetation, supplemented by insects, and it is a ground-dwelling bird known for elaborate courtship displays. A fun fact is that it has been traditionally hunted by falconers across its range for centuries.
House bunting: House buntings have brown streaked backs, pale eyebrow stripes, and short conical bills. They inhabit human settlements like villages, farms, and gardens across Europe and Asia. They eat seeds and insects, often foraging in flocks on the ground. A fun fact is that they commonly nest in the eaves or chimneys of buildings.
House crow: House crows are entirely black birds with a sleek appearance and strong, dark beaks. They thrive in urban and suburban areas worldwide, foraging widely for food. Their diet includes scraps, insects, eggs, and fruits, and they are highly social, noisy birds often seen in groups. A fun fact is that they solve complex puzzles to access food, demonstrating notable intelligence.
House sparrow: House sparrows have brown streaked backs, gray heads in males, and a black bib. They live in human settlements worldwide, nesting in buildings and foraging in open areas. Their diet consists of seeds and insects, and they are social, noisy birds often seen in flocks. They are one of the most widespread bird species due to human introduction.
Humes leaf warbler: Humes leaf warblers have olive-green upperparts and pale yellow underparts with a pale eye ring. They inhabit coniferous forests in mountainous regions of Central Asia during breeding season. They feed on insects while actively foraging in trees and are often mistaken for similar leaf warblers due to their similar appearance.
Iberian chiffchaff: The Iberian chiffchaff is a small, olive-brown warbler with a pale eyebrow and dark eye stripe. It inhabits coniferous and mixed forests, particularly in mountainous regions of the Iberian Peninsula. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, foraging actively in trees and shrubs. Its distinctive "chiff-chaff" call is the source of its common name.
Iberian grey shrike: The Iberian grey shrike has grey upperparts, white underparts, a black mask, and black wings with white patches. It inhabits open woodlands and scrublands across the Iberian Peninsula, feeding primarily on insects, small reptiles, and birds. It is known for impaling prey on thorns to store or eat later, a behavior earning it the nickname butcher bird. A fun fact is that it uses sharp thorns to secure its food, creating a unique food storage system.
Iceland gull: The Iceland gull has a pale grey back, white head and underparts, and black wingtips with white spots. It breeds in Arctic regions like Iceland and Greenland and winters along northern coasts. Its diet includes fish, invertebrates, and human food waste, and it is highly social, often gathering in large flocks. Its distinctive call sounds like a loud kree-ee.
Icterine warbler: The icterine warbler has yellow underparts, a pale yellow eyestripe, and olive-brown upperparts. It breeds in reedbeds and wetlands across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists mainly of insects caught while foraging in shrubs, and it is typically solitary and vocal with a loud repetitive song. A fun fact is that its distinctive "kik-kik-kik" call is often heard before the bird is seen.
Isabelline shrike: The Isabelline shrike has pale sandy-brown plumage with a distinctive black mask and white wing patches. It inhabits dry steppes, semi-desert, and open woodlands across southern Europe and Asia. It hunts insects and small vertebrates, often impaling prey on thorns. It is sometimes called a butcher bird due to this feeding habit.
Isabelline wheatear: The Isabelline wheatear has a sandy-brown back, pale face, and dark eye stripe. It inhabits dry, open steppes and deserts across central Asia and southern Europe. It feeds primarily on insects hunted from low perches and is known for its distinctive call. Its name comes from the bird's habit of calling while perched on stones.
Italian sparrow: The Italian sparrow has a darker crown and less black in the male compared to the house sparrow. It inhabits urban areas and farmland across Italy. Its diet includes seeds and insects, and it forms social flocks. It is the only sparrow species native to Italy.
Ivory gull: Ivory gulls are entirely white birds with black eyes and a yellow-tipped bill, appearing stark against Arctic ice. They inhabit sea ice and coastal waters across the high Arctic, breeding on remote islands and cliffs. Their diet includes fish, scavenged seal carcasses, and marine invertebrates, and they are known for opportunistic feeding near ice edges. They nest on sea ice floes, a rare behavior among birds.
Jack snipe: Jack snipes have mottled brown and black plumage that camouflages them in wet grasslands and marshes. They feed on insects, worms, and small invertebrates by probing mud with their long bills, often at dawn or dusk. Their secretive behavior includes explosive takeoffs when disturbed, and they produce a distinctive winnowing sound during courtship flights.
Kentish plover: The Kentish plover is a small, sandy-brown shorebird with a black forehead band and white face. It nests on open sandy beaches and coastal mudflats across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists of small insects, worms, and crustaceans found on shorelines, and it exhibits ground nesting behavior with alarm calls to warn of danger. A fun fact is that it performs a broken wing display to distract predators from its nest.
Killdeer: The Killdeer has a brown back, white underparts, and a distinctive black band across its breast. It inhabits open areas like fields, lawns, and beaches across North America. It feeds on insects and worms, often foraging by walking and pecking, and uses distraction displays like a broken-wing act to protect its nest. Its loud "kill-deer" call gives the bird its common name.
King eider: Male King eiders have striking black and white plumage with a large orange bill. They breed in Arctic coastal areas and winter in marine habitats along northern coasts. They dive for shellfish and other invertebrates, often forming large flocks during migration. Their distinctive call resembles a loud "kree-ee".
Kittlitzs plover:
Kittlitz's plover has pale brown upperparts, a white breast, and a distinct dark eye mask. It inhabits coastal beaches, mudflats, and estuaries across southern Africa and Australia. Its diet consists of insects and small invertebrates, which it finds by running and probing the sand.

This plover exhibits a distinctive courtship display where males perform a sky-pointing leap.
Lady Amhersts pheasant: Male Lady Amherst's pheasants display vibrant iridescent green and white plumage with long tail feathers. They inhabit dense forests in Southeast Asia, including China and Myanmar. Their diet consists of insects, seeds, and plant matter, and they are shy, ground-foraging birds. Males possess extremely long tail feathers that can exceed three meters in length.
Lanceolated warbler: This small warbler has brown upperparts with pale streaks, a pale eyebrow, and a white throat. It inhabits dense reedbeds and marshy wetlands across eastern Asia during breeding. It feeds on insects and spiders, foraging quietly in thick vegetation. Its sharp "tseep" call sounds like a high-pitched insect buzz.
Lanner falcon: Lanner falcons have a gray back, barred chest, and a dark facial mask. They inhabit open landscapes including cliffs, grasslands, and farmlands across Africa, Europe, and Asia. They hunt birds like pigeons and doves on swift, agile flights, often perching on high structures to survey their territory. They were historically used in falconry for hunting game birds.
Lapland longspur: Lapland longspurs have streaked brown plumage in winter with darker streaks and a distinctive long bill. They breed in Arctic tundra and migrate to grasslands and agricultural fields in temperate regions. Their diet consists of seeds year-round and insects during the breeding season, and they form large flocks in winter. A fun fact is that males perform a fluttering courtship flight while singing a thin, high-pitched song.
Lappet-faced vulture: The Lappet-faced vulture has a large size, bald red head with prominent fleshy lappets, and a strong hooked bill. It inhabits open savannas, deserts, and semi-arid regions across Africa and the Middle East. It primarily feeds on carrion, often dominating feeding sites despite arriving later than other vultures due to its slow flight. A fun fact is that it helps prevent disease spread by rapidly consuming carcasses that might otherwise attract harmful bacteria.
Laughing dove: The laughing dove has a pale grey body, a distinctive black neck ring, and a white tail with black tips. It inhabits urban areas, gardens, and farmlands across Europe, Asia, and Africa, feeding mainly on seeds and grains. It is social and often seen in pairs, with a soft cooing call that sounds like laughter. This species has rapidly expanded its range in recent decades, colonizing new areas across Europe.
Laughing gull: Laughing gulls have black heads and white bodies during breeding season with gray wings. They inhabit coastal areas across North America, nesting on beaches and feeding on fish, insects, and human scraps. Their distinctive high-pitched call sounds like human laughter, giving the species its name.
Laurel pigeon: The Madeiran laurel pigeon has dark gray plumage with a pinkish head and inhabits dense laurel forests on Madeira Island. It feeds primarily on fruits, seeds, and leaves, foraging in social groups on the forest floor. A fun fact is that it is the largest pigeon species native to the Madeira Islands.
Leachs storm petrel: Leach's storm petrels are small dark seabirds with a white rump and black plumage that breed on remote Atlantic islands and spend most of their lives at sea. They feed on plankton and small fish by skimming the ocean surface and are nocturnal at nesting sites to avoid predators. A fun fact is they are the smallest seabirds in the North Atlantic and often follow ships for food.
Least sandpiper: The Least sandpiper has brown streaked back, pale breast, and a short dark bill. It inhabits muddy shores, marshes, and beaches across North America during migration. It feeds on small insects and invertebrates by probing mud with its bill. This species is the smallest sandpiper in North America.
Lesser black-backed gull: The Lesser black-backed gull has a gray back, white underparts, yellow bill with a red spot, and pale eyes. It inhabits coastal areas, estuaries, and inland lakes during breeding, and winters along coastlines. It feeds on fish, insects, and scavenged food, often foraging in groups and stealing food from other birds. A fun fact is that they are known to steal food from other birds like crows.
Lesser crested tern: The Lesser crested tern has gray upperparts, white underparts, and a black cap during breeding season. It inhabits coastal areas including shores, estuaries, and islands, forming large nesting colonies. It feeds primarily on small fish caught by plunge-diving and exhibits strong territorial defense. A fun fact is that it aggressively dives at intruders to protect its nest.
Lesser grey shrike: The Lesser grey shrike has grey upperparts, pale underparts, and a distinct black mask across its eyes. It inhabits open woodlands, scrublands, and farmlands across Europe and Asia. It hunts insects and small vertebrates from perches, impaling prey on thorns, and is known for its habit of storing food on sharp branches. A fun fact is that it is sometimes called a "butcher bird" due to this impaling behavior.
Lesser kestrel: The Lesser kestrel has brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a distinctive dark eye stripe. It inhabits open farmlands and grasslands, nesting colonially on buildings or cliffs. It primarily feeds on insects like grasshoppers, hunting by hovering before diving. A fun fact is that males perform dramatic aerial displays during courtship, including steep dives and wing claps.
Lesser scaup: Male Lesser scaup have a glossy green head and white body, while females are brown with a pale face. They inhabit freshwater lakes and ponds in summer and coastal waters in winter, feeding on aquatic plants and invertebrates by diving. They form large flocks during migration and are known for their rapid, direct flight. A fun fact is that they are smaller than the similar greater scaup, hence their name.
Lesser spotted eagle: The Lesser spotted eagle has brown plumage with a pale neck patch and a white-tailed band. It inhabits open woodlands, grasslands, and wetlands across Europe and Asia, migrating to sub-Saharan Africa for winter. It hunts small mammals, reptiles, and insects while soaring or perching, often solitary except during breeding. Its high-pitched "kree-ee" call distinguishes it from similar eagles.
Lesser spotted woodpecker: This small woodpecker has gray-brown plumage with black barring and a red crown patch in males. It inhabits mature forests across Europe and Asia, foraging for insects on tree trunks and branches. It produces rapid drumming sounds and can climb down trees headfirst, a rare ability among woodpeckers.
Lesser white-fronted goose: This small goose has a white forehead and pale face, gray-brown upperparts, and white underparts. It breeds in Arctic tundra regions and winters in grasslands across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists mainly of grasses and seeds, and it forms large, noisy flocks during migration. A fun fact is that its distinctive high-pitched call sounds like a rapid "kwee-kwee" unlike other geese.
Lesser whitethroat: The Lesser whitethroat is a small gray-brown warbler with a pale throat and distinctive eye ring. It breeds in scrubland, hedgerows, and woodland edges across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on insects like flies and aphids, foraging actively in bushes while singing its characteristic buzzy song. A fun fact is that it is one of the few songbirds capable of singing while in flight.
Lesser yellowlegs: The Lesser yellowlegs has yellow legs, a slender body, and brown-streaked upperparts. It breeds in northern wetlands and winters along coastlines and large lakes. It feeds on insects, worms, and small fish by probing shallow water with rapid movements. A fun fact is that its call sounds like "tew-tew-tew," often mistaken for the similar Greater yellowlegs but higher pitched.
Levant sparrowhawk: The Levant sparrowhawk has dark gray upperparts and reddish barred underparts in males, while females are browner. It inhabits woodlands, forests, and urban parks across the Levant region. It hunts small birds and insects using agile flight through dense vegetation, often perching to ambush prey. A fun fact is that this hawk frequently hunts in city parks, adapting well to human environments.
Lichtensteins sandgrouse: Lichtenstein's sandgrouse has sandy-brown plumage with black wing and tail markings. It inhabits dry grasslands and scrublands across sub-Saharan Africa. Its diet consists mainly of seeds, and it forms flocks that travel to waterholes at dawn. Males carry water in special belly feathers to nourish chicks.
Little auk: This small black-and-white seabird has a black head and white underparts. It nests on Arctic coasts and feeds primarily on plankton while diving underwater. A fun fact is that their calls sound like a soft 'dovekie' when they gather in large breeding colonies.
Little bittern: This small heron has brown and buff plumage with dark streaks, typically found in dense reed beds of freshwater wetlands. It feeds on small fish, insects, and amphibians, often hunting by standing motionless in vegetation. Its loud call can be heard at dawn and dusk, and it is known for being extremely difficult to spot due to its excellent camouflage.
Little bunting: Male Little buntings have streaked brown backs and pale underparts, while females are duller brown. They inhabit open grasslands and farmlands across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists of seeds and insects, and they forage on the ground in flocks. A fun fact is their distinctive 'tink-tink' call that sounds like tiny bells.
Little bustard: The Little Bustard has brown and white streaked plumage for camouflage in open landscapes. It inhabits grasslands, steppes, and cultivated fields across Europe and Asia, feeding primarily on insects and seeds. Males display aggressively during breeding season, and they are ground-foraging birds. A fun fact is that males produce a loud wing-clapping sound during courtship displays.
Little crake: The Little crake has a brown back, reddish-brown flanks, and a pale face with a dark eye stripe. It inhabits freshwater wetlands with dense reeds and vegetation across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists of insects, worms, and small aquatic invertebrates, and it is secretive, active at dawn and dusk. Its distinctive call is often heard before the bird is seen.
Little curlew:
This medium-sized wader has brown streaked plumage, a long curved bill, and feeds in shallow wetlands across Asia and Australia.  
It forages for invertebrates in mudflats and coastal areas, often in small groups.  
Fun fact: Its migration route spans over 10,000 kilometers between breeding grounds in Siberia and wintering sites in Southeast Asia.
Little egret: The little egret is a small white heron with long black legs and yellow feet. It inhabits freshwater and coastal wetlands worldwide, feeding on fish, insects, and amphibians by standing motionless or slowly stalking prey. A fun fact is that they sometimes drop bread crumbs to attract fish, then catch them.
Little grebe:
The Little grebe has dark brown upperparts, a rusty neck, and a white throat. It inhabits still freshwater ponds and lakes with dense vegetation.  
It feeds on aquatic insects, small fish, and crustaceans, diving frequently to forage while remaining secretive.  
A fun fact is that it can tuck its head underwater to hide from predators while floating.
Little gull: The Little gull has a dark grey back, white underparts, and a black head in breeding season. It breeds near freshwater and coastal habitats, foraging by skimming water for insects and small fish. Known for high-pitched chattering calls, it often travels in large flocks during migration.
Little owl: The Little owl has brown plumage with white spots and a distinct facial disc. It inhabits open countryside, farmland, and woodland edges across Europe and Asia. It hunts insects, small mammals, and birds at night, often perching prominently on trees or fence posts. Its call sounds like a repeated "little owl" phrase.
Little ringed plover: This small shorebird has pale brown upperparts, white underparts, a black band across the eye, and a distinctive black ring around the neck. It inhabits sandy or gravelly shores, riverbanks, and lakeshores, feeding primarily on insects and small invertebrates. It exhibits a broken-wing display to distract predators and is not a true plover despite its name.
Little stint: The Little stint has a brownish back, white underparts, and a short black bill. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters on coastal mudflats and estuaries globally. It feeds on small invertebrates like insects and worms, foraging in quick, darting movements within flocks. A fun fact is that it undertakes one of the longest migrations of any small shorebird, often flying non-stop across the Pacific Ocean.
Little swift: The Little swift has dark brown plumage with a distinctive white throat patch and a streamlined body built for swift flight. It inhabits sub-Saharan Africa, nesting in cliff crevices or buildings near open habitats like rivers and woodlands. It feeds entirely on flying insects while exhibiting highly aerial behavior, rarely landing except to nest. A fun fact is that it can sleep while flying, spending nearly its entire life airborne.
Little tern: Little terns have pale gray backs, white fronts, and a black cap during breeding. They nest on sandy beaches and gravel spits near coastal waters and inland rivers. They eat small fish caught by plunge-diving and are highly social, nesting in colonies. They are known for their loud, sharp alarm calls when predators approach their nests.
Long-billed dowitcher: Long-billed dowitchers have a long, straight bill, brown and streaked plumage in breeding season, and a stocky build. They inhabit shallow wetlands, mudflats, and coastal areas during migration and winter. They feed on invertebrates by probing mud with rapid movements and run short distances when alarmed. They can run briefly across water surfaces when startled.
Long-billed pipit: The Long-billed pipit has brown streaked upperparts and pale underparts with a distinct pale eye stripe. It inhabits open grasslands, agricultural fields, and pastures across its range. It feeds primarily on insects and seeds, foraging on the ground with characteristic head-bobbing movements. Its common name comes from the distinctive "pipit" call it makes while foraging.
Long-eared owl: Long-eared owls have distinctive ear tufts, reddish-brown plumage with dark streaks, and large yellow eyes. They inhabit dense coniferous and mixed forests across temperate regions, roosting in thick foliage during the day. Their diet consists primarily of small mammals like voles and mice, and they are nocturnal hunters. A fun fact is that they often roost in large groups with other owls during cold weather.
Long-legged buzzard: Long-legged buzzards have pale brown plumage with a pale head and dark wingtips. They inhabit open grasslands, steppes, and agricultural areas across Europe and Asia. They hunt small mammals, birds, and insects by soaring and perching, often hovering to spot prey. Fun fact: They can hover motionless for extended periods while scanning the ground for food.
Long-tailed duck: Males have a long tail and black-and-white plumage while females are browner. They breed in Arctic tundra and winter along temperate coasts. They dive for mollusks and crustaceans in deep water, often in large flocks, and can dive over sixty meters to feed.
Long-tailed jaeger:
Long-tailed jaegers have dark brown upperparts, pale underparts, and distinctive long tail streamers in breeding plumage. They breed in Arctic tundra and migrate to open oceans worldwide.  
They primarily eat fish and squid, often stealing food from other seabirds through kleptoparasitism.  
They are known for aggressively chasing other birds to force them to drop their catch.
Long-tailed tit: The Long-tailed tit has a small body, white and grey plumage, a black cap, and an exceptionally long tail. It inhabits woodlands, gardens, and hedgerows across temperate Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, foraging actively in flocks that constantly move through trees. Its nest is a remarkable hanging structure woven from moss and spider silk.
Long-toed stint: The Long-toed stint is a small shorebird with brown streaked upperparts, pale underparts, and notably long toes adapted for wading in soft mud. It inhabits shallow wetlands, marshes, and coastal mudflats during migration and breeding seasons across Eurasia and Africa. Its diet consists of small invertebrates like insects and crustaceans, and it forages by probing shallow water while moving in flocks. A fun fact is that it produces a very high-pitched, insect-like call during migration that is distinctive among shorebirds.
MacQueens bustard: MacQueen's Bustard has mottled brown and black plumage and inhabits open grasslands and savannas across Africa and Asia. It feeds on seeds, insects, and small vertebrates and is a ground-dwelling bird that runs swiftly and produces a deep booming call during display. A fun fact is that it can fly over 50 kilometers in a single day during migration despite its large size.
Madeira firecrest: The Madeira firecrest has a bright orange crown and white eye stripe contrasting with greenish upperparts and a pale throat. It inhabits laurel forests and woodlands on Madeira Island, foraging actively in trees for insects and spiders. This small bird is often seen in mixed-species flocks and performs acrobatic movements while feeding. A fun fact is that it is one of the rarest birds in Europe, found only on Madeira.
Mallard: Male Mallards feature iridescent green heads and chestnut chests against a grey body, while females are mottled brown. They inhabit freshwater wetlands, ponds, and parks across the Northern Hemisphere. Mallards are omnivorous dabblers feeding on aquatic plants, insects, and small invertebrates, often foraging in groups. Mallards are the wild ancestors of most domestic ducks worldwide.
Manx shearwater: Manx shearwaters have dark brown upperparts and white underparts with a distinctive dark wing stripe. They nest on remote oceanic islands and spend most of their lives foraging at sea. Their diet consists mainly of fish and squid, and they exhibit strong homing behavior to nesting colonies. They can return to the same nesting burrow for decades after migrating thousands of miles.
Marbled duck: Marbled ducks have mottled brown and white plumage with a dark head and pale face. They inhabit shallow freshwater wetlands, lakes, and marshes across Europe, Asia, and Africa. Their diet consists mainly of aquatic plants, seeds, and small invertebrates, and they are adept divers. They can stay submerged for up to 30 seconds while foraging.
Marsh sandpiper: The Marsh sandpiper is a small wading bird with pale gray-brown upperparts, white underparts, a long thin bill, and long legs. It inhabits freshwater wetlands, marshes, and shallow ponds, feeding on insects and small aquatic invertebrates by probing mud. It is highly active and often seen in flocks during migration, covering vast distances. Fun fact: Marsh sandpipers can migrate over 10,000 kilometers between breeding and wintering grounds.
Marsh tit: Marsh tits have a dark grey cap, white cheeks, and a brown back with a pale throat. They inhabit wet woodlands, reed beds, and shrubby areas across Europe and Asia. Their diet includes insects and seeds, and they forage actively in trees and bushes. They cache food in tree crevices for later use.
Marsh warbler: The Marsh warbler is a small, brownish bird with a pale eyebrow and throat. It breeds in reedbeds and wet meadows across Europe and Asia, migrating to sub-Saharan Africa for winter. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, foraging actively in dense vegetation while singing from reed tops. A fun fact is that it is an exceptional mimic, often incorporating other birds' songs into its own complex vocalizations.
Masked shrike: The Masked shrike has a distinctive black mask across its eyes and white face, with gray upperparts and reddish-brown wings. It inhabits open woodlands, scrublands, and parklands across Europe and Asia. It hunts insects like beetles and grasshoppers from perches, often impaling prey on thorns, and is known for its loud, repetitive song. A fun fact is that it sometimes mimics the calls of other birds while hunting.
Meadow pipit: Meadow pipits are small brown birds with streaked backs and pale eyebrow stripes. They live in open grasslands, meadows, and farmland across Europe and Asia. They eat insects and seeds, often foraging on the ground while singing a high-pitched song from perches. Their name comes from the distinctive "pipit" sound they make while flying.
Mediterranean gull: The Mediterranean gull has a white head with a black eye patch, gray back, and black-tipped wings. It inhabits coastal areas and wetlands, feeding on fish, insects, and invertebrates while displaying agile flight and scavenging behavior. A fun fact is that it often nests on small islands to avoid ground predators.
Mediterranean short-toed lark: This small lark has brown streaked upperparts, a pale eyebrow, and a short bill. It inhabits open grasslands, farmlands, and dry scrub across southern Europe and North Africa. It feeds mainly on seeds and insects, foraging on the ground and singing from low perches. Its distinctive song sounds like a rapid "tsee-tsee-tsee".
Melodious warbler: The Melodious warbler has olive-green upperparts, pale yellow underparts, and a prominent white eye-ring. It breeds in deciduous and mixed forests across Europe and western Asia, migrating to sub-Saharan Africa for winter. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, foraging actively in tree canopies. Its distinctive musical song resembles a series of clear, rising notes.
Merlin:
Merlins are small falcons with brown upperparts, pale underparts marked with dark bars, and a dark head stripe. They inhabit open country including tundra, grasslands, and coastal areas across the Northern Hemisphere.  
They primarily hunt small birds and insects on the wing, using fast, direct flight and sudden dives to capture prey.  
Merlins can pursue prey at speeds exceeding 100 kilometers per hour during aerial chases.
Middle spotted woodpecker: This small woodpecker has black and white barred plumage with a red crown patch in males. It inhabits mature deciduous forests with old trees across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists mainly of wood-boring insects, and it forages by climbing tree trunks while drumming loudly. Its drumming pattern is a distinctive rapid "tata-tat" sound.
Mistle thrush: The Mistle thrush is a large brown bird with white underparts marked by dark spots. It inhabits woodlands, parks, and gardens across Europe and Asia. It eats berries, insects, and worms, and is known for aggressively defending territories, especially around mistletoe. Its name comes from its habit of eating mistletoe berries.
Mountain chiffchaff: Mountain chiffchaffs are small olive-brown birds with pale yellowish underparts and a distinct pale eye stripe. They inhabit coniferous and mixed forests in mountainous regions across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists mainly of insects and spiders, and they actively forage by gleaning leaves and branches. Their name comes from their characteristic repetitive "chiff-chaff" call.
Moustached warbler: The Moustached warbler has a brown back, pale underparts, and a prominent black stripe through the eye. It inhabits dense reedbeds near water in Europe and Asia. It feeds mainly on insects and spiders, moving stealthily through vegetation. Its loud, repetitive song is surprisingly loud for such a secretive bird.
Mute swan: Mute swans have white plumage, an orange bill with a black knob, and a long neck. They inhabit freshwater lakes, rivers, and ponds across Europe and Asia, often in protected wetlands. Their diet consists mainly of aquatic plants, and they are highly territorial, especially during nesting. A fun fact is that despite their name, they are not completely silent and can hiss or make low grunting sounds when threatened.
Namaqua dove: The Namaqua dove has pale pinkish-brown plumage with a dark neck band and brown wings. It inhabits arid and semi-arid regions including deserts and scrublands across southern Africa. It primarily eats seeds and insects while being shy and often seen alone or in pairs. Its distinctive call sounds like a ticking clock.
Naumanns thrush: Naumann's thrush has a brown upper body with pale streaked underparts and a distinct white eye ring. It breeds in Siberian coniferous forests and migrates to East Asia, foraging on the forest floor for insects and berries. Its distinctive flute-like song is often heard during migration.
Northern bald ibis: The Northern bald ibis has dark plumage, a bare red head and neck, and a long curved beak. It inhabits arid cliffs and semi-desert areas in parts of North Africa and the Middle East, often nesting in colonies. It feeds on insects, worms, and small amphibians, foraging in groups and displaying strong social bonds. A fun fact is that it was historically known as the "Lark of the Nile" in ancient Egyptian culture.
Northern fulmar: Northern fulmars are gray and white seabirds with long wings and a hooked beak. They nest on coastal cliffs and spend most of their lives flying over open ocean. Their diet consists mainly of fish, squid, and plankton, and they glide effortlessly on wind currents. A fun fact is that they can regurgitate a foul-smelling oil to deter predators.
Northern gannet: Northern gannets are large white seabirds with black wingtips and a yellow head. They nest colonially on rocky Atlantic coasts and hunt fish like herring by plunging from great heights. Their dramatic dives reach speeds over 60 miles per hour, making them one of the fastest diving birds.
Northern goshawk: Northern goshawks have dark gray backs, barred white underparts, and a pale eyebrow stripe. They inhabit mature forests across northern continents. They hunt birds and mammals like squirrels using stealth and speed in dense woodlands. Their ability to pursue prey through thick trees earns them the nickname forest falcon.
Northern harrier: Northern harriers have long wings, a slender body, and a pale gray or brown back with a white rump. They inhabit open grasslands, marshes, and agricultural fields across North America and Eurasia. They hunt small mammals like voles by flying low and silently, using their facial disc to hear prey, and their asymmetrical ears help locate sounds precisely. A fun fact is that their ear placement allows them to pinpoint prey movements even underground.
Northern hawk-owl: Northern hawk-owls have a distinct facial disc, no ear tufts, and streaked brown and white plumage. They inhabit dense boreal forests across northern North America and Eurasia. They hunt primarily small mammals like voles during daylight hours, perching or flying low while remaining highly territorial. A fun fact is they can rotate their heads nearly 180 degrees to scan for prey.
Northern lapwing: Northern lapwings have a brown body, black crest, and white underparts. They inhabit open grasslands, farmlands, and wet meadows across Europe and Asia. They eat insects, worms, and small invertebrates, often foraging by probing the ground and displaying aerial displays during breeding. Their courtship flight involves dramatic dives and calls known as "sky-dancing."
Northern pintail: Male Northern pintails have a distinctive long neck, brown head, and white chest. Females are mottled brown with a shorter, less curved tail. They breed in northern wetlands and migrate to freshwater ponds and marshes across temperate regions. Their diet includes aquatic plants, seeds, and small invertebrates. They feed in groups while swimming or dabbling. Northern pintails are among the fastest flying ducks.
Northern shoveler: Male Northern shovelers have iridescent green heads and chestnut bodies while females are mottled brown. They inhabit freshwater wetlands, ponds, and lakes across North America, Europe, and Asia. They feed by dabbling and filtering water through their large, spatulate bills to consume plants and small invertebrates. Their bill is one of the largest relative to body size among ducks.
Northern wheatear: The Northern wheatear has a distinctive black-and-white appearance with a white rump and black wings. It breeds in open tundra and rocky habitats across northern Europe and Asia, migrating to sub-Saharan Africa for winter. It feeds primarily on insects caught in flight or gleaned from the ground and is known for its active, perch-hunting behavior. It undertakes one of the longest annual migrations of any songbird, traveling up to 15,000 kilometers.
Nubian nightjar: The Nubian nightjar has mottled brown and gray plumage for camouflage in sandy or rocky arid habitats across East Africa. It feeds on flying insects caught at dusk and night, often perching low on the ground during the day. Its distinctive loud churring call resembles a motorbike and can be heard at night.
Olive-backed pipit: The Olive-backed pipit has olive-brown upperparts, pale underparts with dark streaks, and a pale eye stripe. It inhabits open grasslands, agricultural fields, and scrublands across South and Southeast Asia. It forages on the ground for insects and seeds, often bobbing its tail while moving. Its name comes from its distinctive "pip-it" call.
