Olive-tree warbler: This small warbler has olive-green upperparts and yellowish underparts with a pale eye ring. It inhabits Mediterranean olive groves, scrublands, and open woodlands. It feeds primarily on insects gleaned from leaves and branches, often moving quietly in pairs or small groups. Its distinctive song is a rapid series of high-pitched notes sounding like "tsee-tsee-tsee."
Oriental cuckoo: The Oriental cuckoo has brown upperparts, pale underparts with dark streaks, and a white eye-ring. It breeds in forested areas across Asia and winters in Southeast Asia. It eats insects, especially caterpillars, and is a brood parasite, laying eggs in other birds' nests. Its call mimics the common cuckoo to avoid detection by host birds.
Oriental skylark: The Oriental skylark has streaked brown upperparts and pale underparts. It inhabits open grasslands, agricultural fields, and wetlands across South and Southeast Asia. It feeds primarily on seeds and insects, foraging on the ground while displaying aerial song flights. Its distinctive high-pitched song is often sung while ascending steeply into the air during flight.
Oriental turtle dove: The Oriental turtle dove has a grey-brown body with a pinkish breast and a distinctive white patch on its neck. It inhabits forests, woodlands, and gardens across South and Southeast Asia. It feeds mainly on seeds and fruits, forms long-term pairs, and produces a soft cooing call. Its name comes from the repetitive "turtle-turtle" sound it makes while calling.
Ortolan bunting: The Ortolan bunting has a brown body with dark streaks on its back and breast, a pale eyebrow stripe, and a short, conical bill. It inhabits open woodlands, farmlands, and grasslands in Europe and Asia during breeding, migrating to sub-Saharan Africa for winter. It feeds primarily on seeds and insects, often foraging in flocks on the ground. A fun fact is that it was historically considered a delicacy in French cuisine, traditionally served whole and eaten in one bite.
Osprey:
Ospreys have dark brown upperparts and white underparts with a distinctive dark eye stripe. They nest near water bodies including coasts, lakes, and rivers.  
They primarily eat fish, diving feet-first to catch them with specialized reversible outer toes.  
Ospreys can rotate one foot backward to grip slippery fish more effectively.
Pacific golden plover: Pacific golden plovers have a golden-brown back and white underparts in summer, becoming mottled brown in winter. They breed in Arctic tundra regions and migrate to coastal areas across the Pacific, including Hawaii and Australia. Their diet consists of insects, worms, and small invertebrates, and they forage in flocks on mudflats and beaches. They undertake remarkable non-stop flights across the Pacific Ocean during migration.
Paddyfield warbler: This small brown warbler has a pale eyebrow stripe and short bill. It inhabits wet grasslands and rice paddies across Asia during breeding. It feeds primarily on insects and is active in dense reeds. Its loud repetitive "pik-pik" song is a common sound in its breeding habitat.
Pale rockfinch: Pale rockfinches have pale brown plumage with dark streaks on their backs and a pale eyebrow. They inhabit rocky deserts, scrublands, and cliffs across South Asia, feeding mainly on seeds and insects. These birds are social, foraging in small groups on the ground. Their distinctive call sounds like a soft "tink-tink" repeated rapidly.
Palestine sunbird: The Palestine sunbird has a male with green upperparts, a red throat patch, and a black mask, while females are duller olive-green. It inhabits open woodlands, gardens, and scrublands across the Middle East and Africa. It feeds primarily on nectar and small insects, exhibiting active, territorial behavior while foraging. A fun fact is that it hovers like a hummingbird while feeding on flowers.
Pallass gull: The Pallass gull has a large size with a pale gray back, white head, and black-tipped wings. It inhabits coastal areas, estuaries, and inland water bodies across Asia. It feeds on fish, insects, and human scraps, often gathering in large groups. A fun fact is that it nests on deserted islands, sometimes laying eggs on bare ground.
Pallass leaf warbler: The Pallass leaf warbler has greenish-yellow upperparts and pale yellow underparts with a distinct white eye ring. It breeds in coniferous forests across northern Asia and winters in dense broadleaf forests in Southeast Asia. It feeds on insects and spiders while foraging actively in tree foliage and is known for its high-pitched song. A fun fact is that it is one of the most abundant leaf warblers in its breeding range across Siberia.
Pallid harrier: The Pallid harrier has pale brown upperparts and pale underparts with a distinctive pale face. It inhabits open grasslands, steppes, and agricultural fields across central Asia and Europe. It hunts small mammals and insects by low, slow flight over open ground. This species undertakes one of the longest migrations of any harrier, traveling over 10,000 kilometers annually.
Pallid scops owl: This owl has pale brown plumage with dark streaks and a pale face. It inhabits open woodlands, gardens, and agricultural areas across South and Southeast Asia. It hunts insects and small vertebrates at night using silent flight and a distinctive call. Its name comes from the sound of its call, which resembles "scop-scop."
Pallid swift: The Pallid swift has pale brown plumage, a dark tail, and a deeply forked tail. It inhabits open areas near cliffs or buildings, feeding exclusively on insects caught while flying. It is highly aerial, rarely landing except to nest, and produces loud chattering calls. Fun fact: Pallid swifts spend almost their entire lives in flight, only descending to nest in rock crevices or buildings.
Parasitic jaeger: Parasitic jaegers have dark brown plumage with white wing patches and a forked tail. They breed in Arctic tundra regions and migrate to open oceans worldwide. They are aggressive predators that steal food from other seabirds and hunt fish and invertebrates. They mimic the calls of other birds to lure them closer for theft.
Parrot crossbill: Parrot crossbills have a distinctive crossed bill and display bright red or orange plumage in males with greenish females, inhabiting coniferous forests across northern Europe and Asia. They primarily consume conifer seeds, using their specialized bills to extract seeds from cones, and are highly nomadic, moving frequently to locate food sources. A fun fact is that their crossed bills allow them to twist seeds out of cones more efficiently than other birds.
Pechora pipit: The Pechora pipit is a small brown bird with a streaked back and pale throat, breeding in wet grasslands across northern Siberia and migrating to southern Asia for winter. It feeds primarily on insects and seeds, foraging on the ground and singing a high-pitched song from exposed perches. Its distinctive call is frequently mistaken for other pipit species during migration.
Pectoral sandpiper: Pectoral sandpipers have streaked brown backs, white underparts, and a distinctive breast streak. They breed in Arctic tundra and migrate to wetlands, mudflats, and grasslands worldwide. They feed on insects and small invertebrates while foraging actively along shorelines. Males perform dramatic aerial display flights during courtship.
Peregrine falcon: Dark gray backs and barred white underparts characterize this bird. It inhabits cliffs and urban structures globally, feeding primarily on birds like pigeons. Known for diving at over 200 miles per hour to catch prey, it holds the title of fastest animal.
Pied avocet: The Pied avocet has black and white plumage with a long, upturned bill. It inhabits shallow wetlands, estuaries, and coastal lagoons across Europe and Asia. It feeds on small invertebrates by sweeping its bill side-to-side in water. Its distinctive feeding motion creates a unique visual display while foraging.
Pied kingfisher: The pied kingfisher has striking black and white plumage with a black eye stripe and white underparts. It inhabits freshwater habitats across Africa and Asia, hunting small fish by hovering before diving headfirst. It often feeds alone but sometimes cooperates with others to drive fish into shallow water, a rare social behavior among kingfishers.
Pied wheatear: The pied wheatear has black and white plumage with a prominent white wing patch and inhabits open, rocky areas across Europe and Asia. It primarily eats insects, foraging by hopping on the ground and perching on rocks to spot prey. It undertakes long migrations, with some populations traveling over 10,000 kilometers annually to Africa. A fun fact is that it is one of the smallest birds to migrate across the Sahara Desert.
Pied-billed grebe: The Pied-billed grebe has dark brown plumage with a distinctive white band on its thick, black bill during breeding season. It inhabits freshwater ponds, lakes, and marshes across North America, often hiding among dense vegetation. It feeds on fish, insects, and aquatic plants, diving quickly and remaining secretive. A fun fact is that it can swallow small fish whole and submerge rapidly to avoid predators.
Pin-tailed sandgrouse: Pin-tailed sandgrouse have brownish plumage with a long, pointed tail and a pale breast. They inhabit arid deserts and dry grasslands across Africa and Asia. They feed mainly on seeds and travel in flocks to water sources at dawn and dusk. Males carry water to their chicks by soaking their belly feathers.
Pine bunting: Pine buntings have streaked brown upperparts and a pale eyebrow stripe, typically found in coniferous forests across northern Europe and Asia. They feed mainly on seeds and insects, forming large flocks in winter while singing from exposed perches during breeding. Their distinctive two-note song sounds like 'pew-pew' and is often heard in their forest habitats.
Pine grosbeak: Pine grosbeaks have a stocky build with males displaying vibrant rose-red plumage and females appearing brownish with pale streaks. They inhabit coniferous forests across northern North America and Eurasia, often in mountainous regions. Their diet consists primarily of conifer seeds, buds, and berries, and they are known for being relatively tame and social. A fun fact is that they sometimes consume berries even in deep winter when other food is scarce.
Pink-footed goose: Pink-footed geese have gray-brown bodies, pale heads, and distinctive pink legs and feet. They breed in Arctic regions and winter in temperate grasslands and agricultural areas across Europe. Their diet consists mainly of grasses, grains, and crops, and they travel in large noisy flocks during migration. A fun fact is they are known for their loud, honking calls that can often be heard during their long migratory flights.
Pomarine jaeger: Pomarine jaegers have dark brown plumage, a long forked tail, and a hooked bill. They breed in Arctic tundra and migrate to open oceans for winter. They primarily eat fish caught by diving or stolen from other seabirds through aggressive kleptoparasitism. They are known for harassing gulls to force them to drop their catches.
Purple heron: Purple herons have grayish-purple plumage with a long neck and legs. They inhabit freshwater wetlands, including reed beds and marshes across Africa, Asia, and Europe. Their diet consists of fish, amphibians, and insects, and they hunt by standing motionless or slowly stalking prey. They sometimes nest in trees, a rare behavior among herons.
Purple sandpiper: Purple sandpipers have grayish-brown plumage with a pale eyebrow and dark legs. They breed in Arctic tundra and winter along rocky coastlines in Europe and North America. They feed on small invertebrates like insects and crustaceans, foraging in flocks along shorelines. They can survive Arctic winters by eating frozen prey on ice-covered shores.
Pygmy cormorant: The Pygmy cormorant has dark brown plumage, a slender neck, and a small size compared to other cormorants. It inhabits shallow freshwater wetlands, lakes, and marshes across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on small fish, diving to catch them and often foraging in groups. A fun fact is that they can fly in tight, coordinated flocks while migrating.
Razorbill: Razorbills have black backs and white fronts with a thick black bill edged in white. They nest on rocky Atlantic and Pacific coastlines and spend most of their lives at sea. Their diet consists of fish like herring and sand eels, and they dive underwater using their wings to swim. Razorbills can dive over 100 meters deep to catch prey.
Red crossbill: Male Red crossbills are bright red with dark wings, while females are greenish-yellow. They inhabit coniferous forests across northern regions, moving nomadically to follow cone crops. Their diet consists mainly of conifer seeds, and they use their crossed bills to extract seeds from cones while foraging in flocks. A fun fact is that their calls vary regionally, helping scientists identify distinct populations.
Red kite: Red kites have reddish-brown plumage, a deeply forked tail, and broad wings with black tips. They inhabit open woodlands, farmlands, and grasslands across Europe and Asia. They primarily eat carrion and small mammals, often soaring high to spot food. A fun fact is that they were nearly extinct in the UK but have rebounded due to successful conservation programs.
Red knot: Red Knots have reddish-brown breeding plumage and gray-brown non-breeding feathers. They nest in Arctic tundra and migrate to coastal mudflats worldwide. Their diet consists of invertebrates like worms and mollusks, and they feed by probing mud with their bills. A fun fact is they rely on horseshoe crab eggs during migration stopovers in Delaware Bay.
Red phalarope: Red phalaropes have a distinctive red-brown breeding plumage with a white neck and black cap, turning grayish-brown in winter. They breed in Arctic tundra and spend most of the year on open oceans, feeding on plankton and small marine invertebrates by spinning rapidly in circles. Females are larger and more aggressive, competing for mates while males incubate the eggs, a rare behavior among birds. A fun fact is that they are among the few bird species where females initiate courtship and defend territories.
Red-backed shrike: The Red-backed shrike has a grey head, reddish-brown back, black wings with white patches, and a white throat. It inhabits open woodlands, scrublands, and hedgerows across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on insects, impaling them on thorns to store or eat later. Its habit of storing prey on thorns gives it the nickname "butcher bird."
Red-billed chough: This black bird has a bright red bill and legs, living in mountainous regions across Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects and invertebrates, often flying in noisy groups with acrobatic maneuvers. A fun fact is its historical association with St. Kevin in Irish folklore.
Red-breasted flycatcher: The Red-breasted Flycatcher has a reddish breast in males with gray head and brown back, while females are duller with a pale breast. It inhabits deciduous and mixed forests across Eurasia, migrating long distances to tropical regions for winter. It feeds primarily on flying insects caught mid-air, displaying agile foraging behavior. A fun fact is that it often joins mixed-species bird flocks during migration.
Red-breasted goose: The Red-breasted goose has a black head and neck, a bright red breast patch, white rump, and gray back. It breeds in Arctic tundra regions of Russia and winters in grasslands and agricultural fields across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on grasses and sedges, forming large noisy flocks during migration. Its loud, distinctive "kree" call is often heard in flocks.
Red-breasted merganser: Male Red-breasted mergansers have a reddish breast, green head, and a long thin serrated bill. They breed in northern lakes and winter along coasts, diving for fish in large groups. Their call sounds like a rusty gate hinge.
Red-crested pochard: Male Red-crested pochards have a bright red head with a black crest, while females are brownish. They inhabit shallow freshwater lakes and ponds across Europe and Asia. They feed on aquatic plants and invertebrates by diving, often forming large flocks. A fun fact is that males perform a distinctive head-bobbing display during courtship.
Red-flanked bluetail: The Red-flanked bluetail has a male with bright red flanks and a blue tail, while the female is brown with pale streaks. It breeds in forested areas across northern Asia and migrates to Southeast Asia for winter. It feeds primarily on insects gleaned from the ground or low vegetation and is typically active and short-lived. A fun fact is that it is a common visitor to gardens in Southeast Asia during its migration.
Red-footed falcon: Red-footed falcons have reddish legs and feet, with males displaying reddish-brown upperparts and pale heads, while females are browner. They breed in open habitats like grasslands and farmlands across Europe and Asia, migrating to sub-Saharan Africa for winter. Their diet consists mainly of insects such as grasshoppers and beetles, and they hunt by hovering or from perches, often forming large colonies. A fun fact is that they sometimes nest in colonies alongside other birds like swallows.
Red-fronted serin: The Red-fronted serin has a bright red forehead patch, olive-green upperparts, and yellow underparts. It inhabits montane forests and woodlands in East Africa, often foraging in small flocks. Its diet consists mainly of seeds, and it is typically active and vocal in its habitat. A fun fact is that it produces a distinctive high-pitched "see-see-see" call while feeding.
Red-headed bunting: Male Red-headed buntings have striking red heads and breasts, while females are brown and streaked. They inhabit open grasslands, farmlands, and scrublands across eastern Asia. Their diet consists mainly of seeds and insects, and they form loose flocks outside the breeding season. A fun fact is that males sing a distinctive high-pitched "tsee-tsee" song during courtship.
Red-knobbed coot: The Red-knobbed coot has a dark black body, a white frontal shield, and distinctive red knobs on its forehead. It inhabits freshwater lakes, marshes, and rivers across sub-Saharan Africa. It feeds on aquatic plants, insects, and small invertebrates, often foraging in groups while displaying aggressive territorial behavior. Its loud, honking calls can carry over long distances in wetland habitats.
Red-legged partridge: The Red-legged partridge has brown and grey plumage with a white face and distinctive red legs. It inhabits open farmland, grasslands, and scrubby areas across southern Europe. Its diet includes seeds, insects, and plants, and it is ground-dwelling, often seen in coveys. It is a popular game bird hunted for sport in many regions.
Red-necked grebe: Red-necked grebes have a reddish neck and face in summer, gray back, and white underparts. They inhabit freshwater lakes and ponds in summer, moving to coastal waters in winter. Their diet consists mainly of fish and aquatic invertebrates, and they are skilled divers that build floating nests. They can compress their bodies to sink rapidly underwater when threatened.
Red-necked nightjar: This bird has a reddish neck patch and mottled brown plumage for camouflage. It inhabits open woodlands and savannas across Africa and Asia, feeding on insects at dusk and nesting on the ground. Its distinctive chuckling call often echoes at night, a sound that mimics human laughter.
Red-necked phalarope: The Red-necked phalarope has a reddish neck and breast in breeding plumage, a gray back, and white underparts. It breeds in Arctic wetlands and winters on open oceans, feeding primarily on marine invertebrates and plankton by spinning in circles to create feeding currents. Females are larger and more brightly colored than males and take the lead in courtship. A fun fact is that females compete for males and leave the nesting duties to them.
Red-necked stint: The Red-necked stint has a brown back, pale underparts, and a distinct reddish neck during breeding season. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters on coastal mudflats and wetlands across Africa, Asia, and Australia. It feeds on small invertebrates like insects and worms, often foraging in large flocks. It undertakes one of the longest non-stop migrations of any bird, flying over 10,000 kilometers across the Indian Ocean.
Red-rumped swallow: The Red-rumped swallow has a dark blue upper body, white breast, and a prominent red patch on its lower back. It nests in colonies under bridges or on buildings in open countryside near water. It feeds on flying insects while foraging in flocks. This bird is known for its swift, agile flight patterns that allow it to catch insects mid-air with remarkable precision.
Red-rumped wheatear: The Red-rumped wheatear has brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a striking red rump patch. It inhabits open, rocky landscapes across Asia and Africa. It feeds primarily on insects and small invertebrates, foraging on the ground and singing from exposed perches. This bird undertakes remarkable long-distance migrations, sometimes exceeding 5,000 kilometers between breeding and wintering grounds.
Red-tailed shrike: The Red-tailed shrike has a gray back, white underparts, a black facial mask, and a distinctive red tail. It inhabits open grasslands, farmlands, and scrublands across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and small vertebrates, often impaling prey on thorns or barbed wire. A fun fact is that it regularly uses thorns to impale and store food, a behavior known as caching.
Red-tailed wheatear: It has pale brown upperparts, a white throat, and a bright red tail. It inhabits arid grasslands and deserts across Asia and Africa, foraging for insects on the ground. Its loud, distinctive call inspired the common name 'wheatear'.
Red-throated loon: The Red-throated loon has a grey back, white underparts, and a distinctive red throat patch during breeding season. It inhabits Arctic coastal waters and open oceans year-round, nesting on tundra lakes. It feeds primarily on fish and invertebrates, diving underwater to hunt with great agility. This bird can swim submerged for up to two minutes while hunting.
Red-throated pipit: The Red-throated pipit has a pale brown back, white underparts, and a distinct red throat patch in breeding season. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters in open grasslands, farmlands, and wetlands across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists of insects and seeds, and it forages on the ground with short flights. A fun fact is that its repetitive call sounds like "pip-pip," giving the species its common name.
Red-throated thrush: The Red-throated thrush has a brown back, white underparts, and a distinctive reddish throat patch. It inhabits coniferous and mixed forests in northern regions during breeding. Its diet consists of insects, worms, and berries, and it forages on the ground while singing from perches. This species undertakes long migrations to winter in sub-Saharan Africa.
Red-wattled lapwing: The Red-wattled lapwing has brown upperparts, white underparts, and distinctive red facial wattles. It inhabits open farmlands, wetlands, and grasslands across South Asia, feeding primarily on insects and small invertebrates. It is highly vocal with loud alarm calls and aggressively defends its ground nest. A fun fact is that it is known to attack snakes near its nest.
Redhead: Redheads have a distinctive reddish head in males, contrasting with a gray body and black breast. They inhabit freshwater lakes and ponds across North America, migrating to coastal waters in winter. Their diet consists mainly of aquatic plants and invertebrates, and they are social, forming large flocks. A fun fact is that Redheads often lay eggs in the nests of other ducks, a behavior known as brood parasitism.
Redwing: Redwings have brown upperparts with distinctive reddish wing patches and a pale eye stripe, living in open woodlands, farmlands, and gardens across Europe. They eat insects, worms, and berries, forming noisy flocks during migration and singing from high perches. Their melodious song is a characteristic sound of European spring woodlands.
Ring ouzel: The Ring ouzel is a dark grey-brown thrush with a prominent white crescent on its breast and white tail corners. It inhabits upland areas like mountains and moors across Europe and Asia, feeding on berries and insects. It is migratory, often seen in flocks during winter. A fun fact is that its white breast patch resembles a ring, giving it the name "ring ouzel."
Ring-billed gull: Ring-billed gulls have white bodies, gray wings, and a yellow bill with a distinct black ring. They live near water bodies, coastlines, and urban areas like landfills and parks. They eat fish, insects, and human food scraps, often foraging in noisy groups. They are known to collect shiny objects such as coins.
Ring-necked duck: Male Ring-necked ducks have a black head with a subtle white neck ring, a dark back, and a white belly. They inhabit freshwater lakes, ponds, and marshes across North America. They feed on aquatic plants and invertebrates, diving underwater to forage in groups. A fun fact is that the white neck ring on males is often hard to see, making the common name somewhat misleading.
River warbler: The River Warbler has brown upperparts with pale streaks and a pale eyebrow, often seen in dense reed beds near water. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, remaining hidden while singing from cover. Its loud, repetitive song is frequently heard before the bird is spotted in its wetland habitat.
Rock bunting: Rock buntings have streaked brown plumage with yellow facial patches and underparts. They inhabit rocky cliffs, mountainsides, and open farmlands across Europe and Asia. They feed primarily on seeds and insects, foraging on the ground and often forming small flocks. Their distinctive trilling song is commonly heard in their rocky habitats.
Rock martin: Rock martin has dark brown upperparts and pale underparts with a forked tail. It nests in colonies on cliffs, buildings, and bridges across open landscapes. It feeds on flying insects caught mid-air and is highly social, often seen in flocks. A fun fact is that Rock martins can hover briefly like hummingbirds while feeding.
Rock pigeon: Rock pigeons have gray bodies with iridescent neck feathers and white rumps. They live in cities and towns nesting on buildings and bridges. They eat seeds, grains, and human food scraps while forming large social flocks. Pigeons can navigate using the Earth's magnetic field to find their way home.
Rock pipit: Rock pipits have brown streaked backs and pale undersides, often seen on rocky seashores. They feed on insects and small invertebrates picked from the ground or shorelines. Their behavior includes running along coastlines and short, low flights, and they are often mistaken for other pipits but are exclusively coastal. A fun fact is that they can be found nesting on cliff faces far from water in some regions.
Rock ptarmigan: Rock ptarmigans have white plumage in winter and brown in summer for camouflage, inhabiting Arctic and alpine tundra regions. They primarily eat plant material like willow buds and berries, and are ground-dwelling birds that form flocks during cold months. A fun fact is their feet are covered in feathers to prevent sinking into snow.
Rock sparrow: Rock sparrows have streaked brown backs and pale underparts with a prominent black bib on the throat. They inhabit rocky outcrops, cliffs, and human structures across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists mainly of seeds and insects, and they are social birds often seen in small groups. They are known to mimic sounds from their surroundings.
Rook: Rooks are entirely black birds with a bare grey head and neck, featuring a distinctive hooked bill. They inhabit open countryside with trees, often forming large communal roosts in woodlands or farmlands. Their diet includes insects, grains, and carrion, and they are highly social, often seen in noisy flocks. Rooks are known to use tools, such as dropping nuts onto roads to crack them open.
Roseate tern: Roseate terns have pale gray backs, white underparts, and a black cap during breeding season with a pinkish tinge on the breast. They nest colonially on coastal islands and beaches worldwide, migrating to temperate zones for breeding. They feed primarily on small fish caught by plunge-diving and exhibit strong pair bonds with both parents caring for young. A fun fact is that their courtship involves a distinctive aerial display where pairs fly in a tight V formation while calling.
Rosss gull: Ross's gull has a white body, black wingtips, and a bright red bill. It breeds in Arctic regions and winters along coastal areas. Its diet includes fish and invertebrates, and it is typically solitary and shy. This gull is one of the rarest gull species globally.
Rosy starling: Rosy starlings have pinkish plumage in summer with a dark head, nesting in colonies on cliffs or in tree holes across open farmlands. They feed on insects and fruits, often foraging in noisy flocks that perform agile aerial displays. A fun fact is that their name comes from the rosy hue they display during the breeding season.
Rough-legged buzzard: Rough-legged buzzards have feathered legs and a brownish body with a pale belly. They breed in Arctic tundra and migrate to open fields and grasslands in temperate regions. They hunt rodents like voles by hovering motionless in the air. A fun fact is they can hover for extended periods while searching for prey.
Royal tern: Royal terns have white bodies, gray backs, black caps, and long orange bills. They nest on sandy beaches and islands in coastal regions worldwide. They feed primarily on fish caught by plunge-diving and often forage in groups. Royal terns can drink seawater due to specialized salt-excreting glands.
Ruddy duck: Male Ruddy ducks have a distinctive reddish-brown body and a blue bill in breeding plumage. They inhabit freshwater ponds and lakes across North America and Europe. Their diet consists of aquatic plants, insects, and small invertebrates, and they are skilled divers. Males perform an unusual courtship display by inflating their chest feathers and making a squeaky sound.
Ruddy shelduck: Ruddy shelducks have a reddish-brown body, white wings, and a distinctive white head with a dark patch around the eyes. They inhabit freshwater lakes, rivers, and wetlands across Asia, often nesting in burrows near water. Their diet consists mainly of aquatic plants and seeds, and they are social birds that forage in groups. They are known for loud whistling calls during flight.
Ruddy turnstone: Ruddy turnstones have brown and white plumage with black markings on their backs and faces. They inhabit shorelines, mudflats, and beaches worldwide, feeding on invertebrates by flipping stones and shells. These birds are highly active foragers with a distinctive habit of turning over objects to find food. They undertake remarkable long-distance migrations, traveling from Arctic breeding grounds to South American wintering sites.
Ruff: Ruffs have a stocky build with males displaying elaborate, colorful ruffs during breeding season. They inhabit wetlands and grasslands across Europe and Asia, feeding on insects, worms, and small aquatic invertebrates. Males gather in leks to perform aerial displays. A fun fact is that male Ruffs can have different colored ruffs on each side of their neck.
Rufous-tailed scrub robin: This bird has a reddish-brown tail and brown upperparts with pale underparts, found in dry scrublands across sub-Saharan Africa. It forages for insects on the ground, often flicking its tail while moving. Its loud, melodious song is surprisingly powerful for its small size.
Ruppells vulture: Ruppell's vulture has a pale head with a dark cap, a bulky body, and a white band on its tail. It inhabits open savannas and grasslands across sub-Saharan Africa, feeding primarily on carrion. These birds soar high for long periods and gather in groups at carcasses. They hold the record for the highest recorded flight altitude of any bird.
Rustic bunting: Rustic buntings have streaked brown upperparts and pale underparts, with males showing a black crown and bib during breeding. They breed in open woodlands and scrub across northern Asia, migrating to southern Asia for winter. Their diet consists mainly of seeds and insects, and they are shy birds that forage in dense vegetation. A fun fact is their song is a series of sharp, high-pitched notes often described as sounding like "tsee-tsee-tsee."
Sabines gull: Sabine's gull has a black head and white forehead in summer, gray back, and white underparts, breeding in Arctic tundra and migrating to coastal waters in winter. It feeds on insects, fish, and marine invertebrates while flying low over open water. A fun fact is that it is one of the few gull species that nests in the Arctic and has a distinctive sickle-shaped wing profile.
Saker falcon: Saker falcons have dark brown upperparts and pale underparts with a pale face. They inhabit open grasslands and steppes across Eurasia. They hunt birds and small mammals using high-speed aerial pursuits. They were historically prized in Central Asian falconry for their hunting prowess.
Sand martin:
Sand martins have brown upperparts, a pale throat, and white underparts. They nest in colonies on sandy riverbanks or gravel pits.  
They eat flying insects caught in swift, agile flight.  
A fun fact is that they form massive nesting colonies, sometimes with hundreds of burrows in a single bank.
Sand partridge: It has sandy brown plumage that blends with desert soils. It inhabits open dry scrublands and deserts across North Africa and the Middle East. It feeds on seeds and insects while moving in small flocks on the ground. It can run very fast to evade predators.
Sanderling: Sanderlings are small sandpipers with gray-brown upperparts and white underparts in breeding season, becoming uniformly pale gray in winter. They inhabit sandy beaches globally, migrating long distances between Arctic breeding grounds and coastal wintering areas. They feed on small invertebrates by running rapidly along the water's edge, probing the sand. A fun fact is that they are among the most widespread shorebirds, found on every continent's coast.
Sandwich tern: Sandwich terns have a distinctive black cap, yellow-tipped black bill, and white plumage. They nest on sandy coasts and islands, often in large colonies. They feed primarily on small fish by plunge-diving and are highly social, often flying in groups. A fun fact is that they were named after Sandwich, England, where early naturalists first described them.
Sardinian warbler: Sardinian warblers have gray-brown backs and pale undersides, with males showing black heads and white throats. They inhabit Mediterranean scrublands, coastal thickets, and maquis vegetation. Their diet consists of insects and berries, and they are active, territorial birds often seen in pairs. Fun fact: their loud repetitive song sounds like "swee-swee-swee" and is commonly heard during the breeding season.
Savis warbler: Savi's warbler is a small brown bird with a pale eyebrow and thin bill. It inhabits dense reed beds near wetlands, feeding on insects and small invertebrates. This secretive bird sings a loud repetitive song from hidden perches, and its call often sounds like a buzzing insect.
Sedge warbler: This small brown warbler has streaked upperparts and a pale eyebrow. It breeds in wet grasslands and reed beds across Europe, feeding on insects while singing from dense cover. Its song includes mimicry of other birds, making it a vocal mimic.
See-see partridge: The see-see partridge has brown plumage with white spots and a distinctive red bill. It inhabits dry savannas and scrublands across sub-Saharan Africa. Its diet consists of seeds, insects, and small invertebrates, and it forages in small groups on the ground. Its name comes from its repetitive call sounding like "see-see".
Semicollared flycatcher: The Semicollared flycatcher has a distinctive black head and white collar, with grayish-brown back and white wing patches. It inhabits deciduous and mixed forests across Europe and Asia, nesting in tree cavities. It feeds primarily on insects caught in flight and is territorial during the breeding season. A fun fact is that males sing complex songs to attract females, and their songs vary regionally like human dialects.
Semipalmated plover: This small shorebird has brown upperparts, white underparts, and a distinct black breast band. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters on sandy beaches, feeding on insects and worms by running and stopping abruptly. It undertakes one of the longest migrations among shorebirds, traveling over 10,000 kilometers annually.
Semipalmated sandpiper: This small shorebird has a brown streaked back, pale breast, and short dark bill. It breeds in Arctic tundra and winters along coasts from North America to South America. It feeds on small invertebrates by probing mudflats and forms large migrating flocks. It undertakes one of the longest nonstop flights of any bird, covering up to 6,000 miles during migration.
Senegal coucal: The Senegal coucal has dark brown plumage with a reddish head and a long tail. It inhabits open woodlands and savannas across sub-Saharan Africa. It feeds primarily on insects and small invertebrates, foraging stealthily on the ground while being known for its loud, repetitive calls. Its distinctive "kook-kook" call is often heard before the bird is spotted.
Senegal thick-knee: The Senegal thick-knee has mottled brown plumage, large yellow eyes, and long yellow legs adapted for walking in open terrain. It inhabits savannas, grasslands, and open woodlands across sub-Saharan Africa, feeding primarily on insects, small reptiles, and invertebrates at night. This nocturnal bird is known for its loud, distinctive call and often remains motionless during the day to avoid detection. A fun fact is that its common name comes from the loud, repetitive "thick-knee" call it makes, especially at dusk.
Sharp-tailed sandpiper: Sharp-tailed sandpipers have brown streaked backs, pale underparts, and a distinctive pointed tail. They breed in Siberian wetlands and migrate to coastal mudflats in Australia and Southeast Asia. Their diet consists of insects and small invertebrates, and they feed in flocks while foraging. They undertake one of the longest migrations of any shorebird, traveling over 10,000 kilometers annually.
Short-billed dowitcher: Short-billed dowitchers have brown streaked backs and pale underparts with a short, straight bill. They inhabit wetlands and mudflats across North America during migration and breeding seasons. They feed on invertebrates by probing mud with their bills and often forage in flocks. Their distinctive loud "peep" call is easily recognizable.
Short-eared owl:
Short-eared owls have brown and pale streaked plumage, short ear tufts, and large yellow eyes. They inhabit open grasslands, marshes, and tundra, often nesting on the ground.  
They primarily hunt small mammals like voles, flying low and silently with a distinctive buoyant flight pattern.  
Fun fact: They are known for their spectacular long-distance migrations across continents.
Short-toed snake eagle: This bird has dark brown plumage with a pale head and white wing patches. It inhabits open grasslands, farmlands, and scrublands across Europe, Asia, and Africa. It specializes in hunting snakes, often spotting them from high soaring flights before striking. A fun fact is that it can safely eat venomous snakes without harm.
Short-toed treecreeper: This small brown bird has streaked upperparts, a pale throat, and a long curved bill. It inhabits mature forests, especially coniferous woodlands, where it forages on tree trunks and large branches. It eats insects and spiders by climbing vertically in a spiral pattern, often following woodpeckers to catch disturbed prey. A fun fact is that it sometimes uses its stiff tail feathers to brace itself while climbing trees.
Siberian accentor: The Siberian accentor has brown upperparts, a pale eyebrow, and a white eye ring. It breeds in dense coniferous forests across Siberia and winters in East Asia. It eats insects and berries, foraging quietly in undergrowth. Its distinctive song sounds like sharp, repeated notes.
Siberian crane: The Siberian crane is a large white bird with black wingtips and a distinctive red face patch. It breeds in wetlands across Siberia and migrates to wintering grounds in China, India, and Iran. Its diet includes aquatic plants, insects, and small fish, and it travels in family groups during long migrations. A fun fact is that it performs an elaborate courtship dance involving head-bobbing and jumping.
Siberian jay: Siberian jays have a gray body with blue wing patches and a black mask around their eyes. They inhabit dense boreal coniferous forests across northern Eurasia. Their diet includes insects, seeds, and berries, and they are highly social, forming family groups that cache food for winter. They can recognize individual humans and distinguish between friendly and threatening people.
Siberian rubythroat: Male Siberian rubythroats have a distinctive bright red throat patch against dark brown upperparts. They breed in dense shrubs within Siberian taiga forests and migrate to Southeast Asia for winter. These insectivorous birds feed on flying insects and sing from exposed perches during the breeding season. A fun fact is that males produce a unique metallic tinkling note in their song.
Siberian sand plover: The Siberian sand plover has brown upperparts and a pale breast with a dark chest band in breeding plumage. It breeds in open Siberian tundra and winters on sandy beaches and mudflats across Asia and Africa. It feeds on insects and small invertebrates by running and pecking, often in small groups. This species undertakes one of the longest migrations of any shorebird, traveling over 10,000 kilometers annually.
Siberian stonechat: The Siberian stonechat has a distinctive black and white head and back in males, with a chestnut breast, while females are brown with pale streaks. It breeds in open habitats like steppes and tundra edges across northern Asia and winters in Africa and South Asia. It feeds primarily on insects caught by hawking from low perches and is known for its bold, territorial behavior. Its name comes from its sharp, stone-like call.
Sichuan tit: The Sichuan tit has gray upperparts, white underparts, and a distinctive black facial mask. It inhabits coniferous forests in Sichuan province, China, feeding primarily on insects and seeds while moving actively in small flocks. Its loud distinctive call sounds like 'pik-pik'.
Sinai rosefinch: This small finch has a pinkish head and breast with a distinct black face patch, inhabiting rocky scrublands in the Sinai Peninsula. It primarily eats seeds and forages in small social groups. A fun fact is that it thrives in the Sinai's harsh desert environment where few other birds survive.
Slender-billed gull: This gull has a pale grey back, white head with dark eye patches, and a slender black bill. It inhabits coastal lagoons and estuaries across Europe and Asia, feeding on fish and invertebrates while foraging in flocks. A fun fact is that its high-pitched call sounds like a soft 'kree-ee' alarm.
Smew:
Male Smews have striking black and white plumage with a pointy crest. Females are browner with a pale face. They breed in northern forested lakes and winter along coasts.  
Smews dive underwater to catch fish, their primary diet. They are solitary or form small groups during breeding.  
Smews are sometimes called water turkeys in certain regions.
Snow bunting: Snow buntings have white wings and backs with dark streaks, and brownish underparts. They nest in Arctic tundra and migrate to open fields and agricultural areas in temperate zones. Their diet is primarily seeds and insects, and they are social birds that form large flocks. They breed farther north than any other songbird.
Snow goose:
Snow geese have a white body with black wingtips and orange legs. They form large noisy flocks during migration and nesting.  
They breed in Arctic tundra, wintering in agricultural fields across North America. Their diet consists mainly of grasses, grains, and aquatic plants.  
A fun fact is that they undertake one of the longest migrations of any bird, traveling thousands of miles between breeding and wintering grounds.
Snowy owl: Snowy owls have pure white plumage with black barring, especially on females and juveniles, and inhabit open Arctic tundra. They primarily eat small mammals like voles and lemmings, hunting actively during daylight hours. Their large clutch size can reach up to ten eggs, making them one of the most prolific owl species.
Sociable lapwing: The Sociable lapwing has brown upperparts, white underparts, a black-and-white head pattern, and a long tail. It breeds in Central Asian grasslands and steppes, migrating to wintering grounds in the Middle East and Africa. It feeds on insects and seeds while foraging in flocks, known for forming very large social groups. A fun fact is that it often gathers in flocks of thousands during migration.
Solitary sandpiper: This bird has gray-brown upperparts, a pale eye stripe, and white underparts. It nests in wooded wetlands and forages along forest streams and ponds. It eats insects and small aquatic invertebrates while foraging alone, often walking slowly. A fun fact is it is one of the few shorebirds that nests in trees or dense vegetation.
Sombre tit: The Sombre tit has a dark grey head, white cheek, and pale body with a distinctive black eye stripe. It inhabits woodlands and forests across Europe and Asia, feeding on insects, seeds, and berries while foraging actively in trees. A fun fact is that it caches food in tree bark crevices to retrieve during winter.
Song thrush: The Song thrush has a brown back with black spots, a pale breast, and a yellow beak. It inhabits woodlands, gardens, and parks across Europe and Asia. Its diet includes worms, snails, and insects, and it is known for smashing snails on stones. It sings a loud, melodious song from high perches during the breeding season. A fun fact is that its song is one of the most recognizable and beloved bird sounds in European gardens.
Sooty falcon: The Sooty falcon has dark grey-brown plumage with a pale face and a distinct dark eye stripe. It inhabits arid coastal cliffs and islands across the Middle East and Africa. It hunts insects and small birds on the wing, migrating long distances and known for its remarkable annual journey exceeding 10,000 kilometers.
Sooty gull: The Sooty gull has dark grey plumage with a pale head and white eye rings. It inhabits coastal areas, islands, and shorelines across the Indian Ocean region. It feeds on fish, invertebrates, and scavenged food, often gathering in noisy groups. These birds are known for their loud, harsh calls that can be heard over coastal winds.
Sooty shearwater: Sooty shearwaters are dark brown or black birds with a white belly and long wings. They inhabit open oceans worldwide, breeding on remote southern hemisphere islands and migrating vast distances. They feed on fish, squid, and plankton, using dynamic soaring to glide efficiently over waves. Their annual migration covers over sixty thousand kilometers, making them among the longest-distance animal travelers.
Sooty tern: Sooty terns have dark gray plumage with a white forehead and underparts. They nest on tropical oceanic islands and forage over open seas. Their diet consists mainly of small fish and squid, and they are highly social, often forming large colonies while feeding on the wing. A fun fact is they undertake some of the longest migrations of any seabird, traveling thousands of miles annually between breeding and feeding grounds.
Sora: The Sora has a dark head, brown back, white throat, and a short bill. It inhabits freshwater marshes and wet meadows across North America. Its diet includes seeds, insects, and small aquatic invertebrates, and it moves stealthily through dense vegetation. Its distinctive call sounds like "sora-sora," giving the bird its common name.
Spanish imperial eagle:
Dark brown with a pale golden nape and a distinctive white tail patch, it inhabits open woodlands and grasslands in Spain and Portugal.  
It primarily hunts rabbits and small mammals, often soaring or perching to spot prey.  
They produce loud, raspy calls during courtship displays.
Spanish sparrow: Spanish sparrows have a brown back, pale underparts, and a warm orange-brown face with a dark stripe through the eye. They inhabit urban areas, farmlands, and coastal zones across southern Europe and North Africa. Their diet consists mainly of seeds and insects, and they are social, noisy birds often seen in groups. A fun fact is that they readily nest in buildings and have expanded their range significantly into new regions due to human settlements.
Spectacled warbler: This small warbler has brown upperparts, pale underparts, and distinctive white eye rings. It inhabits dry scrublands, farmlands, and coastal areas across southern Europe and North Africa, feeding mainly on insects while being active and restless. Its song is a characteristic high-pitched 'tsee-tsee' call.
Spotless starling: Spotless starlings have glossy black plumage with no spots in adult birds and inhabit open woodlands, farmlands, and urban areas across Europe and introduced regions. They feed on insects, fruits, and seeds while foraging in large, noisy flocks. A fun fact is that they were introduced to New York City in 1890 to represent all birds mentioned in Shakespeare's works.
Spotted crake: The Spotted crake has a brown and white spotted back, reddish-brown breast, and a short, dark bill. It inhabits dense freshwater wetlands like reed beds and marshes across Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects, worms, and small aquatic invertebrates, being secretive and active at dawn and dusk. Its distinctive call sounds like a rapid "chuck-chuck" repeated in a low, rhythmic pattern.
Spotted flycatcher: Spotted flycatchers have brown upperparts with white underparts and two pale wing bars. They inhabit woodlands, gardens, and parks across Europe and Asia. They hunt insects by sallying from perches and eat flies, beetles, and other small flying insects. Their soft repetitive "pew" call is a distinctive sound in summer gardens.
Spotted nutcracker: The Spotted nutcracker has white plumage with black spots and streaks, a large black bill, and a prominent crest. It inhabits coniferous forests across Eurasia, especially in mountainous regions. Its diet consists mainly of conifer seeds, which it caches extensively for later use. This caching behavior aids forest regeneration as forgotten seeds often germinate.
Spotted redshank: Spotted redshanks have a long red bill, dark legs, and distinctive spotted upperparts in breeding plumage. They inhabit coastal mudflats, estuaries, and wetlands during migration and winter. They probe mud for insects, worms, and small crustaceans and are often seen in flocks. Their loud, distinctive "tchick" call is commonly heard during flight.
Spotted sandgrouse: Spotted sandgrouse have mottled brown and white plumage for camouflage in dry landscapes. They inhabit arid grasslands, deserts, and scrublands across Africa and Asia. They primarily eat seeds and gather at water sources at dawn and dusk. Males carry water in specialized belly feathers to their chicks.
Spotted sandpiper: Spotted sandpipers have brown backs with white spots, white breasts, and a distinctive tail-bobbing walk. They inhabit shorelines of ponds, rivers, and lakes, feeding on insects, worms, and small aquatic invertebrates. Males incubate eggs and care for young while females often seek additional mates. Males perform a unique courtship display where they offer food to females while flying in a figure-eight pattern.
Spur-winged lapwing: Spur-winged lapwings have gray and white plumage with black wingtips and distinctive black spurs on their wings. They inhabit wetlands, lakes, and rivers across Africa, often near human settlements. They eat insects, worms, and small aquatic animals, and are highly vocal and territorial defenders. Their wing spurs are used aggressively in fights with other birds.
Squacco heron: The Squacco heron has brown plumage with a pale head and white underparts, often appearing as a small, stocky heron. It inhabits shallow freshwater wetlands like marshes and ponds, feeding on small fish, insects, and amphibians while hunting by standing still or walking slowly. Its name comes from an Italian cloth describing its mottled brown color, and it is often mistaken for a juvenile heron.
Stellers eider: Steller's eider has a distinctive black and white plumage in males, with females being brownish. It nests on Arctic tundra islands and winters in coastal marine waters. Its diet consists mainly of mollusks and crustaceans, which it dives to find. A fun fact is that its loud, trumpeting call can be heard over long distances across the frozen Arctic seas.
Steppe eagle:
Steppe eagles have dark brown plumage with pale underparts and a pale wing patch. They inhabit open grasslands and steppes across Eurasia.  
Their diet consists mainly of rodents and small birds, and they hunt by soaring or perching.  
A fun fact is that they undertake one of the longest migrations of any eagle, traveling over 10,000 kilometers annually.
Stilt sandpiper: Stilt sandpipers have long, pale legs, a slightly upturned bill, and brown-streaked upperparts in breeding plumage. They nest in Arctic tundra and migrate through wetlands and mudflats across North America. Their diet consists of insects, worms, and small crustaceans, and they forage actively by probing or picking from the surface. A fun fact is that they undertake one of the longest migrations of any shorebird, traveling over 10,000 miles annually between Arctic breeding grounds and South American wintering sites.
Stock dove: Stock doves have gray bodies, black wing patches, and a white neck ring. They inhabit woodlands, farmlands, and urban areas, nesting in tree cavities or cliffs. Their diet consists mainly of seeds and grains, and they are social birds often seen in flocks. Their soft, repetitive cooing is a common sound in European countryside.
Streaked scrub warbler: The Streaked scrub warbler has brown streaked upperparts and pale underparts. It inhabits dry scrublands and grasslands across parts of Asia. It forages on the ground for insects and spiders, moving with quick, restless movements. Its loud, repetitive song resembles "chick-a-dee" and can be heard from dense cover.
Striated heron: The Striated heron has dark grey plumage with white streaks on its back and a white throat, commonly found near freshwater and coastal wetlands. It feeds on small fish, insects, and crustaceans by standing motionless to ambush prey. A fun fact is that it sometimes uses bait like bread crumbs to attract fish.
Striolated bunting: The Striated Bunting has brown streaked plumage on its back and pale underparts with dark streaks. It inhabits grasslands and scrublands across central Asia, feeding primarily on seeds and insects while foraging in small groups. Its song consists of repeated high-pitched "tsee" notes often heard during spring.
Surf scoter: Surf scoters are large, dark sea ducks with distinctive white patches on the male's head. They inhabit coastal waters along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, breeding in boreal forests and wintering in sheltered bays and estuaries. They primarily feed on marine invertebrates like mussels and clams by diving deep, often forming large flocks. A fun fact is that they produce a characteristic "sucking" sound while feeding underwater.
Swainsons thrush: Swainsons thrush has brown upperparts, a pale spotted breast, and a white eye ring. It inhabits forests in North America during summer, nesting in dense undergrowth and migrating to Central America for winter. Its diet consists of insects and berries, and it forages quietly on the forest floor, often singing a flute-like song. A fun fact is that its song is considered one of the most beautiful among North American songbirds.
Swinhoes storm petrel: Swinhoes storm petrel has dark brown plumage with a distinctive white rump and black legs. It inhabits the open Pacific Ocean, breeding on remote rocky islands in the western Pacific. Its diet consists of plankton and small fish, and it forages by skimming the water surface. A fun fact is that it can walk briefly on the ocean surface while feeding.
Sykess warbler: Sykes's warbler has a brown back with pale streaks and a pale eyebrow. It inhabits dry scrublands and desert edges across India and Pakistan. It feeds primarily on insects and is known for its secretive behavior in dense vegetation. A fun fact is that it was named after the British naturalist William Sykes who collected specimens in the 1800s.
Syrian serin: The Syrian serin has green upperparts, yellow underparts, and a black face patch. It inhabits open woodlands, scrublands, and agricultural areas across the Levant region. It feeds mainly on seeds and insects, often foraging in small flocks with active, social behavior. Its cheerful, repetitive call sounds like "see-see-see" and can be heard throughout its range.
Syrian woodpecker: The Syrian woodpecker has black and white barred plumage with a red crown patch on males. It inhabits deciduous woodlands, orchards, and parklands across its range in the Middle East. It feeds primarily on insects, especially larvae, by pecking tree bark and uses drumming for communication. This species is known to visit bird feeders for suet.
Taiga bean goose: Taiga bean geese have brownish body plumage, a pale face, and a dark head patch. They breed in Siberian taiga forests and winter in wetlands across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists mainly of grasses and sedges, and they form large, noisy flocks during migration. A fun fact is their distinctive call resembles the word "bean," giving them their common name.
Taiga flycatcher: The Taiga flycatcher has grayish-brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a dark eye stripe. It breeds in coniferous forests across northern Eurasia. It catches insects mid-air, often perching low to hunt, and migrates long distances to winter in Southeast Asia. A fun fact is that it travels over 5,000 kilometers each way during migration.
Tawny eagle: The Tawny eagle has a brown body with a pale neck and dark tail, inhabiting open grasslands, deserts, and savannas across Africa and Asia. It primarily scavenges carrion but also hunts small mammals and birds, often soaring high or stealing food from other raptors. A fun fact is that they frequently follow large mammals like elephants to catch insects disturbed by the animals.
Tawny owl: Tawny owls have brown mottled plumage and a distinct facial disk. They inhabit woodlands, forests, and sometimes suburban parks across Europe and Asia. They hunt small mammals like mice at night, using silent flight and sharp talons. Their head can rotate nearly 270 degrees to scan for prey.
Tawny pipit: The Tawny pipit has brown streaked upperparts, pale underparts, and a distinct pale eyebrow. It inhabits open grasslands, farmlands, and coastal areas across Europe and Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and seeds, foraging on the ground by hopping and running. Its distinctive song is a series of high-pitched notes often given while hovering. A fun fact is that it sometimes mimics the calls of other birds.
Temmincks stint: Temminck's stint is a small shorebird with streaked brown upperparts and pale grey underparts in breeding plumage. It breeds in wetlands and migrates to coastal mudflats, feeding on insects and small invertebrates while foraging in flocks. This species undertakes remarkable long-distance migrations, often covering over 10,000 kilometers annually.
Tenerife blue chaffinch: This bird has bright blue plumage in males and duller grayish-brown in females. It lives exclusively in the high-altitude pine forests of Tenerife, Canary Islands. It primarily eats pine seeds and is social in winter but territorial during breeding. Its population is critically low, making it one of the rarest birds globally.
Terek sandpiper: Terek sandpipers have a slender build, gray-brown back, white underparts, and a long, slightly downcurved bill. They inhabit shallow wetlands, mudflats, and coastal areas across Europe, Asia, and Africa during migration and winter. They feed primarily on insects and small invertebrates, foraging actively by running and probing the ground. A fun fact is that they often flick their tails upward while feeding.
Thick-billed lark: The Thick-billed lark has brown streaked upperparts, pale underparts, and a pale eyebrow. It inhabits dry grasslands and open areas across sub-Saharan Africa. It feeds on seeds and insects while foraging on the ground and is known for its loud, distinctive song. Its song can often be heard over long distances in open habitats.
Thick-billed murre: Thick-billed murres have black backs and white fronts with a thick black bill. They breed on Arctic sea cliffs and spend winters on open ocean. They dive for fish like capelin and herring, often in large groups, and nest closely together on rocky ledges. They can dive over 200 meters deep to catch prey.
Thick-billed warbler: The Thick-billed warbler has a brownish upper body, pale underparts, and a notably thick bill. It breeds in wet grasslands and reedbeds across central and eastern Europe and Asia, migrating to southern Asia for winter. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, foraging stealthily in dense vegetation while being shy and elusive. Its loud, distinctive song is often heard before the bird is seen.
Tree pipit: Tree pipits have brown streaked backs and pale underparts. They inhabit open woodlands, farmlands, and grasslands across Europe and Asia. They eat insects and seeds, foraging on the ground and singing from tree tops. Their song is often mistaken for a meadow pipit's but is typically delivered from a higher perch.
Tristrams starling: Tristram's starling was a small bird with gray plumage and black wings. It lived in desert scrub habitats across the Sinai Peninsula, feeding on insects and berries. This social bird is now extinct, known only from museum specimens collected in the 1890s. A fun fact is it was last reliably recorded over 120 years ago.
Trocaz pigeon: The Trocaz pigeon is a large dark bird with a pinkish breast and white wing patches. It inhabits native laurel forests on São Miguel Island in the Azores. Its diet consists of forest fruits and seeds, and it is typically seen in pairs or small groups. It is the national bird of the Azores.
Trumpeter finch: The Trumpeter finch has a brown-streaked body, pale eyebrow, and a white throat patch. It inhabits dry rocky scrublands and farmlands across northern Africa and the Middle East. It feeds mainly on seeds and insects, often foraging in flocks while singing loudly from perches. Its name comes from its repetitive, trumpet-like call.
Tufted duck: Males have a black head with a distinctive rear tuft, while females are brown. They inhabit freshwater lakes and ponds across Europe and Asia. They dive for aquatic invertebrates and plants, forming large flocks in winter. Fun fact: Tufted ducks can stay underwater for up to 30 seconds while foraging.
Tundra bean goose: Tundra bean geese have brown bodies, pale heads, and distinctive black-and-white wing patterns. They breed in Arctic tundra and winter in grasslands and agricultural areas across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists of grasses and sedges, and they form large, noisy flocks during migration. A fun fact is that they undertake some of the longest annual migrations of any goose species.
Tundra swan: Tundra swans are large white birds with black legs and a dark bill base. They breed in Arctic tundra, migrate long distances to coastal wetlands and lakes in temperate zones, and feed primarily on aquatic plants. They are highly social, forming lifelong pairs and migrating in noisy V-formations. Their distinctive high-pitched whooping call can be heard for miles during migration.
Turkestan short-toed lark: The Turkestan short-toed lark has sandy-brown plumage with dark streaks on its back and head, blending into its open steppe environment. It inhabits dry grasslands and cultivated fields across Central Asia, feeding primarily on seeds and insects while foraging on the ground. It sings a distinctive musical song from low perches or during flight displays. A fun fact is that its song is often heard as a rising, warbling series of notes during its characteristic hovering display flight.
Twite: Twite have brown streaked upperparts, pale underparts, and a distinctive yellow bill. They inhabit open grasslands, heaths, and coastal areas across Europe and Asia. Their diet consists mainly of seeds, and they form large flocks in winter. A fun fact is that their name comes from their characteristic "twit" call.
Two-barred crossbill: The Two-barred crossbill has a distinctive crossed bill and shows two dark bars on its wings. It inhabits coniferous forests across northern North America and Eurasia. Its diet consists primarily of conifer seeds, and it moves nomadically to find food sources. A fun fact is that its crossed bill allows it to efficiently extract seeds from pine cones without opening them.
Two-barred warbler: The Two-barred warbler has two distinct dark bars on its wings and a pale eyebrow stripe. It inhabits dense coniferous and mixed forests during breeding season in eastern Europe and Asia, migrating to Southeast Asia for winter. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, foraging actively in the understory by flitting through foliage. A fun fact is that it undertakes one of the longest migrations of any small warbler species.
Upland sandpiper: Upland sandpipers have brown-streaked backs and white underparts with a long neck and legs. They inhabit open grasslands and prairies across North America, feeding mainly on insects and worms. Their loud, whistled call and distinctive courtship display, where males soar high before parachuting down, are notable behaviors.
Ural owl: Ural owls have brown plumage with pale streaks and lack ear tufts. They inhabit mature forests across Eurasia, nesting in tree cavities. Their diet consists mainly of small mammals like voles, and they are nocturnal hunters with loud territorial calls. They can rotate their heads nearly 270 degrees.
Veery: Veery has a brown back, reddish tail, and a streaked pale breast. It inhabits moist deciduous forests in eastern North America during breeding season. Its diet includes insects and berries, and it forages on the forest floor, often singing from low perches. Its name comes from its distinctive downward-sloping song that sounds like "veer."
Velvet scoter: Velvet scoters have dark black plumage with a glossy purple sheen on males and brownish females, featuring bright yellow eyes. They breed in freshwater lakes and rivers across northern Europe and Asia, then migrate to coastal marine waters for winter. Their diet consists mainly of aquatic invertebrates like mussels, crustaceans, and worms, which they dive to forage. A fun fact is that they produce a distinctive soft chuckling call during courtship.
Verreauxs eagle: Verreaux's eagle is predominantly black with white wing and tail patches and a white rump. It inhabits rocky mountainous regions across southern Africa. Its diet consists almost entirely of rock hyraxes, which it hunts by soaring high and diving with precision. A fun fact is that pairs perform dramatic aerial courtship displays involving locked talons and tumbling dives.
Wallcreeper: Wallcreeper has a reddish-brown back, white underparts, and black wings. It inhabits rocky mountain cliffs and buildings in Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects and spiders, moving vertically on rock faces using its stiff tail for support. A fun fact is that it is one of the few birds capable of climbing straight up vertical rock surfaces without flapping its wings.
Water pipit: Water pipits have brown streaked backs and pale underparts with a white eye stripe. They inhabit wet grasslands, meadows, and marshy areas across Europe and Asia. They feed primarily on insects and seeds, foraging on the ground while often bobbing their tails. A fun fact is that they undertake some of the longest migratory journeys among small passerines, traveling over 5,000 kilometers annually.
Water rail: The Water rail has a dark brown back, barred chest, and a red bill. It inhabits dense reed beds and marshes across Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects, worms, and small aquatic creatures while being secretive and active at dawn and dusk. Its loud, repetitive call sounds like "wheep-wheep" often heard before the bird is seen.
Western Orphean warbler:
This warbler has gray-brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a pale eyebrow. It breeds in scrublands and open woodlands across southern Europe and North Africa. It feeds mainly on insects while actively foraging in dense vegetation.

Its song is a distinctive flute-like series of notes.
Western black-eared wheatear: This small bird has pale brown upperparts and a distinctive black ear patch. It inhabits dry open habitats like steppes and rocky deserts across North Africa and the Middle East. It feeds primarily on insects while foraging on the ground, often perching on rocks to scan for prey. A fun fact is that its common name refers to its habit of flicking its tail like a wheat stalk when perched.
Western capercaillie: The Western capercaillie is a large forest grouse with males displaying dark plumage and a prominent white throat patch. It inhabits mature coniferous forests across northern Europe and Asia, feeding primarily on conifer needles, berries, and insects. Males perform loud lekking displays on forest clearings to attract females. A fun fact is that males produce a distinctive loud "koo-koo" call during these displays to attract mates.
Western jackdaw: Western jackdaws have a grey body, black head, and a pale eye ring. They inhabit open countryside, farmlands, and urban areas across Europe and western Asia. Their diet includes insects, seeds, and human food scraps, and they are highly social, forming large noisy flocks. They can recognize individual human faces and remember them for years.
Western marsh harrier: This bird has brown plumage with long wings and a long tail, commonly seen over wetlands like marshes and grasslands. It hunts small mammals, birds, and insects while flying low and steadily. A fun fact is that males perform aerial courtship displays called 'sky-dancing' to attract females.
Western olivaceous warbler: This small warbler has olive-brown upperparts and a pale throat. It inhabits scrubland, gardens, and woodland edges in southern Europe and North Africa. It feeds on insects and spiders, foraging actively in bushes. Its distinctive song helps distinguish it from similar species.
Western reef heron: Western reef herons have white plumage with a black cap during breeding and greyish in non-breeding seasons. They inhabit coastal mangroves and shorelines, feeding primarily on fish while foraging alone. A fun fact is they can remain motionless for over an hour waiting to catch prey.
Western rock nuthatch: The Western rock nuthatch has a grey back, black cap, white face, and pale underparts. It inhabits rocky cliffs, boulders, and arid scrubland in the Middle East and Central Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, foraging by climbing vertically on rock faces and moving headfirst down surfaces. This species is known for its ability to descend trees headfirst, a rare trait among birds.
Western sandpiper: Western sandpipers are small brownish shorebirds with buffy underparts and dark streaks. They breed in Arctic tundra and migrate to coastal mudflats, beaches, and estuaries worldwide. Their diet consists of insects, worms, and small crustaceans, which they probe for in wet sand or mud. They are known for their incredibly long migrations, traveling up to 10,000 miles annually between breeding and wintering grounds.
Western subalpine warbler: This small warbler has brown upperparts and pale yellow underparts. It inhabits mountainous scrublands and forests during breeding, feeding primarily on insects while foraging actively in dense vegetation. Its loud, repetitive song sounds like "whee-oo."
Western swamphen: The Western swamphen has striking purple-blue plumage, a bright red bill, and red legs. It inhabits freshwater wetlands like reed beds and marshes across Europe, Asia, and Africa. It eats plants, insects, and small aquatic animals and is known for being social and noisy. Its loud, distinctive call can carry over long distances.
Western yellow wagtail: The Western yellow wagtail has bright yellow underparts and a greenish back in breeding plumage, with a distinctive tail-wagging behavior while foraging. It inhabits wet grasslands, meadows, and agricultural fields across Europe and Asia during breeding. Its diet consists mainly of insects like flies and beetles, and it is highly active and vocal. A fun fact is that some populations migrate over 10,000 kilometers annually between breeding grounds in Europe and wintering areas in sub-Saharan Africa.
Whinchat: The Whinchat has a brown back, pale underparts, and a prominent white eyebrow. It inhabits open habitats like heathlands, grassy fields, and hedgerows. It feeds mainly on insects caught by sallying from perches and often perches prominently while singing. Its name comes from its characteristic call note.
Whiskered tern: The Whiskered tern has a dark cap, pale grey back, and white underparts with distinctive black "whiskers" below its eyes. It inhabits freshwater and coastal wetlands, nesting in colonies on floating vegetation or mudflats. Its diet consists mainly of insects and small fish caught while flying, and it exhibits agile, acrobatic foraging behavior. A fun fact is that it can plunge-dive underwater to catch fish, unlike many other tern species.
White stork: White storks have white plumage, black wingtips, and red legs and feet. They inhabit open habitats like grasslands, wetlands, and farmlands across Europe and Africa, often nesting on tall structures. Their diet consists mainly of insects, amphibians, and small mammals, and they migrate in large flocks. A popular cultural myth associates them with bringing babies.
White wagtail: White wagtails have a distinctive black and white plumage with a white head and underparts. They inhabit open country including fields, gardens, and riverbanks across Europe and Asia. They eat insects and are known for constantly wagging their tails while foraging. A fun fact is that they are among the most widespread wagtail species, breeding across much of the Northern Hemisphere.
White-backed woodpecker: The White-backed woodpecker has a black body with a distinctive white back and a red crown patch. It inhabits mature forests with old trees, primarily in Europe and Asia. It feeds on wood-boring insects, foraging by pecking and drumming on tree trunks. Its drumming pattern is notably loud and rhythmic for communication.
White-cheeked tern: The White-cheeked tern has a white face with a black eye patch, grey upperparts, and white underparts. It inhabits coastal areas, nesting on sandy or rocky shores in the Indian Ocean region. It feeds primarily on small fish caught by plunge-diving and exhibits colonial nesting behavior. Its sharp kree call is a distinctive feature.
White-crowned wheatear: This bird has a distinctive white crown, dark wings, and a brown back. It inhabits dry, rocky areas across Africa, feeding mainly on insects while foraging on the ground. Its name 'wheatear' is a misnomer as it primarily eats insects, not wheat seeds.
White-eared bulbul: The White-eared bulbul has a brown body with distinctive white ear patches and inhabits forests and woodlands across Southeast Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and fruits while foraging in social groups within tree canopies. Its loud, varied calls help maintain group cohesion in dense habitats.
White-faced storm petrel: The White-faced storm petrel has a dark brown body with a distinctive white face and forehead. It inhabits the open southern oceans, rarely coming to land except to breed on remote islands. It feeds on plankton and small fish by skimming the water surface, often flying low with rapid wing beats. A fun fact is that it can "patter" on the water with its feet while feeding, creating a distinctive splashing motion.
White-headed duck: The White-headed duck has a white head with a black cap and a reddish-brown body. It inhabits shallow freshwater lakes and ponds with dense vegetation across Europe and Asia. It feeds on aquatic plants, insects, and small invertebrates, often diving to forage, and is social in winter but territorial during breeding. Its population is critically endangered due to habitat loss and hybridization with introduced ruddy ducks.
White-rumped sandpiper: This small shorebird has a brown-streaked back and a distinctive white rump patch, breeding in Arctic tundra and migrating to South American coasts. It feeds on insects and small invertebrates while foraging in flocks along shorelines and mudflats. Fun fact: It holds the record for the longest non-stop flight among shorebirds, covering over 10,000 miles during migration.
White-rumped swift: The White-rumped swift has dark brown plumage with a distinctive pale rump patch and long, swept-back wings. It inhabits open country, grasslands, and urban areas across much of Asia and Africa, often seen flying high. It feeds exclusively on flying insects while in constant motion, forming noisy flocks. A fun fact is that it can sleep while flying for extended periods.
White-spectacled bulbul: This bird has olive-brown upperparts, a pale yellow underbelly, and distinctive white eye rings. It inhabits forests, scrublands, and gardens across South Asia. It feeds on insects, fruits, and berries, often foraging in small groups with active, social behavior. Its loud, distinctive call sounds like "whit-ee-whit."
White-tailed eagle: White-tailed eagles have dark brown bodies, pale heads, and distinctive white tails. They inhabit coastal areas, lakes, and rivers across northern Europe and Asia. They primarily eat fish but also hunt birds and mammals, often soaring on thermals to spot prey. A fun fact is that they were nearly wiped out in Britain but have successfully returned due to conservation efforts.
White-tailed lapwing: This bird has a white tail, brown upperparts, and a distinct black breast band, inhabiting open grasslands and wetlands across sub-Saharan Africa. It feeds on insects and small invertebrates while foraging on the ground in groups, often making loud alarm calls. Its distinctive whistling call, sounding like 'wheet-wheet', gives it its common name.
White-throated dipper: This bird has a brown back, white throat, and white belly, and it inhabits fast-moving streams across Europe and Asia. It feeds on aquatic insects and larvae, often bobbing its body while perched on rocks near water. It can dive underwater to catch prey, making it one of the few songbirds that forages underwater.
White-throated kingfisher: The White-throated kingfisher has a bright blue back, orange underparts, and a distinctive white throat patch.
