It inhabits open country near water sources like rivers, ponds, and irrigated fields across South Asia and Africa. It feeds primarily on fish, insects, and small amphibians, often hunting by perching and diving. This species can swallow small fish headfirst to avoid throat blockage.
White-winged lark: The White-winged lark has brown streaked plumage with prominent white wing patches visible in flight. It inhabits open grasslands, steppes, and agricultural fields across Europe and Asia. Its diet consists mainly of insects and seeds, and it forages on the ground while singing from elevated perches. This bird can run swiftly across the ground, often faster than it flies.
White-winged redstart: The White-winged redstart has a striking black body with prominent white wing patches and a bright red tail in males, while females are browner with similar white markings. It inhabits open woodlands and scrublands in the Himalayas and adjacent mountain ranges, feeding primarily on insects caught mid-air or gleaned from vegetation. This active bird often flits through branches while foraging and displays its red tail when excited. A fun fact is that it frequently fans its red tail to flash the color during courtship or to startle predators.
White-winged scoter: The White-winged scoter has a dark plumage with prominent white wing patches visible in flight. It inhabits coastal waters, lakes, and rivers across northern North America and Eurasia, migrating to open oceans in winter. It feeds primarily on mollusks and crustaceans, diving to forage in shallow waters while often forming large flocks. A fun fact is that it produces loud, raspy calls described as "kuk-kuk" during breeding displays.
White-winged snowfinch: This bird has gray-brown plumage with prominent white wing patches visible in flight. It inhabits high mountain grasslands and rocky slopes across central Asia. It feeds primarily on seeds and grasses, often foraging in flocks. Its soft call resembles a gentle 'tsee' sound.
White-winged tern: White-winged terns have white wings with black tips, a dark head and neck in breeding plumage, and a white body. They inhabit freshwater wetlands including lakes, marshes, and rivers across Europe and Asia. They feed primarily on insects and small fish caught in flight, often hovering or dipping while foraging in colonies. A fun fact is that they can perform acrobatic aerial displays while hunting insects mid-air.
Whooper swan: The Whooper swan is a large white bird with a distinctive yellow-and-orange bill and black legs. It inhabits northern wetlands for breeding and migrates to temperate lakes and coastal areas in winter, feeding mainly on aquatic plants. It forms strong lifelong pairs and produces loud trumpeting calls during migration. A fun fact is that its call is one of the loudest among birds, audible over three kilometers.
Willow ptarmigan: Willow ptarmigans have seasonal plumage changing from white in winter to mottled brown in summer. They inhabit Arctic tundra, boreal forests, and mountainous regions across northern continents. Their diet consists mainly of plant material like willow buds and berries, and they are ground-dwelling birds known for drumming displays during breeding. They can eat snow to obtain water in winter.
Willow tit: Willow tits have a black cap, white cheeks, and a pale throat with a dark stripe through the eye. They inhabit wet woodlands, parks, and shrubby areas near water across Europe and Asia. They eat insects, spiders, seeds, and berries, foraging actively in trees and bushes, often in small noisy groups. A fun fact is that their call sounds like a repeated "whee-oo" or "wheet" note.
Willow warbler: Willow warblers have greenish-yellow upperparts and pale yellow underparts with no distinct markings. They breed in shrubby habitats like willow thickets and open woodlands across Europe and Asia. They feed primarily on small insects and spiders, constantly moving through foliage while foraging. Their song sounds like a repetitive sweet sweet sweet.
Wilsons phalarope: Wilson's phalarope has a distinctive appearance with a pale gray body, reddish breast and neck in breeding plumage, and a long, thin bill. It breeds in freshwater wetlands across North America and winters along marine coasts in South America. This species feeds on aquatic insects and zooplankton, often spinning rapidly in water to stir up food. Females are larger and more brightly colored than males and compete for mates.
Wilsons storm petrel: Wilson's storm petrel is a small dark seabird with a white rump and a distinctive white band across its tail. It inhabits open oceans worldwide, breeding only on remote subantarctic islands. It feeds on plankton and small fish by skimming the water surface with rapid wingbeats. Its name comes from the belief that it foretells storms when seen near shore.
Wood sandpiper: Wood sandpipers have gray-brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a distinctive dark eye stripe. They breed in wetlands across northern Europe and Asia and migrate to Africa and South Asia for winter. They feed on insects and small aquatic invertebrates while foraging actively along water's edges. They undertake remarkable long-distance migrations, sometimes covering over 10,000 kilometers non-stop.
Wood warbler: The Wood warbler has a greenish-yellow back and pale yellow underparts with a distinct pale eye ring. It inhabits mature deciduous forests across Europe during the breeding season. It feeds primarily on insects gleaned from leaves and branches while being highly active and often seen high in trees. Its distinctive high-pitched song sounds like a soft sibilant whistle.
Woodchat shrike: The Woodchat shrike has a striking black head and mask contrasting with white underparts and grey wings. It inhabits open woodlands, scrublands, and farmlands across southern Europe and northern Africa. It hunts insects and small vertebrates from high perches, often displaying territorial aggression. A fun fact is that it frequently impales prey on thorns to store or soften it.
Woodlark: The Woodlark has brown upperparts with a pale eyebrow stripe and buff underparts. It inhabits open woodlands, heathlands, and grassy areas across Europe and Asia. It feeds on insects and seeds, foraging on the ground and singing from elevated perches. Its distinctive courtship display involves a spiraling flight while singing high above the ground.
Yelkouan shearwater: This seabird has dark brown upperparts and a pale belly with white underwings. It nests on rocky Mediterranean islands and forages over open ocean. Its diet consists of fish and squid, and it feeds by surface dipping while flying long distances. A fun fact is that it performs a distinctive synchronized courtship display involving mutual wing flapping and calling.
Yellow-billed cuckoo: The Yellow-billed cuckoo has brown upperparts, pale buff underparts, and a distinctive yellow bill. It inhabits deciduous forests and riparian areas across eastern and central North America. Its diet consists primarily of insects like caterpillars and cicadas, and it is typically secretive and solitary. This bird consumes large numbers of cicadas during their summer emergence.
Yellow-billed loon: The Yellow-billed loon has a black back, white breast, and a distinctive yellow bill. It breeds in Arctic lakes and winters in open ocean, feeding primarily on fish by diving. It undertakes one of the longest migrations among birds, traveling up to 6,000 miles annually.
Yellow-breasted bunting: This bird has a bright yellow breast, brown streaked back, and a black face with white stripes. It breeds in open grasslands and agricultural areas across northern Eurasia and migrates to southern Asia and Africa for winter. Its diet consists mainly of seeds and insects, and it is highly social, often forming large flocks during migration. A fun fact is its loud, repetitive song sounding like "tsee-tsee-tsee" heard during the breeding season.
Yellow-browed bunting: The Yellow-browed bunting has a brown back, white underparts, and a prominent yellow stripe above its eye. It breeds in Siberian forests and winters in agricultural areas across East Asia. It primarily eats seeds and forms large, noisy flocks during migration. A fun fact is that it is one of the most common wintering seed-eating birds in Japan.
Yellow-browed warbler: The Yellow-browed warbler has a bright yellow eyebrow stripe, olive-green upperparts, and pale yellow underparts. It breeds in coniferous forests across northern Asia and winters in forested regions of South Asia. It feeds primarily on insects and spiders, foraging actively in tree foliage. Its remarkable migration covers over 5,000 kilometers annually between breeding and wintering grounds.
Yellow-legged gull: The Yellow-legged gull has a gray back, white head and underparts, and prominent yellow legs. It inhabits coastal areas, estuaries, and urban environments across Europe and North Africa. It feeds on fish, insects, carrion, and human food waste, often scavenging boldly in groups. These gulls are famous for stealing food directly from people at beaches and parks.
Yellow-throated sparrow: The Yellow-throated sparrow has a brown body, white cheeks, and a distinctive bright yellow throat patch. It inhabits forests and gardens across South Asia, often foraging in small groups on the ground. Its diet consists of insects, seeds, and fruits, and it is known for being highly social and vocal. A fun fact is that it produces a loud, repeated "chik-chik" call that is easily heard in its habitat.
Yellowhammer: Yellowhammers have bright yellow heads and throats in males, with streaked brown backs and wings. They inhabit open farmland, grasslands, and hedgerows across Europe. Their diet consists of seeds and insects, and they sing from prominent perches while forming winter flocks. A fun fact is that their name directly references their striking yellow plumage.
Zitting cisticola: The Zitting cisticola is a small brown bird with a pale eyebrow stripe and a white throat. It inhabits grasslands, wetlands, and cultivated fields across Asia and Africa. It feeds primarily on insects gleaned from vegetation and is known for its persistent, high-pitched song while perched low in grass. Its loud, repetitive "zitting" call gives the species its common name.
